#3551. Netflix’s ‘The Body’ Explores Queer Girlhood, Catholic Guilt, and the Teenage Search for Faith

“Confess!” yells a teen as she stares into a pack of wide-eyed Catholic schoolgirls.

“I made out with Katie’s dad,” one reveals. “I masturbate to Daddy Franklin!” another cries, a black cross still smudged on her forehead.

Welcome to The Body, a new Netflix series that recalls a holy trinity of inspirations: Carrie, Jennifer’s Body, and Heavenly Creatures. But while all three were reference points for the show’s star, Geena Meszaros, she also wants her character to stand alone. “I really wanted her to be her own thing,” she told VF in October.

“It was kismet,” Meszaros says of landing the role of Lisbeth. “I feel like she was my dream character to play before I even realized it.”

The Body is set in a Catholic girls school circa the early 2000s—complete with Juicy Couture pajamas, Yahoo! Messenger, teenage devilry, secret lesbian relationships, and plenty of Catholic guilt. Meszaros plays Lisbeth, a gawky reject whose desperation to join the dance team leads her to some fairly sinful decisions. On Halloween night, mutually pining co-captains Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany) stage a team initiation that goes wildly wrong—and maybe accidentally summons the devil.

Amid the chaos of their drunken houseparty, Lisbeth takes one for the team and buries a body—literally. Before long, high school devolves into Crucible-style mania as the girls start seeing visions.

Though showrunner Quinn Shephard has described The Body as a love letter to the female-centered horror of the early 2000s, and it arrives amid a similarly themed Carrie remake and the Nov. 20 return of Yellowjackets; the series might be less of a Y2K echo than something entirely new: a snapshot of Gen Z’s faith in 2026.

“There's a sense of faith in each other, that you need to have, that you just don't get if you're not part of a team,” Meszaros says about connecting with her costars.

Meszaros calls the show a mix of horror, comedy, and grittiness, all smushed together. There’s also a bit of romance overseen by Chala Hunter, the same intimacy coordinator who worked on Heated Rivalry. Meanwhile, a very pregnant Gabby Windey makes her acting debut as the team’s coach. (“I don’t know if I’ve met anyone who’s just so themselves all the time,” Meszaros says of her costar.).

Like Meszaros, almost everyone else in the cast is an up-and-comer: Kristina Bogic, who plays the popular high school sweetheart Anya; Sara Boustany, who plays her wicked best friend (and secret lover) Elise; Sofia Wylie, the doomed preacher’s niece; and Nnamdi Asomugha, an NFL cornerback turned actor who plays that very preacher (and the school’s principal): Father (Daddy) Franklin.

“I'm more of a spiritual person, but I think having faith in anything outside of yourself, whether that's God or whether that's something else, I think that's important,” Meszaros says.

In the months before filming, the team bonded just like their characters do: through dance team training, which sometimes lasted seven hours a day. “There was no pretending with the friendships on the show,” Meszaros says, even if the rehearsals were so intense that they cost her two toenails.

Unlike the other girls, though, Meszaros was playing a pariah. “I love a flawed human,” she says. “I love kind of being able to dive into the psyche of someone that maybe some people find awful.”

It wasn’t hard for Meszaros to feel empathy for Lisbeth. Her character has roots in a rural West Virginia congregation famed for their serpent handling rituals, where worshippers handle live snakes to prove their faith. Lisbeth’s Stephen King-esque arc kicks off when her dad dies and she and her mentally ill mother move to a new town to start over. Their bad luck follows.

On some level, Meszaros could relate. “My parents divorced when I was a baby, and so at my dad’s house, I was raised Christian, and at my mom’s house, she was just more spiritual,” she says. “I went through a dark period where I didn’t [believe]. I just kind of abandoned it all, which is very Lisbeth.” Her own experienced gave her a bit of a blueprint for the character: “I [kept] that feeling of like a hole left over from her world being turned upside down after her dad died, and just what it does to someone when you don't have some sort of faith, and you don’t really believe in anything. That desperation.”

Gen Z shares that desperation. Research shows that young people are plagued by mental health crises at higher rates than any previous generation. And although experts today differ on whether there’s an actual religious revival among Gen Z, there’s no denying that the way young people approach religion is rapidly evolving.

Meszaros’s feed is divided about the show, even before its premiere: “People are gonna love it or hate it,” she says, laughing. But she’s mostly just excited for people to see it, even though it’s coming out too late to inspire Body-themed Halloween costumes.

“I kind of wish people could be Lisbeth,” she says with a sigh. “But maybe next year.”

Sometimes not even a hedge can keep a good friend out…especially when that friend is Adam Sandler. I don’t think anyone has more fun than him when it comes to having his closest pals live nearby. So, naturally, while he’s out walking with the family, he makes time to ensure neighbor Conan O’Brien knows he’s there. However, while the good friends may be tight, they can admit that it gets weird living behind Hollywood hedges.

Part of this has to do with the fun gesture Sandler makes to ensure his friend knows he’s over the hedge. While it isn’t as sweet as his Mother’s Day gesture to long-time ‘friend’ Jennifer Aniston, it’s definitely one of his funniest ones. Sandler and O'Brien dished about the weird perk of being neighbors when the Happy Gilmore actor stopped by his friend’s podcast, Conan O’Brien Needs A Friend. That’s when O’Brien shared the Sandman's ritual for every single time he walks by his pal’s house:

Everyone lives near each other, but everyone lives behind a hedge. Everyone's real cool about where everyone else lives, and one of my favorite things is this man, when he's outside your house, he'll go, 'Conie!'

While hedges may permit celebrities personal space, this doesn’t stop Sandler from making sure his friend hears him going by. Though it’s clearly in good fun, as the actor is often a guest at O’Brien’s house, even for his Christmas bash. The host reassures him that he’s always wants him at the party. So it doesn't shock me that he gives his pal, "Conan!" a shout out whenever he’s walking by. Also, this is so on brand, given Sandler is known for his quirky hijinks, such as wearing socks while swimming in the pool.

Sandler's eccentric gestures are certainly one of the reasons his friend circle hasn’t changed much over the years, and his jokey tendencies often seem to get zanier when he’s around old celebrity pals. For instance, I can imagine there are lot of zingers, shouts, and one-liners while he’s palling around with his celebrity friends in New Jersey filming Grown Ups 3. Such funny traits are also so common that Sandler's daughters come to expect them:

My kids wait for me to say it now. They just go, ‘alright he’s going to do his thing.’ Conan! Conan! And then they go back to tell me something in their life.

By now, Sadie and Sunny know how their dad, right down to his classic laidback red carpet style while they’re dressed to impress. However, while Sandler is most known for his comedic and outlandish antics, I can also say the man contains multitudes. While he may make funny gestures in public and participate in wild antics on screen, he also has depth and can play the heck out of a dramatic role The actor’s performances in Scott Cooper’s psychological drama Time Out, Punch Drunk Love and Uncut Gems could've won him Oscars.

In the same way, O'Brien is also quite complex. While he's a the definition of a funnyman and can deliver a funny performance in Toy Story 5, he can also surprise us with a dramatic film like If I Had Legs I'd Kick You. Maybe it's the complexity that helps bond O'Brien and Sandler? Regardless, it’s sweet to think that while the two remain busy, a simple shout over the hedge (whether it be weird or not) helps to serve as a sweet reminder of their friendship.

Of course, given the holiday season is upon us, it’s safe to say that Sandler will once again be on the guest list for the party. However, the real question is: Will he be shouting "Conan" instead of singing Christmas carols?

#3549. Does Marvel's VisionQuest Have A Post-Credits Scene? A Spoiler-Free Guide

The end of a trilogy that started back in 2020 is upon us. The "WandaVision" trilogy is one of the most significant pieces of Marvel's Multiverse Saga, focusing on Wanda Maximoff and Vision's complicated relationship and the characters who are connected to them. With "VisionQuest" reaching its conclusion, the trilogy has been capped off. But is it all over once the credits start to roll on the final episode? Or is there more to it?

This series brings back Paul Bettany as Vision for what is presumably one last ride. It also brings back James Spader as Ultron more than a decade later. How exactly is Ultron alive in "VisionQuest?" That's one of many questions the show has answered during its run.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is notorious for including post-credits scenes in its movies and TV shows. Some of them have been very good and consequential, such as Thanos arriving in "The Avengers." Some of Marvel's worst post-credits scenes? Not so good. Whatever shape they take, it's always reasonable to wonder whether or not a given MCU project contains a credits scene or two.

That brings us back to the "VisonQuest" season finale. We're here to offer up a spoiler-free guide to the show's credits scene situation. Do you need to stick around? Or can you find something else to watch once the credits roll? Seriously, we're not going to spoil anything significant. We're just here to arm viewers with necessary information. With that out of the way, let's get into it.

Yes, "VisionQuest" does have a post-credits scene that fans should be aware of. In fact, there are two scenes. One of the scenes is important enough that viewers who made it all the way through the series shouldn't skip it. It helps put a button on the events that transpired in the show. Without spoiling anything, it's not a throwaway gag or anything like that. In fact, go ahead and watch both scenes. It's worth it.

This shouldn't come as a huge surprise. "WandaVision" also had a pretty significant credits scene. The "WandaVision" post-credits scene was sneakily altered by Marvel Studios, though that's another conversation entirely. Still, it stands to reason that the finale to this trilogy would include a credits scene as well.

This show had a lot to accomplish and was rather ambitious. "VisionQuest" explained the biggest plot hole from "Avengers: Age of Ultron," and also had to serve as a satisfying end for a character who has been with the MCU since its earliest days. No pressure.

Christopher J. Byrne, Gandja Monteiro, Vincenzo Natali, and Terry Matalas directed episodes of the series. The cast also includes Ruaridh Mollica (Tommy Maximoff), Todd Stashwick (Paladin), T'Nia Miller (Jocasta), Lauren Morais (Lisa Molinari), Orla Brady (F.R.I.D.A.Y.), Diane Morgan (The Handler), Polly Frame (Fiona Guthrie), Henry Lewis (D.U.M.-E.), Jonathan Sayer (U.), Emily Hampshire (E.D.I.T.H.), and James D'Arcy (J.A.R.V.I.S.).

"VisionQuest" is streaming now on Disney+.

#3548. Meghan Markle’s Mother, Doria Ragland, Helped the FBI Investigate Thomas Markle, Meghan’s Father

New details have emerged regarding the arrest of Thomas Markle, Meghan Markle’s father, on charges of possessing child pornography. According to People magazine, Doria Ragland, mother of the Duchess of Sussex, assisted the FBI and played a key role in identifying her ex-husband, leading to his arrest in Florida on November 6. (Thomas Markle has previously denied any possession of child sex abuse material.)

The Sun also reports that she played a central role, one that, as the outlet writes, involved reviewing a series of photographs obtained by federal agents. Ragland was reportedly shown a series of blurred images depicting alleged sexual abuse of minors, and she identified the man in the photographs as her ex-husband. Markle, now 82, was reportedly between 30 and 40 years old at the time the photos were taken, during a period when he may not have even been married to Ragland yet (they were married from 1979 to 1987, while Meghan was born in 1981). Markle was also reportedly recognized by another person, whose name has not been disclosed. This person is said to be a witness who spent a great deal of time with him around the time the photos were allegedly taken.

The photographs in question were found among the material seized from a storage unit that Markle rented in Los Angeles. According to statements from the Department of Justice, this was a space where the man allegedly stored “child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls.” The FBI took action following the suspicious discovery of alleged child pornography at Markle’s home in Cebu, Philippines, where he lived for a year—until last May—before returning to the United States due to health issues. After a court appearance in Tampa following his arrest, he was released on the condition that he remain at the Maravida Senior Living nursing home in Lakeland, Florida—the same facility from which he had been taken into custody.

The investigation was initiated by Thomas Markle Jr., whom Meghan’s father had with his first wife, Roslyn Loveless, along with another daughter, Samantha. The man told police that he had found a great deal of compromising material among the family mementos, which was why he had filed a complaint against his father. Markle Jr. was initially considered a person of interest by investigators, with Juanito Victor Remulla, secretary of the Philippine Department of the Interior, saying, “There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well.” However, the Philippine police have since publicly apologized to Markle Jr. after interviews with his fiancée and others in his circle reportedly exonerated him.

Meanwhile, following Ragland’s intervention, Meghan is also reportedly willing to cooperate with the FBI in the investigation into her father, a source told The Sunday Times. The Duchess of Sussex no longer has any relationship with her father, and—as was revealed when the story about the alleged child pornography surfaced—it is precisely for this reason. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” Meghan said in a statement on the matter. “I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.” She continued: “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” This is a story with many unresolved issues. More will be known after the first hearing, the date of which has not yet been set.

#3547. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

90 Day: Florida is the latest entry in the 90 Day Fiancé franchise, and I have to ask if we've lost the plot. Sure, it seems and feels like the average TLC spinoff we'd expect to see on the 2026 TV schedule, minus the cornerstones of what makes this franchise what it is. Yes, beginning Monday, December 14th, those with TLC or an HBO Max subscription can see all the 90 Day couples living in Florida jam-packed into one show. This season teases a wedding between Cortney Reardanz and Phil, as well as a celebration for Jasmine Pineda. It sounds fun, but I'm still on the fence about it due to these two principles.

90 Day: Florida gives me pause for a couple of reasons, and they have to do with the foundation of the franchise. One detail is the fact that this entire spinoff takes place in one location. While we've seen this done before with 90 Day: The Last Resort or Hunt For Love, the resort was a matter of convenience rather than a series focused on individuals all living in one area. I mean, should a franchise that focuses on people finding love abroad have a spinoff based solely in one part of the United States?

It doesn't feel like we're going to get the best storylines with couples in the franchise, or that this is a handpicked selection of the best 90 Day has to offer. It's just all the cast members who live in Florida, which feels like this was just made out of convenience rather than actual fan interest.

90 Day: Florida feels like TLC attempting to make 90 Day Fiancé like the Real Housewives franchise. The problem is, what they're doing already exists, and in making a spinoff based solely on the fact that all these couples live in the same state, I question if it'll pull in the core audience that shows up for these shows.

I'm Shocked By How Much 90 Day Fiancé's Sarper Reportedly Made Doing Stand-Up Comedy

All this to say, it's not my money, so I'm curious to see how 90 Day: Florida will do and how audiences will respond. I do know there are rumors that Yara Dufren will be accused of cheating on Jovi, which is something I would love to know more about.

I also can't help but notice the timing of this spinoff lines up perfectly with Libby and Andrei Castravet announcing their exit from the franchise. They're also based in Florida, so is it possible they ended up leaving after not receiving an invite to appear? I'd love to know the details on that, especially in the aftermath of their feud with Alexei and Loren Brovarnik.

Whether I'm on board or not, though, I'll be watching 90 Day: Florida when it premieres, and I hope I'm wrong about this franchise not really feeling like it falls under the 90 Day Fiancé umbrella. I'll be eager to see what other viewers say as well, and if this ends up being a format that TLC sticks with for other states.

#3545. VisionQuest: The Identity Of The Client, Explained

Spoilers ahead for "VisionQuest" Episode 8, "Forever."

Ultron (James Spader) may have no strings on him anymore, but someone has been manipulating the events of "VisionQuest" like a puppetmaster. That someone is The Client, who hired the bounty hunter Paladin (Todd Stashwick) to capture Vision (Paul Bettany). We've gotten glimpses of The Client all season, but only as a digitally altered voice or a faceless avatar ... until Episode 7, "Immolation."

At the episode's end, Vision and Ultron's gynoid lover Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) are delivered to The Client's doorstep. Out of said door walks ... someone who looks just like Ultron's human avatar. Huh?

"Forever" clarifies it. "The Client" is Virgil Horton, grandson of Phineas Horton (Bettany), the scientist who created the Synthetic Man/Human Torch (Bettany again) in the 1940s. As Virgil explains, the Synthetic Man's uncontrolled fire powers mean that Dr. Horton was considered a failure. Years ago, Virgil joined with Dr. Josephine Carrington (Miller) to perfect AI in hopes of redeeming the Horton family legacy. They scanned their own brainwaves to create the genesis of what Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.) completed.

Horton and Carrington also fell in love. After Carrington's death from a terminal illness, Horton revived her as Jocasta. As Virgil explains, he was one of the engineers hired by SWORD to rebuild Vision back in "WandaVision." After that, he created a robotic body for Carrington's mind-scanned AI. Jocasta being a recent creation helps explain why she looks like feminine Ultron, but why did Virgil then erase her memories of him and her creation?

Virgil believes the only worthy lover of a "goddess" like Jocasta is a god. So, he intends to delete Vision's personality and then upload himself into Vision's shell, so he and Jocasta can rule an Earth infected with Jocasta's hive mind nanites.

Virgil's borderline-incestuous romance plan echoes the central influence of Ultron: "Frankenstein," specifically when the Creature asks Doctor Frankenstein to make him a companion. Virgil's plan is rather similar to Kenneth Branagh's 1994 "Frankenstein" film adaptation, where Victor Frankenstein (Branagh) tries to resurrect his dead wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) through the same process by which he made the Creature (Robert De Niro).

There's an implication that Virgil scanning his brainwaves for his and Josephine's AI embedded his personality into the AI code. That's why Ultron basically has his same flamboyant personality, his voice, and why Ultron wears Virgil's face as his human avatar. "VisionQuest" showrunner Terry Matalas has said giving Ultron a human form in "VisionQuest" was about getting the most out of Spader's performance. Now, we know, it was also essential to the pay off of this twist about the Client's identity. But "Forever" breaks out Ultron's robotic form, too.

Virgil's plan fails because Jocasta has fallen for Ultron and wants him to be her eternal partner. Using the nanites, Ultron recreates his physical form and crushes Horton to death with a hug. It's a very Oedipal move: Ultron's defining goal has always been killing his father, whether it be Hank Pym (in Marvel's comics) or Tony Stark (in the Marvel Cinematic Universe). He comes close to that by killing the man of whom he's an artificial echo.

Ultron being based on Virgil also explains why fell for Jocasta in the first place. This restores some of the mirroring of the creator and creation that's present in comics Ultron. In the "Avengers" comics, Ultron created Jocasta from the brainwaves of Hank Pym's wife: Janet van Dyne, the Wasp, and his spiritual mother. Since Ultron is based on Hank's personality, he inherited his father's affections for Janet though extremely twisted means. The same logic applies to Spader's Ultron falling for this Jocasta.

Now, it's worth noting that while Phineas Horton and his Human Torch originated in Marvel Comics, Virgil did not. Rather, he's an original creation of this series, and "VisionQuest" seems to be using him as a proxy for the original Dr. Horton. Previously, Steve Englehart and George Tuska's "Avengers" #135 tied Horton and the Ultron-Vision lineage together, with the issue revealing that Ultron had abducted Phineas Horton and forced him to rebuild the inert Human Torch into the Vision.

Keep in mind, Ultron and Vision debuted in 1968. At that time, it was plausible that a scientist active in World War II would be living in retirement. But not so much in 2026, where it makes much more sense to use a descendant of Horton in the present day. It's the same time creep that led to Captain America originally missing only two decades of time while frozen to awakening almost a century later.

#3544. Jensen Huang Did: Have an Ill-Advised Affair. He Did Not: Wear Vintage Saint Laurent.

Jensen Huang, the president, cofounder, and CEO of Nvidia is making headlines this week. Not for developments in AI technology—for all the wrong reasons.

On Sunday, Nvidia said it had opened an investigation into Huang regarding his relationship with a woman whom intelligence agencies have said is a Chinese spy. (The Chinese government has denied that the woman is a spy.) That same day, Huang sent an email to the company’s employees apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife and for “hurting” her and their children with the affair. He also apologized to his colleagues and the company’s board and shareholders. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility,” he wrote. “I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.” He said he’d cooperate with the investigation opened by Nvidia’s board of directors. “I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security,” he wrote. “I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

The news of Huang’s affair filled X with memes about Chinese spies and mistresses in a variety of configurations. By Monday evening, Huang had reached the fashion world’s stylish netizens: The Instagram account @hidden.ny, an anonymous digital mood board and cultural platform, posted a series of images of Huang in a studded leather jacket. The caption read, “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy.”

It’s well-known that Huang is a leather-jacket enthusiast, and he is seldom seen in public without one. In July Sotheby’s auctioned one of his pre-worn jackets, this one by Tom Ford. The auction house originally estimated its sale price between $40,000 and $60,000, but it sold for a whooping $960,000.

Despite Huang’s penchant for a black-leather moment, it appears that he was, in fact, not wearing the Saint Laurent jacket as previously shared by Hidden and a variety of other accounts on both Instagram and X. A quick run through an AI image detector debunked Huang’s being a “Slimaniac”—what Slimane’s fervent fans often call themselves—at least in this particular case. SynthID, the detector created by Google DeepMind to identify AI-generated or enhanced media by OpenAI, Google, Kakao, and, of course, Nvidia, detected that the images posted by Hidden and other users online had been generated or edited with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. To burst the bubble even further, it appears that the images used as the base for this particular edit weren’t taken following the disclosure of Huang’s affair, but from a trip to South Korea in June. (He was wearing a Dior jacket by Jonathan Anderson then.)

Just last week, a Free Press reporter went viral on X for posting an image she had not disclosed as enhanced by AI as part of her election-night reporting, which was also debunked by VF. It’s not necessarily fun being the AI fashion police, and the stakes of netizens giving Huang the fashion-meme treatment versus a reporter using AI to illustrate a point are not the same. But as the use of AI becomes harder to detect, disclosure has become paramount.

Apologies to the menswear crowd for ruining the fantasy—but did you all really want Huang to be a certified “Hedi boy” after this news? As one comment under the original post read, Huang might be the “first person in history to have negative aura wearing archive Hedi.”

#3543. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3542. 2024's Most Controversial Western Thriller Is Suddenly a Hit on Prime Video

The divisive Alec Baldwin film is riding high on streaming despite its troubled history

Alec Baldwin has spent decades as one of Hollywood's most recognizable actors, moving between blockbuster movies, acclaimed dramas, and television comedy. From The Hunt for Red October and Glengarry Glen Ross to The Departed and The Aviator, Baldwin has built an extensive filmography, while his Emmy-winning role as Jack Donaghy in 30 Rock remains one of his most memorable performances.

Baldwin has remained a familiar face in Hollywood for decades, but one of his more recent movie projects has attracted attention for reasons beyond its cast. A Western thriller led by the veteran actor is now finding an audience on streaming, giving viewers an opportunity to check out a film that generated considerable controversy before it ever reached theaters.

The 2025 Western Rust, directed by Joel Souza, has climbed into Amazon Prime Video's U.S. movie top 10, according to FlixPatrol. The film recently reached No. 5 on the platform's U.S. chart and is having massive success internationally right now, finding a second life on streaming a year after its release.

Set in 1880s, Wyoming, Rust follows Harland Rust (Baldwin), an infamous outlaw who comes to the rescue of his 13-year-old grandson, Lucas Hollister (Patrick Scott McDermott), after the boy is sentenced to hang for accidentally killing a rancher.

With his grandson facing execution, Harland breaks him out of prison, and the pair flee toward Mexico. Their journey quickly becomes a dangerous fight for survival as they attempt to evade U.S. Marshal Wood Helm (Josh Hopkins) and ruthless bounty hunter Fenton "Preacher" Lang (Travis Fimmel).

Despite its renewed streaming attention, Rust received a mixed reception from critics. The movie currently holds a 56% critics' score and 68% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. The site's critics' consensus describes it as a middling drama with impressive visuals, but little that distinguishes it from other Westerns.

Rust made headlines after cinematographer Halyna Hutchins was fatally shot on set in October 2021 when a revolver Baldwin was holding discharged during a rehearsal. Director Joel Souza was also wounded in the incident.

Baldwin was charged with involuntary manslaughter, but the case was dismissed with prejudice in July 2024 after the judge found prosecutors had improperly withheld evidence. The film eventually resumed production and arrived in theaters in May 2025.

#3541. VisionQuest's Finale Finally Pays Off A Story Marvel Started In Avengers: Age Of Ultron

What is grief if not spoilers persevering? This article discusses major plot details from the season finale of "VisionQuest."

An argument could be made that the "VisionQuest" finale was a confrontation over a decade in the making. Clearly, the well-received Disney+ series has marketed itself as a "WandaVision" sequel and a trilogy-capper to the story continued in "Agatha All Along." But there's no way around its biggest and most pressing concern: providing a fitting epilogue to the 2015 blockbuster "Avengers: Age of Ultron." In an inspired choice, "VisionQuest" showrunner Terry Matalas understood there was still plenty of unfinished business between James Spader's megalomaniac robot Ultron and Paul Bettany's synthezoid Vision, which finally pays off spectacularly in the eighth and final episode of the show.

Once Vision and Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) realize that the mysterious Client dogging their steps is actually Virgil Horton (also played by Spader), the descendant of Phineas Horton (aka the mind behind the Synthetic Man, as portrayed by Bettany), this sets up the finale's most compelling battle. No, it's not Horton's toxic, twisted love for Dr. Jo Carrington and his desire to inhabit Vision's body so they may live forever together. It's the apparent murder of Ultron's lover Jocasta, setting off Ultron's malevolence towards humanity and one last showdown with Vision.

This is precisely the kind of potential that shared universes were meant to fully realize — not cameos and references for the sake of it or disposable narratives to throw on in the background as white noise, but as meaningful additions to ongoing arcs for viewers willing to take the time to explore them. That may go down as the greatest accomplishment of "VisionQuest" in its finale, delivering the perfect button on the Ultron saga that "Age of Ultron" simply couldn't pull off.

Amazing what eight hours of storytelling can do that studio-meddled blockbusters never could, eh? In spite of its obvious shortcomings and compromises, we here at /Film are long-suffering defenders of "Avengers: Age of Ultron." Arguably the last time the Marvel Cinematic Universe was able to be as weird and messy and introspective as the comics themselves, the movie still managed to find moments of quiet poignancy amid all the mind-numbing spectacle. To no surprise, that's something showrunner Terry Matalas and his writers have carried over into "VisionQuest," and nowhere is that more confidently on display than in the finale.

We're not only talking about the moment when a dying Jocasta merges Ultron with the horde of killer nanobots and allows him to regain his physical form, fighting Vision in a well-staged battle that ought to be many a nerd's dream come to life. What puts the finale over the top is when it somehow combines the best of "Age of Ultron" with "WandaVision." Vision traps Ultron inside a sitcom-set mindscape where the two artificial beings can hash out their differences without throwing hands and trading particle beams at each other. If previous episodes filled in some Ultron-centric plot holes, then this one brings us back to their best moment of all — when, in the midst of Sokovia's destruction, the two land in an idyllic forest to talk about humanity's doomed fate, the grace found in their failings, and the fact that nothing beautiful is meant to last forever.

Here, the big climactic fight becomes a treatise on Ultron's all-consuming grief, his unresolved malevolence towards human beings, and, deep down, his debilitating fear of being alone.

To the credit of "VisionQuest," this season-long epilogue suggests there's more to his emotional journey than a single movie could ever explore. The finale digs even deeper to prove this, completing Ultron's transformation into something much more human by giving him someone to love. Despite the changes made to the comics' origins, the Ultron/Jocasta romance is a defining moment in Ultron's portrayal in the MCU. Finally, he can understand Vision's own progression to becoming an individual in his own right, along with all the joy and loss and humanity that comes with it.

That's probably why, even after he retreats back to his old ways and attempts to cause our extinction again, "VisionQuest" posits that Ultron isn't beyond redemption. Sure, it isn't until he's confronted with his own mortality that he finally decides to spare the world's population. But even that is as human as it gets. Vision helps him come to terms with what life has to offer. And when we leave him, eager to appreciate human art and perhaps even rebuild Jocasta, it's a perfect period to the end of his sentence ... or, perhaps, an ellipsis.

"VisionQuest" is now streaming on Disney+ in its entirety.

Adam Driver and Miles Teller are the co-leads of a particularly thrilling entry on the 2026 movie schedule. The two actors – alongside the show-stopping Scarlett Johansson – headline Paper Tiger, the latest film from director James Gray. It tells the story of a family that gets wrapped up in shaky business dealings and, as a result, some characters keep secrets. CinemaBlend caught up with Teller and Driver and asked about their secret-keeping abilities, and it seems as far as their wives are concerned, they just can’t do it.

In the film, Teller and Driver play Irwin and Gary Pearl, respectively, who embark on a business venture (at Gary’s suggestion) involving the Gowanus Canal in 1980s New York. The two ultimately find themselves contending with the forces of the Russian mafia and, amid a portion of the conflict, Irwin’s wife, Hester (Johansson) is left in the dark. When CB caught up with the two leading men and asked if they would be able to keep big secrets from their significant other, and Driver dropped a funny take:

Would I have told her right away? Oh, yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah…. My wife is kind of a [clairvoyant]. She can see into the future a little bit. No literally, but she can just tell….

Since 2013, Driver has been married to Joanne Tucker, with whom he shares two children. Based on his comments, it sounds like the Ferrari star knows better than to try to keep something from his wife. The sentiments drew laughs from Teller, but he also seemed to be able to empathize with the thoughts. Teller is married to Keleigh Sperry (who’s known for sharing fun videos online), and they’ve been married for over seven years. While discussing whether he’d keep a big secret from Sperry, Teller had this to say about his wife:

Yeah, Keleigh, can always sense when something’s… Even if I just eat something wrong, she's like, ‘Everything OK?’ I’m like, how did you…

It’s great to hear that the two stars strive to maintain transparency with their wives, though that also begs another question. Our Jeff McCobb went on to ask if the two would tell the truth only because they knew they couldn’t get away with a lie. However, they both clarified their thoughts on that front:

Considering their attitudes, I wonder if that tendency not to keep secrets also extends to the actors’ work. I mean, was Tucker aware that Driver was developing a Kylo Ren movie with Steven Soderbergh for a time, or is Sperry privy to any details regarding Teller’s involvement in Top Gun 3? I’d also like to know if the pair’s co-star, Johansson, also kept secrets from hubby Colin Jost while she was “wrapped up” in Marvel movies. I could just be overthinking this, and maybe the stars’ spouses don’t even care to know such information. Regardless, it’s still interesting to consider.

What isn’t a secret, though, is that Paper Tiger is proving to be an extremely buzzy title, and James Gray and co. are receiving considerable praise from critics. The Armageddon Time director seems to have delivered yet another classic, and it may even yield some recognition this awards season. For now, though, anyone who wants to see Adam Driver and Miles Teller keep secrets (on screen and not in real life) can check out their new movie, which opens in limited release on November 13 and opens nationwide on November 20.

#3539. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

#3538. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3 Opening Credits Have A Hidden Connection To HBO's White Lotus [Exclusive]

As viewers make their long-awaited return to Middle-earth in Season 3 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power," they will inevitably find things a bit different compared to where they last left off. The war that was teased at the conclusion of Season 2 has finally arrived, led by Charlie Vickers' Sauron unmasked in all his Dark Lord, uh, lordliness. A five-year time jump has reset the board considerably, putting heroes like Elrond (Robert Aramayo) and Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) on their back foot. But, as of Episode 2, fans will notice a significant tweak has been made to the opening credits sequence — one which contains an unseen connection to another popular streaming series.

Prior to the premiere, I recently attended the press junket for "The Rings of Power" and spoke with co-showrunner Patrick McKay about the third season. In our limited time together, I wanted to address the noticeably darker edge to the title sequence this time around and whether there might be any Easter eggs worth paying attention to, as has been the case in the prior two seasons. The creative team worked with studio and creative consultant Plains of Yonder, who crafted the sand-based vibrational look for the opening credits of "The Rings of Power" and apparently pitched a new approach for Season 3. Here's a behind-the-scenes featurette showcasing their previous work:

But observant fans may recognize the fingerprints of another haunting title sequence. Fans of HBO's "White Lotus," this one's for you. As proudly displayed on their website, Plains of Yonder was also involved in everyone's favorite dramedy about "when everybody goes to the hotel" (as McKay hilariously put it in our interview) and, specifically, the wallpaper-focused title sequence with some seriously unsettling imagery. Not surprisingly, the designers pulled a similar trick with "The Rings of Power."

In keeping with the theme of Season 3 of "The Rings of Power," Patrick McKay explained that Plains of Yonder pitched a different approach for the episodes to come. Where Seasons 1 and 2 contained hidden references and symbols pointing towards specific events of the story, the designers felt called to go in another direction. "They're really serious artists," McKay told me with obvious admiration for their skills. "They're really wonderful people to work with. I mean, we find [their work on Season 2] hypnotic."

Episode 2 provides our first glimpse of the newly-revamped opening credits sequence, with the familiar-looking particulates now taking on a much darker color palette as they reform into all sorts of different visuals: evocative landscapes, elemental imagery, and plenty more examples of abstract art. According to McKay:

"Season 3, they're like, 'We want to do something different. We want to change the entire thing. We want to revisit the concept and make it feel like this season feels [emotionally], rather than reference things that happen in the season.' So it's a little different this time. It's a little more dramatic, has a little more darkness to it."

The visuals certainly help strike a different tone for Season 3, although the stirring musical theme by "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy composer Howard Shore remains perfectly intact. This seems to suggest that, even in its darkest moments, Middle-earth always retains a glimmer of hope. New episodes of "The Rings of Power" stream on Prime Video every Wednesday.

#3537. Model Alex Consani on Starring in American Horror Story and Pursuing a Career as an Actress

Alex Consani, a mainstay of the runways and one of the most emblematic supermodels of her generation, was notably absent from the spring-summer 2027 shows in September and October, bar a few exceptions. That’s because the California native, 23, has been busy broadening her horizons: Consani is following in the footsteps of many supers before her—including Cindy Crawford, Gisele Bündchen, and Tyra Banks—and trading the runway for the silver screen to pursue a career as an actress. She’s currently starring in American Horror Story: 13, the latest installment of Ryan Murphy’s stylish horror anthology series. Up next, Consani will appear in Molly Gordon’s Peaked and Janicza Bravo’s Preppy.

On Saturday night, Consani joined Demna and his Gucci crew at the 15th annual LACMA Art + Film Gala, where she says she had to do a “Hannah Montana”–style wardrobe change so that her voluminous gown could make it to the step-and-repeat before changing again to “pump it in a side-slit” in the look she wore on the runway in September. Yesterday, the model and newly minted actress Zoomed in after touching back down in New York to break down her film ambitions.

Alex Consani at the 2026 LACMA Art + Film gala.

José Criales-Unzueta: I’m not going to lie, I miss you on the runway. But you’re busy and otherwise occupied!

Alex Consani: I miss being on the runway. I’ve been busy. I’ve been doing a lot of cool projects. You might not see me on the runway, but you’ll definitely see me on the silver screen.

I mean, American Horror Story, all the episodes just came out. I don’t know if you watched, but that was obviously super fun. I also have two projects that are coming out next year, Preppy and Peaked. I’m just really excited. I’m in this era now where I’m kind of shifting into a different space, and it’s exciting to be able to do it specifically with people that understand that. For fashion and film, there are many places where both come together in such a natural way, and I think the LACMA [gala] really is that.

I worked with Sarah Paulson for American Horror Story, and then I sat next to her at LACMA, and we’re both wearing witchy outfits. Sarah and I were looking at Demna and he was like, “Look at my witches,” [laughs]. I love that the fashion world and the film world come together in such a fun way. I think Demna specifically is really big into characters—it’s not just the clothes, but it’s the woman in the clothes.

Did you always intend to go into acting, or was it something that unfolded as you went into fashion?

It’s something that I’ve always been interested in. And I think, in a way, fashion for me has always been acting. I mean, what I enjoy most about fashion is being able to become the character, being able to ask the designer, who is the woman that’s wearing this? It gives me the most gratification when I’m able to build the world around the clothing. [Acting] came naturally, but obviously it was in the back of my head. When I was a kid, I did classes and stuff. With fashion, the time constraints or the time needed to be in fashion is a lot. So I think it was just difficult. I’m blessed to be at a point in my fashion career and also in the [acting] projects that are coming to me, that it isn’t impossible to do both.

I’m putting work into being a better actress. It’s a really exciting endeavor for me, especially considering all the projects that I’ve done that are coming out. There’s a lot of diversity within the projects. I did American Horror Story, which is obviously a horror TV show, and then I have a comedy movie coming out, and then I also have a period piece coming out. It’s fun to be able to bounce around those. And fashion-wise, fab, honestly, the fashion in the films that I’ve done is quite fun. It’s nice because then I get to give my insight as someone in fashion to all the teams, and it feels like a real collaboration, which is my favorite part of any creative job.

Alex Consani with Sarah Paulson (left) and Leslie Grossman (right) in the sixth episode of American Horror Story: 13.

You and I are from the generations that grew up on Ryan Murphy shows.

Coven, for me, is my favorite American Horror Story season by far. What was it like to join the project? Did you audition? Did you get a call?

I’m signed with a really incredible agency that manages that facet of my career, and they expressed that Ryan had some interest in seeing me. I sent in an audition and it fell into place in that way. I definitely was auditioning and going through that script a lot before I got to filming. It was really important for me to really understand the character. And so when I got there, it was obviously super exciting, but I was also a little bit nervous considering the fact that I’m with some of the most seasoned actors in the industry. It was so gratifying and comforting hearing how supportive these women were. My biggest takeaway from this experience is that the reason that those women and those people in Coven are so acclaimed, on top of being incredibly talented, they’re kind and they’re open arms to anyone that wants and that puts in the effort into the acting industry.

What I find so exciting about it is that it doesn’t feel as exclusive as fashion does, in a way. It opens up the conversation to anyone that’s willing to work for it. Fashion is being the right person in the right place at the right time. I think that acting is being the right person, yes, but putting the right energy and the right time into the job. It was just such an incredible experience. Jessica Lange, Emma Roberts, Sarah Paulson, Gabourey Sidibe… it was fab. It was fab! I have so many iconic memories made on that set that I’m going to have forever. I got so much knowledge from these women. I think that it was just really reassuring to see how kind and open-minded these people were, especially Billie Lourd. She’s an icon of mine, but then I got to work with her, and she was just so open and honest about how she’s felt in her first roles. It’s just really gratifying to hear this stuff.

There’s a long legacy of supermodels trying to crack into the silver screen. A lot of models have done it, some very successfully, some have done it once and then moved on. Do you feel any sort of pressure for this to work?

I think I was really ready to just lock in and have fun, but for me, what I was most excited about was being able to be ugly. I see this a lot in models and actresses, where it becomes difficult when you’re so aware of the camera, and you grow up being so aware of the camera to then unlearn that awareness. It was so exciting to be able to go into a space where I was able to get into the character without there being the perception of others there. Obviously there’s a camera, but it’s not a fashion show where you hear like, yeah, work! [laughs] It was a real experience that I worked on within myself.

I was reading The Artist’s Way, which, not to be all corny, I think I realized that the feeling of gratification and the feeling of completing something is only as good as that feeling. I think that perception, especially now with social media and [giving] a numeric value to art, it’s really important to be able to feel like you did the best you could and that’s enough. I think for me, that was really where it kind of progressed. I was able to lock down away from the facet of just being pretty. I didn’t get the touch-ups before set, I didn’t get the lighting right. I wasn’t asking to see the playback, which, as a model—I know you’ve been on many sets where you see the girls and with every single shot we’re looking at the screen, there’s a mirror behind the photographer— it’s very not that. I do the day, and I don’t know if I did a good job. I felt like I did a good job, and that’s enough for me. I’m excited to see it in seven months when it comes out. But that really took a lot of the pressure away. I was just enjoying the experience and doing my best. I think that that’s the beauty of it and that’s the beautiful difference between fashion and film.

I love a lot of animated characters. I was watching Rio yesterday. Did you know Anne Hathaway is the love interest? That’s my dream. Honestly, I would love to do some really fab, cool animation because I think that in itself is a challenge. It’s nice to be able to build a character with just your voice.

Fundamentally, I would really love to have a role that really personifies someone different for me. I also watched Catwoman yesterday with Halle Berry. I think powerful women roles are obviously exciting for any female actress. Having the opportunity to do that would be incredible. I’m very “divine timing” when it comes to this stuff, so I believe everything will happen and run its course in the way it should. But there’s also a lot of really interesting biopics that I would love to see. Maybe I write them, maybe I act. Who knows?

Consani arriving at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

A polaroid of the final glam for the night.

So you want to get into writing too, or have you been writing?

Yeah, I actually have. I have been in the background of my mind thinking about this and maybe moving into that space as well. I think it’s quite exciting. In my whole career, it’s always been if you’re not given the opportunity, you make it yourself. I think of other actresses, and the behind-the-camera work that goes into the shows that they do.

That’s a really good point. A lot of the actors that we grew up with—Nicole Kidman, Reese Witherspoon—have really gone into production, or are part of the writing process. Do you have a dream director to work with? Do you have a bucket list?

Totally. Wes Anderson is a really big one... I love Wes Anderson. I think he’s an incredible director. But on top of that, I just worked with Janicza Bravo, and I’m such a big fan. She’s so incredible with the way that she thinks. Lena Dunham [is another]. There’s so many incredible people, but I think I like the way that each different director works. My favorite part about working with Janicza was just the youth in her perspective. I’ve worked with multi-generations of directors at this point, and to see the difference between how Ryan works versus how Janicza works versus how Molly Gordon works, it’s just quite interesting. There’s a lot of directors that I’m a big fan of, people who are obviously focused on cinematography, but also understand how to have fun.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. #3534. 32 Years Later, The Santa Clause's Line On Believing Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote

Ah, "The Santa Clause." The holiday classic where Tim Allen (making his leading man debut in a movie) accidentally murders Jolly Old Saint Nick, featuring a title that tricked an entire generation into misspelling "Santa Claus." In the 1994 film (which ended up having to cut a risque joke), Allen plays Scott Calvin (Get it? His name has the same initials as SANTA CLAUS!), a divorced, work-obsessed marketing exec spending the holidays with his son, Charlie (Eric Lloyd).

Christmas Eve rolls around, and when the real Santa accidentally falls off Scott's roof and dies, Scott is forced to become the new Santa. Scott doesn't like this idea, especially when he starts growing a magical beard and a magical fat belly. It doesn't help that everyone around him — except Charlie — thinks he's gone insane. The film then unfolds over a year leading up to the following Christmas, where Scott has to come to terms with his new career.

Will Scott learn to be a better father, embrace the Christmas spirit, and thrive as the new Santa Claus? Of course he will, and then they'll make a string of sequels (and a streaming TV series reboot as well)! Happy holidays!

"Seeing isn't believing. Believing is seeing."

"Seeing is believing" is an age-old saying, but "The Santa Clause" flips this a bit. When Scott becomes Santa, he ends up in the North Pole, where the Elves who toil away in the workshop try to give him some help. One of those elves, Judy (Paige Tamada), utters our quote of the day: "Seeing isn't believing. Believing is seeing." This quote is later embraced wholeheartedly by Scott's son Charlie, who has to keep reminding Scott that all he has to do is look around to witness the reality of his new magical life.

Belief is a big part of "The Santa Clause." Scott has to believe in himself, while everyone around Scott has to believe he's really the new Santa. The hard-headed realists of the world understandably have trouble with all of this, and that includes Scott himself. He's a gruff American businessman! He doesn't believe in Christmas magic, gosh darn it! All Scott needs to do is open his eyes, both literally and metaphorically, to see the reality of his new situation. And isn't that what Christmas is all about? That and drinking way too much nog? Thank you,"The Santa Clause," for making us believe in Christmas.

"Merry Christmas to all, and to all a good night! And when I wake up, I'm gettin' a CAT scan!"

"We're your worst nightmare. Elves with attitude."

"Everybody likes Denny's, it's an American institution."

"You see, children hold the spirit of Christmas within their hearts. You don't wanna be responsible for killing the spirit of Christmas, now would you ... Santa?"

#3533. All Deku-Nut Bag upgrade locations in Zelda Ocarina of Time

How to get a bigger bag to carry Deku nuts

How to get a bigger bag to carry Deku nuts

Upgrading Link's Deku-Nut Bag increases the number of flashy nuts that you carry in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. As young Link, Deku nuts are extremely useful items, as they stun enemies and create the perfect moment to attack. Unfortunately, you can carry a limited number of nuts early in the game. However, if you know where to look — and which holes to jump into — you can find bigger bags to carry more nuts.

To help you expand Link's arsenal, we've put this guide together explaining where to find all Deku-Nut Bag upgrades in Zelda Ocarina of Time.

When you start the game, you can only carry 20 Deku nuts, but you can increase this number later by finding two upgrades: the Bigger Deku-Nut Bag and the Biggest Deku-Nut Bag. Each one increases the number of nuts you can carry by 10, allowing you to have a total of 40 nuts once you have unlocked the upgrades.

You can find both upgrades in the Lost Woods, but there are a few details to keep in mind before going after them. For the first Deku-Nut Bag upgrade location, you must be young Link and you need the bombs from Dodongo Cavern. As for the second upgrade location, you must have the Mask of Truth, which you get from the Happy Mask Shop.

Here's where you find each Deku-Nut Bag upgrade.

Before you head off, make sure you have some bombs, and you have at least 40 rupees. If you do, you're ready to head to the Lost Woods.

From Kokiri Forest entrance, head right, left, right, left, straight, and left. Alternatively, if you have the Minuet of the Forest, you can play it to warp to Sacred Grove. Enter the Lost Woods and the rock will be in the first room.

Drop a bomb near the boulder to destroy it and reveal a hole in the ground. Jump into it to find an underground cave where two Business Scrubs will be waiting. Deflect their shots with your shield, then talk to the one on the left. It will offer you the first Deku-Nut Bag upgrade for 40 rupees.

To unlock the second Deku-Nut Bag upgrade, you must interact with some Deku Scrubs in a hole in the Lost Woods. There are two paths to this exact location as well. If you're starting from the Kokiri Forest, then go right, left, right, left, and then left. But, if you're coming from the Sacred Grove into the Lost Woods, you want to head left, right, and then right.

Inside the shrubs, you will find a hole in the ground. Enter it to find a cave. Inside, you'll see some small Deku Scrubs and a large one. Climb onto the tree stump wearing the Mask of Truth and the Deku Scrubs will emerge from the ground. Talk to the older Deku Scrub on the right, and it will give you the second Deku-Nut Bag upgrade.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

As for its health hardware, Google left it largely untouched, so you still get heart rate and blood oxygen monitoring, ECG readings, skin temperature, GPS, and sleep tracking, with reportedly accurate findings. The catch is that this remains an Android-only watch, requiring Android 12 or newer, and some of the better AI features work best with a newer Pixel phone.

Physically, the Watch 5 doesn’t stray far from its predecessor, keeping the familiar domed display under 3D Corning Gorilla Glass while adding new watch faces that curve around its edges—with the screen reaching up to 3,000 nits and adjusting to ambient light, so it should remain easy to read during a sunny afternoon run or in a dim room. As for its durability, its IP68 and 5ATM ratings mean you can wear it through a workout, at the beach, or in the pool without worrying about dust or water. And charging shouldn’t necessarily be a nightly routine, either, with the watch lasting up to 56.5 hours in testing. Heavier use will cut into that figure, but you should still have a good chance of making it through two full days with enough power left to track your sleep overnight.
