#3531. Warby Parker and Gentle Monster Are Launching Smart Glasses. Does Anyone Want Them?

This is the November 11, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

It’s been a meme-worthy news week: the new Met Gala theme launched endless online discourse, Jensen Huang ignited the internet with news of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, then fashion netizens had a time memeifying him as a Hedi-boy, and Maybelline changed its slogan with some very confusing punctuation.

IRL, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker are getting into the smart glasses space. Like Meta, they’re working hard to get fashion’s co-sign in order to have tastemakers influence everyone else to wear them, though I have yet to find a fashion person happy to wear these without a check involved. And this week, Alex Consani video-called me to discuss her acting ambitions after her debut in American Horror Story: 13. She’s already filmed two movies coming next year.

Mentioned in this issue: Iron Man, Robert Downey Jr., Kylie Jenner, Timothée Chalamet’s security guard, Steven Meisel, Martine Rose discourse, Luca de Meo, Woke 3.0, Hedi Slimane, Slimaniacs, Sarah Paulson, Ryan Murphy, and many more.

Amelia Gray at the Gentle Monster launch dinner.

Last night Warby Parker and Gentle Monster celebrated the launches of their “intelligent eyewear” lines (not to be confused with Meta’s “smart glasses”), both developed with Google and Samsung. Warby Parker hosted a literary activation with Vogue, and Gentle Monster held a “preview experience” and dinner attended by Alex Consani, Anok Yai, Charles Melton, Joaquin Phoenix, and more.

Snap also tapped Robert Downey Jr. to star in videos showcasing its technology, Iron Man–style. Phoenix appeared in Gentle Monster’s launch campaign in a callback to his role in Her, in which he plays a man who falls in love with an AI voiced by Scarlett Johansson. (In 2024, she had a dispute with OpenAI after learning the company had created a voice that sounded similar to hers for its AI, which she had declined to license for ChatGPT. Sam Altman denied any intentional imitation.) Leveraging two movie stars who’ve been the face of this kind of technology in film to bring their products to the masses is a cunning move from Google and Samsung. Yet it’s possible that no co-sign can combat the anxiety around AI and its surrounding gadgets. There is a budding battle in the smart glasses space—but does anyone actually want them?

Martine Rose is officially taking over from Pierpaolo Piccioli at Balenciaga. I still think he could have been right for the brand, but he came at the wrong time. Balenciaga is essentially Kering’s youth vehicle after a decade under Demna, and Piccioli just wasn’t the designer to fulfill that brief. That his collections seemed to try to honor both Demna’s casualwear range and his own couture-like sensibility only muddled the brand’s remit further. But Rose, who worked with Demna on his Balenciaga menswear early on, is a much better fit in this context, and she has the industry’s goodwill—fans have been advocating her ascent to a role like this one for years.

Rose is the first official hire under Luca de Meo’s tenure as Kering’s CEO, and she is walking into a brave new world. De Meo believes Kering has been overly dependent on its creative directors, and is looking to streamline operations with a new strategy dubbed “ReconKering.” If reports are confirmed that Chemena Kamali will head to Saint Laurent and Virginia Burlina to McQueen, four out of five creative directors at Kering will soon be women. Along with Rose and Louise Trotter at Bottega Veneta, these are designers who are better known as prolific workhorses rather than buzzy household names. De Meo is evidently looking to grow beyond the star creative director strategy that defined fashion in the 2010s, with Demna as an exception. What this means for Rose and Balenciaga, and for Saint Laurent and McQueen, which have historically depended on the persona of their creative leads, remains to be seen.

Balenciaga is back in the news this week with the opening of the first of several activations around the 25th anniversary of its Le City bag, arguably the most enduring of It bags after the Birkin. Damien Hirst has hand-painted 25 bags for the occasion, and Nicole Richie is fronting the campaign in a callback to the aughts. This was planned prior to Piccioli’s exit, yet it’s taking place in between creative directors speaks to an undeniable fact that plays right into ReconKering: These brands are bigger than their designers, despite how important these appointments are to industry insiders and fanatics.

A look from Jun Takahashi’s fall-winter 2024 collection for Undercover, which will be included in the upcoming Met Costume Institute exhibition.

In case you missed it: The Met announced on Thursday the replacement exhibition for the John Galliano blockbuster postponed earlier this year. “ExtraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” will focus on how designers have explored familiar, ordinary garments: jeans, T-shirts, workwear, and more. It sounds like both an ode to normcore and to the ingenuity with which designers like Matthieu Blazy, Demna, Jun Takahashi, and more have reimagined the most simple of clothing. Andrew Bolton, the curator in charge of the Costume Institute, told Vogue he “didn’t have a plan B” after Galliano and that he wanted the replacement show to be “challenging and provocative.” The announcement drew both positive and negative reactions. Its main criticism is its simplicity, especially when compared to Galliano’s extravagance. Bolton has a singular way of placing fashion in larger cultural contexts to underscore its historic importance—I’m curious to see what he’ll do when the fashion he’s dealing with already exists in an atmosphere that requires little explanation.

Maybelline has updated its famous slogan, “Maybe she’s born with it. Maybe it’s Maybelline,” which was first introduced in 1991, to a more democratic, inclusive riff: “Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline.” Confusing punctuation aside, the change feels like it belongs to the late 2010s era of DEI marketing. It’s true that binary pronouns have fallen out of style, particularly at the makeup counter, even if brands shied away from this kind of revamp in the Trump era. But then again, after last week’s blue wave in the midterm elections, maybe Maybelline is just in time.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang waves to the media as he arrives at Gimpo airport in Seoul on June 5, 2026 wearing a Dior jacket. Images from this same outing were modified with AI by fashion netizens.

The news of Jensen Huang’s affair filled X with memes about Chinese spies and mistresses in a variety of configurations. By Monday evening, Huang had reached the fashion world’s stylish netizens: the Instagram account @hidden.ny, an anonymous digital mood board and cultural platform, posted a series of images of Huang in a studded leather jacket. The caption read: “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy.”

It’s well-known that Huang is a leather jacket enthusiast. But despite Huang’s penchant for a black leather moment, it appears he was not, in fact, wearing the Saint Laurent jacket. A quick run through an AI image detector debunked Huang being a “Slimaniac,” at least in this particular case. SynthID detected that the images posted by Hidden and other users online were generated or edited with OpenAI. To burst the bubble even further, it appears the images used as the base for this edit weren’t taken after the disclosure of Huang’s affair, but during a trip to South Korea in June. Apologies to the menswear crowd for ruining the fantasy.

#3530. VisionQuest's Avengers: Doomsday Post-Credits Scene Explained: [SPOILER] Returns

This article contains spoilers for "VisionQuest" Season 1, Episode 8, "Forever."

The season (series?) finale of "VisionQuest" teases that the Vision-Maximoff family still has a future in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. There are two post-credits scenes in "VisionQuest." One is vaguer: Ultron (James Spader), now free and convinced not to kill all of humanity for now, has a backup drive of Jocasta (T'Nia Miller). So, yeah, it looks like this isn't the last we've seen of the Living Automaton in the MCU.

Towards the end of the episode, Tommy Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica) asks Vision (Paul Bettany) if they'll ever see his mom, Wanda Maximoff/The Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen) again. The second post-credit scene all but confirms, yes, they will.

The scene replays the climax of 2022's "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," where Wanda buries herself under the rubble of Mount Wundagore to destroy the grimoire, the Darkhold. But then the scene shows green energy telekinetically lifting the rubble away, as a shadowed, hooded figure stands over Wanda. "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine," he says in a European accent as green light bathes Wanda, and her eyes shoot open. Three guesses who Wanda's savior is and the first two don't count. (But you will get a hint — his name rhymes with "zoom.")

This basically confirms Olsen will be appearing as Wanda in "Avengers: Doomsday," and as a servant of Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) This scene also aligns rather well with a post-credits scene included in the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" rerelease earlier this year, which depicted Doom freeing Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo) from imprisonment after the events of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day."

Many now vindicated Marvel fans refused to believe that Wanda was really dead after Wundagore's destruction. Elizabeth Olsen had previously said she was open to returning as Scarlet Witch, and it seems Marvel must've given her a call.

In "Avengers: Doomsday," Doom will have at least three "Latverian witches" under his command, and they will wear steel masks much like their boss does. That'll be a fitting homage to the three Brides of Dracula — Doom, as a caped, castle-dwelling Eastern European king, is very much a villain modeled in Dracula's image. But there's also rampant speculation the witches' masks hide familiar faces, including Wanda's. This "VisionQuest" post-credits scene all but confirms it.

(In the "Time Runs Out" storyline that "Doomsday" is loosely adapting, Doom had all female acolytes called Black Swans serving him. The Latverian witches might be a simplified version of that concept.)

While I'm hoping Marvel doesn't make Doom, their greatest villain, a literal variant of Tony Stark, the fact is Robert Downey Jr.'s casting means a lot of the audience will read Doom as "evil Iron Man." There'd be some fitting narrative symmetry then if Doom has corrupted Avengers, like Hulk and Scarlet Witch, on his side.

Doom has manipulated Wanda before in the comics, too. "Young Avengers: The Children's Crusade" by Allan Heinberg and Jim Cheung revealed that, after Wanda's infamous "No more mutants" crash-out in "House of M," Doom sheltered her in Latveria to try and gain her powers. This is the storyline that reunited Wanda with Tommy and Billy as well. With how "VisionQuest" leaves the Maximoff boys, and with Marvel Studios having planted the seeds for Young Avengers, I think a "Children's Crusade" adaptation is in the near future.

#3529. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

News broke a few days ago that Universal Orlando’s beloved mascot Earl the Squirrel would be hitting a big milestone this year. He’s headed to the 100th Annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, and if you plan to watch on NBC or with your Peacock subscription, you’ll be able to see him getting his own giant balloon. It’s a big anniversary for the Thanksgiving parade, but it’s also a solid one for Earl, who turns 5 this year. Let’s talk out what we know.

Here at CinemaBlend, we’ve been big fans of Earl The Squirrel for a while. The story behind Earl goes that Earl the Squirrel was a real mammal who burrowed in Universal Studios’ giant Christmas tree in Orlando in the early aughts. One of the best parts of being at Universal Studios around the holidays is the lighting of the Christmas tree, and the original Earl liked to chew on the aforementioned lights.

Someone on the team jokingly put a stuffed squirrel in the Christmas tree in homage, and then in 2021, someone had the bright idea to bring Earl into the parks officially.

Now, he’s the mascot, and most definitely one of the cool Easter egg found throughout the parks. I visited during the holidays last year and saw him cutely burrowing in the big Christmas tree. I’ve also caught Earl in the Tribute store in the past, and a life-size version of Earl does meet-and-greets throughout the holiday season. Finding him on the tree is still a sort of yearly scavenger hunt.

However, I get the sneaking suspicion anyone watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade won’t have any trouble spotting Earl. That’s because he’s going to be 30.4 feet tall and 14.5 feet wide. Literally, you won’t be able to miss him.

I haven’t been to the real-life Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, but Universal Orlando already offers the next best thing: The Holiday Parade Featuring Macys. The theme park actually has had ties to the Macy’s Parade for years, and even if you aren’t normally a parade person, bringing the giant balloons into the theme park is real feat, and impressive to see. A visit around the holiday season is worth it for the parade alone.

The holiday season kicks off this weekend at Universal Orlando, starting on Saturday, November 14th, and Earle will join The Holiday Parade lineup in early December. For now, you can catch The Grinch in action, or check out the Red Coconut Club's alpine makeover. This year, Universal is also once again upping its food game, and you can try out one of the many new cabin-style holiday food kiosks featuring items like Christmas Tree waffles, red-nose reindeer donuts, oh and Earl gets a shoutout there too with Earl The Squirrel’s hazelnut dot cake.

I’m not even getting into the hot chocolate options, which are usually my personal favorite snack this time of year. (Well, as long as it’s not 90 degrees out.)

All in all, there’s a lot to look forward to if you’re planning a trip to the parks, and there are special tickets being offered this holiday season. You can find out more on the Universal Orlando site.

#3527. You Can Get Microsoft Visual Studio Pro 2026 on Sale for Just $30 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3526. Ryan Gosling's R-Rated 2016 Comedy Is Officially Apple TV's Biggest Streaming Hit

I have never seen an actor resist Hollywood stardom more stubbornly than Ryan Gosling. Three years after his 2001 breakout performance as a Jewish skinhead in Henry Bean's incendiary "The Believer," (for which he should've been nominated for an Academy Award), he was transformed into a big-screen heartthrob via his portrayal of Noah Calhoun in Nick Cassavetes' "The Notebook." Gosling could've dined out on hunky leading men roles for the next decade, but, over the next few years, he chose instead to play a freebasing high school teacher in "Half Nelson," a self-destructive husband in the soul-hollowing "Blue Valentine" and an emotionally remote getaway driver in "Drive." "Crazy, Stupid, Love" was a bright box-office spot, but it wasn't the showcase he needed. If he wanted to be a star. Which, in 2011, seemed to be in question.

In 2016, Gosling made a play to become a star on his own off-kilter terms as alcoholic private detective Holland March in Shane Black's "The Nice Guys." The legendary screenwriter behind "Lethal Weapon," "The Last Boy Scout" and "Kiss Kiss, Bang Bang" cooked up an elegantly seared filet mignon for Gosling, and he savored every moment. "The Nice Guys," which pairs Gosling with an over-it Russell Crowe (as a Yoo-hoo swilling enforcer) is an audience movie, but the audience, for whatever reason, didn't show up in 2016.

28 days after "The Nice Guys" went live on Apple TV, it's now the service's most watched movie. I'm thrilled that more people are discovering this shaggy detective classic 10 years after its release, but under Ellison's Skydance rule, Warner Bros. isn't trying to resuscitate commercial misfires. This is it. That said, it's got more going on in its 116 minutes than the entire Marvel Cinematic Universe oeuvre.

I read "The Nice Guys" when it was pitched as a network television pilot by Black and Anthony Bagarozzi (one of these men had the pleasure of watching a stray kitten urinate on my lap). It was sharp, hilarious and fertile ground for a series – if the writers could get around CBS' standards and practices. Not since "The Monster Squad" had Black written with such ease and eloquence at a PG-ish level.

When "The Nice Guys" got greenlit as a film, producer Joel Silver starred it up with Gosling and Crowe. The idea seemed to be that Crowe, a major movie star and Academy Award-winner, would play straight man to Gosling's goofball PI, and the film would sell itself. This just didn't happen. Set in the late 1970s, Black's stumblebum neo-noir is a skillfully plotted romp that finds Gosling and Crowe trying to piece together the disappearance of anti-pollution activist Amelia Kuttner (Margaret Qualley).

Gosling is dopey perfection as Holland March, a single father who's battling against a boozy haze to solve a case that could save his profession and his life. He's funny and heartbreaking in this role. As is Black's wont, you're left with a wacky, whimsically moralistic Donald Westlake riff with blockbuster trimmings. Gosling and Crowe are scrambling to take down men who abuse women. Spoiler: they get their dastardly dudes, and you'll shed tears along the way.

I'm thrilled that Gosling is now an A-lister making films for Lucasfilm, and he was wonderful in "Project Hail Mary," but we've yet to see his best. I just want to watch him blossom.

#3525. All Deku-Seed Bag upgrade locations in Ocarina of Time

Deku-Seed Bag upgrades are a must in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, if you want to be able to beam your opponents from afar without worrying about running out of seeds. Not to be confused with the Deku-Nut Bag, which holds the nuts you can use to flash-stun enemies, the Deku-Seed Bag holds ammo for your Fairy Slingshot.

Below, we explain where to upgrade the Deku-Seed Bag in the Ocarina of Time remake.

After you get the Fairy Slingshot inside the Great Deku Tree, your Deku-Seed Bag will be able to hold 30 Deku seeds. Each upgrade will increase your bag size by 10 seeds, to a total of 50 Deku seeds.

The first upgrade location you'll likely run into is in the Lost Woods and the second upgrade can be found in Hyrule Castle Town, so you can unlock both of these pretty early on in your playthrough.

The Deku-Seed Bag upgrades can only be unlocked as young Link.

The first upgrade location you'll run into is this little shooting range in the Lost Woods. From the Kokiri Forest entrance, head right, and you'll see this target hanging up. (There's also two Skull Kids down below who will give you a Piece of Heart if you play their game.)

Hit the target three times with your Fairy Slingshot and a Deku Scrub will upgrade your Deku-Seed Bag, free of charge. Nice!

The second location is in Hyrule Castle Town.

Head to the shooting gallery, which is to the west of the Happy Mask Shop, and north of the Bombchu Bowling Alley. You can only go in here during the daytime, so sleep or play the Sun's Song to change the time, if you need to.

You'll need to pay 10 rupees per try, and in order to get the bag upgrade, you'll need to hit all 10 targets. You'll only have 15 seeds to try, but if you wipe out, the gallery owner will let you try again for free. The targets will always show up in the same places, so if you do fail, try to memorize where they show up.

Once you do beam all 10 targets, the owner will give you the bag upgrade.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3524. Chris Harrison on Launching The Vow, His Faith-Based Reality Show, and Leaving The Bachelor

“It really has very little to do with being on The Bachelor,” Chris Harrison, the series’s former host, tells me over breakfast at Manhattan’s Whitby Hotel in mid-October. Harrison orders avocado toast with poached eggs on top, then gently redirects the conversation to The Vow, his new faith-based dating series that premieres November 11 on Fox Nation. “It’s what we noticed, reading articles about this revival of young people going to church more than ever,” he says, turning to his wife and fellow executive producer on the show, Lauren Zima, who is seated beside him. “Here in New York, there are youth nights at the Catholic Church, at the temple, that are selling out thousands of kids. Clearly, this generation is searching for something solid—salvation, foundation.”

The six-episode series airs on the conservative-associated Fox Nation, Harrison says The Vow isn’t meant to have a political slant. “We’re not telling you to believe this or follow this path,” says Harrison. “Good shows look into a niche, this one’s about faith-driven people trying to find love. The hookup culture was a big deal and settling down became a cocktail joke. This generation’s really pushing back the other way.”

Faith-based dating shows aimed at Gen Z audiences have begun to infiltrate the reality TV landscape in recent years, from The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives to Hulu’s Ring by Spring Break, an upcoming series “that drops single Christian college students into a steamy spring break in Cabo, where finding ‘The One’ isn’t a dream…it’s a deadline.” But mixing romance and religion can be tricky business, as evidenced by the indeterminate future of the Mormon Wives and a ready-to-release season of The Bachelorette put on pause following allegations made against Taylor Frankie Paul, who leads both shows.

On The Vow, Jace Cates is a 30-year-old devout Christian mortgage-loan officer from Canby, Oregon that 10 similarly faith-driven women compete to marry. The goal is that, “Jace finds love,” says Harrison. “If it leads to marriage and children, we don’t have enough time for all that to happen on the show, but I want to help try and create the real article on TV. And if we don’t, that has to be real as well because this show is not predicated on the fact that it’s guaranteed to work.” But it’s hard to imagine any contenders stand a chance against Sierra, a virgin who lives 20 minutes away from Jace and attends his same Portland church. Her frontrunner status is cemented with a night-one kiss, the filming of which happened to coincide with Sierra’s 26th birthday. “We cast her before we cast Jace,” says Harrison, which feels as telling a reveal as any about producers’ ability to set themselves up for a successful outcome.

In February, before Fox Nation’s public involvement, Harrison shared a casting call for The Vow on Instagram, seeking single men and women aged 21 and older “who want a traditional, marriage-minded partnership built on commitment and shared values.” The description sparked early backlash on social media, but an initially surprised Harrison says he now understands the reaction. “Because in this day and age, we all have our guard up when we hear something that might be controversial,” he explains. “I’m not going to shy away from the fact that [the show] is about faith-based people saying, ‘I really do want to get married. I really do want to have babies’ Even those that might think it’s polarizing, I hope you watch,” Harrison adds. “You might be pleasantly surprised at how unbiased and uncontroversial it really is.”

The 55-year-old Harrison and Zima, who is 16 years his junior, are themselves “on different stages of faith,” she says as her egg-white frittata arrives. “Not drastically, but a bit. He’s probably more traditionally spiritual than I am.” Harrison was raised by a Jewish mother and grandparents, but grew up in a Protestant household during adolescence in the Bible belt of Dallas, Texas. After getting baptized as a Christian in his twenties, Harrison now says he identifies as “a religious mutt.”

“What matters most in our relationship,” the Chicago-born Zima continues, “[are] our values—family, loyalty, wanting to be good to people—those conversations [about] core things that drive you were what we really wanted people to have on the show.” Seeking “a really diverse spectrum of faith” meant casting Christians who ranged from the recently baptized to a first-generation American from Ghana. And the term “tradwife” means something different to everyone—Audrey aspires to be “a woman who makes her own money” as a penile implant sales rep fromin Wisconsin, while California native Mya is a second-grade teacher who one day wants to “do my husband for a living and have a big family.”

“We are always wanting to bring people together,” Zima continues. “And part of the way you bring people together is conversation—giving them dynamic, interesting, layered things to unpack together.”

The couple is open to devoting future seasons to different religions outside Christianity. “The important thing is finding really good, authentic people who have faith in their heart—whatever that faith is—but then really want to get married,” says Harrison. As “one of the rare few that was there on day one back in 2001 when we were inventing what The Bachelor was,” he adds, “it was rough and raw. We shot tons of silly things that never made air because you’re not exactly sure. So there will be some of that on The Vow. As veteran as I am, we’re still asking people to watch our art and accept it.”

The stakes are high for Harrison, who parted ways with The Bachelor franchise following a controversial Extra interview in February 2021, during which he excused racist behavior from one of the show’s contestants. He later issued an apology acknowledging that “by excusing historical racism, I defended it.” After announcing he would be “stepping aside for a period of time” from the series, Harrison also attempted a poorly received daytime TV mea culpa on Good Morning America that anchor Michael Strahan called “a surface response.,” Harrison promptly announced that he would be “stepping aside for a period of time” from the series. He permanently departed the show in June 2021 and reportedly received a “mid-range eight-figure settlement” from ABC, according to Deadline. A follow-up report by Variety adjusted that figure, revealing he received roughly $10 million. Vanity Fair has reached out to Harrison for comment about the payout.

Harrison’s comeback project has already ruffled feathers at his former workplace. In mid-September, Warner Bros, owner of the Bachelor franchise, sent a cease and desist letter against Harrison and Fox Nation, regarding what they viewed as an IP violation on the teaser for The Vow released on September 16. “Sadly, I wasn’t surprised. It’s par for the course. I don’t know why, because in my opinion, you can’t put a cease and desist on finding love,” says Harrison. “So it was unfortunate that’s where they wanted to go in this breakup. I feel a bit like a lover they can’t let go.”

For better or worse, Harrison and Zima’s real-life love story will forever be linked to his time spent hosting The Bachelor. “Oh, the other show?” Zima quips. “All of that, I look back [at it] as a blessing. And blessings don’t always come wrapped in this cute box under the tree,” Harrison says. “Sometimes it’s a humbling and traumatic experience.”

Zima met Harrison while covering The Bachelor franchise as a red-carpet reporter for Entertainment Tonight before things turned romantic in August 2018. “Obviously, what I loved most about her in the beginning was that she was a great interviewer,” says Harrison.

“This is so weird for me. I have to clock myself as being interviewed right now,” says Zima, who brings a bubbly, over-caffeinated energy to Harrison’s politely warm, but largely stoic presence. “By the way, I’m going to shut up. This is his interview,” she says a few times during breakfast, each of them subtly, but noticeably aware that a fellow journalist is meant to be observing their dynamic. They seem more at ease and physically affectionate as the interview wraps up; indeed, it’s only when my recorder stops that Zima dispenses her juiciest morsel of reality TV gossip—a blind item involving Harrison and a certain Real Housewife.

Zima, who earned thousands of views on weekly recaps of the show, credits Harrison’s level of care for those who came on The Bachelor with “how Bachelor Nation was created,” says Zima. “Speaking as someone who watched and reviewed it before we were ever together—he created that energy. What we have together is such a deep understanding of each other’s fields that really adds a passion and joy to our relationship and takes away what could be, in other scenarios, resentment or confusion about a very demanding job.”

Harrison and Zima were both previously married, and he saw two kids off to college in the early years of their relationship. “Maybe it just took the right person, but when she knocked me upside the head with those feelings that I had, that made me want to stop,” Harrison says of his hosting duties on The Bachelor, which often required extended amounts of international travel. “For the first time, I didn’t want to hop on a plane and go to Asia for the next season.”

Coincidentally, his post-COVID epiphany overlapped with Harrison’s exit from his day job. “I’d been on the road for a long time and I felt like something special was happening here with Lauren,” says Harrison, before asking for a reheat of his tea. “I’m just going to hit the pause button and be selfish, fall in love. It allowed me to fall in love and get married. I don’t think she was going to wait around and pine for me while I was on the road shooting another show.” ABC later enlisted former Bachelor, NFL quarterback, and sports commentator Jesse Palmer to replace Harrison as host.

As they celebrate their third wedding anniversary, the Austin-based couple say they’ve come to a peaceful place about “the other show.” Says Harrison, “What a weird thing that I was hosting this show about love and that it allowed me to find love myself. So how can I begrudge that completely?”

As Hollywood weathered hardships of its own, Harrison was happy to employ some of his former Bachelor colleagues, including casting director Lindsay Liles, executive producer Louis Caric, co-EP Deb Read, and director Michael Shea for The Vow. “It’ll probably end up being one of those silly reality TV show drinking games, drink every time someone says ‘intentional’,” says Zima, “but there’s so much meaning behind it and that’s why it gets repeated so much. When we’re kids we read about fairytales and hope to find our love. This guy’s literally bought a house and is filling his savings account for the family he hopes to have one day.”

The show’s dates are grounded in real life. “It’s not too hard to fall in love on a beach in Bora Bora,” says Zima, borrowing a line from Harrison. And there are no elimination rituals where the show’s lead can “hide behind a flower,” says the host. Instead, breakups happen face-to-face and at any time. “It’s what real relationships require,” Harrison tells the participants in the show’s premiere, the only episode provided in advance of our interview. “And honestly, it’s what a gentleman would do.”

That isn’t the only element of The Vow that directly invokes Harrison’s time on The Bachelor. One of the contestants vying for Jace’s heart is Kylee, a 28-year-old who appeared in a post-Harrison season of The Bachelor and now declares herself “on fire for Jesus” following her recent baptism. “There were others. We had a lot of people reach out to us,” from his former franchise, says Harrison. “Kylie was somebody that we were very thoughtful about.”

The showman in Harrison says “it’s fun to poke the bear” with references to his former gig. “It’s reality TV. I’m a TV host. There’s always a side of you that wants to promote the show.” Plus, it’s easier for Harrison to claim his victory in the breakup, given that The Bachelor franchise hasn’t aired a season of its product since March 2025. “And as far as I know, they’re not going to be on the air anytime soon,” says Harrison with a shrug. “So I would just say worry about cleaning up your own mess. Don’t worry about mine.” Roughly two weeks after our mid-October conversation, and just five days before Harrison’s return to TV, ABC announced the official return of The Bachelor in March 2027. No casting has been confirmed.

The search for love is a sensitive one, even for someone as seasoned as Harrison. “I’m not bitter and angry about The Bachelor because I don’t take for granted that I’ve been to the Super Bowl,” he says with a polished kind of sincerity. “I am opening my heart and bearing my soul to everybody, hoping that we could be together again. I do miss that connection and I hope it’s still there. But it’s a very vulnerable thing to do. That’s why I’m not out banging my chest or beating the drum. I’m a producer like anybody else hoping to produce a great television show. My guard is up,” he admits as our plates get cleared away. “Like I was for 20 years before, I will be in front of everybody taking the bullets, and I told [the participants] I will be standing beside you and [we will] do the best we can.”

Behind the scenes, Harrison and Zima often had to convince their young participants that the show wasn’t part of a larger gimmick. “There’s no gotcha—this is really just about you guys finding love,” Harrison recalled. “It was shocking at how low the bar has been set. I don’t mean dating shows, I just mean dating in general. I told the women, ‘I apologize to you on behalf of all men.’ Maybe too arrogant of me and maybe too lofty of a goal, but my hope is that, of all things, maybe we raise the level of debate of what women deserve and what men need to be.”

Zima remembers what it was like to see Harrison return to his element, getting visibly emotional just before our goodbyes. “That first night in the control room, when I saw him on screen, I teared up like I’m tearing up now,” she says with a slightly embarrassed laugh. Harrison reaches over to grab her hand. “It means the world to me that as his wife, more than seeing him on screen, when people stop him in the street and say, ‘Man, you were the thing I could watch with my grandma every week,’” says Zima, “and please come back and do a show because I miss that connection with my family.’ What a meaningful thing to have done in this life, to bring people together.”

#3522. 15 Years Ago Today: Henry Cavill Starred In An Epic Fantasy Movie Before Superman

With now-former DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran's version of the DC Universe coming to a premature end, it's times like these when we would do well to look back at what has worked, and what hasn't worked, when it comes to DC's films. One thing that kinda worked was Henry Cavill, a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie during his run in the DC Extended Universe. Without doubt, the actor had both the charisma and physicality to make you believe a man can fly.

And yet, just two years before debuting as Superman in "Man of Steel," Cavill made audiences believe a man could battle gods with a sword. It was November 11, 2011, and Indian director Tarsem Singh Dhandwar had just released his film "Immortals," an epic fantasy movie inspired by Greek mythology.

In the film, Henry Cavill plays Theseus, a humble stonemason with the physique of a Kryptonian who is chosen by Zeus himself (Luke Evans) to lead humanity in their resistance against Hyperion (Mickey Rourke), a tyrant king wreaking havoc on Greece in search of a mythical bow that would allow him to free the Titans and overthrow the gods of Olympus. No, this movie isn't really based on any particular myth. Rather, it borrows from a number of legends and blends them together in a nonsensical yet very cool tale full of superhero-like action, incredible costumes, and some of the most stunning imagery in any fantasy movie out there.

Back in its day, critics generally praised "Immortals" for its stunning visuals while admitting its story left a lot to be desired. Nowadays, though, the movie represents an underrated entry in Cavill's body of work, as it showed he was ready to be a star and lead a franchise (or two).

"Immortals" is, admittedly, not a well-written movie. And yet, Tarsem Singh Dhandwar went about crafting this movie like it was going to mark the last time he ever set foot on a film set, leaving it all on the screen. Case in point, he tapped Eiko Ishioka ("Bram Stoker's Dracula") to design the movie's impossibly flamboyant costumes, which make the human characters look so extravagant that they almost overshadow the literal gods around them.

Then there's the film's visual style, which Singh once described as "Caravaggio meets 'Fight Club.'" He wanted to make a hardcore action flick in the manner of a Renaissance painting, and it shows, resulting in a movie that blends the desaturated colors and slow motion of something like "300" with a striking painterly aesthetic. When it comes to its spectacle, "Immortals" similarly combines gods with mythical weapons that tear down city walls and intimate, grounded sword clashes, making its violence feel huge in its scope and scale. Indeed, the first scenes involving gods are especially stunning, as they move at full speed while the humans they're reducing to smithereens are slowed way down. It's a great way to illustrate the awesome powers of these deities.

Speaking of awesome powers, "Immortals" is further bolstered by Henry Cavill, who very much proves his ability to carry a big-budget movie ihere. To be sure, his performance matches the wild tone of everything else around him, all while bringing some needed humanity to Theseus. It's enough to make you more than a little excited for Cavill's return to the realm of outlandish fantasy movie adventures with his upcoming "Highlander" reboot.

Warning! The following contains spoilers for the NCIS episode "Speechless." Stream the episode with a Paramount+ subscription, and read at your own risk!

The latest episode of NCIS was a special one for Katrina Law, as the Jessica Knight actress co-starred in it with her daughter. Law told CinemaBlend her kid knocked it out of the park, but she was ready from the moment it was suggested to shut it down if she wasn't ready.

I had a chance to speak to the actress ahead of the episode's airing on the 2026 TV schedule. Law explained that her daughter, Kinley Andreen, actually pitched the idea of coming on the show, so when an opportunity came up, she was asked about having her on. While she was thrilled to give her daughter a chance to be on the series, the actress explained she wanted her kid to earn it through an audition:

There was a part of me going, like, if she's not really good, I'm not going to make [them cast her], I'm not going to, like, put everybody through this experience. She nailed that audition within 20 minutes.

Things went well, and Andreen booked her debut acting appearance as Chloe in NCIS. I was, frankly, a bit surprised to learn it was her first time acting, because I would've assumed she'd been doing it a while based on her performance. However, she'd never done traditional acting outside of school play performances. Did we all just witness the beginning of a future A-lister's career in television?

Due to that lack of experience, Katrina Law said she wanted to have her daughter go through the audition process to see if she's up for the challenge, but told us she couldn't be prouder of how she did:

It was a four-page audition...she picked up all the beats, she had props, she was doing different notes, there was an emotional arc, she memorized all the lines, was completely off book, and I'm like, there are adults who have to spend two days doing this just to prep for this moment, and you got it in 20 minutes. It was amazing.

Law and her daughter also got to display their fluency in Mandarin after the agents were shocked to find the little girl they found was bilingual. It was quite an acting debut, which makes me all the more thankful she pulled it off.

Jessica Knight's run in Season 24 of NCIS is off to a slow start, but the seeds are being planted for her to have a larger role later this season. Her constant monitoring of Tony DiNozzo for Ziva screams that a future team-up is in the works, which I'm very excited to see.

As for what's next for her daughter, who knows where we'll see Kinley Andreen show up next? There's nothing wrong with being a nepo baby when it comes to Hollywood, especially if you have the talent to back it up. Maybe if NCIS can stay on the air another 20+ years, we'll see Andreen come back and play an agent on the series!

For now, I'm just content we have a solid block of NCIS to enjoy on Tuesday nights. Tune in to CBS on those nights for a healthy dose of nostalgia, as the lineup is loaded with classic NCIS actors.

#3520. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3519. How to get the Goron Tunic in Zelda Ocarina of Time

The Goron Tunic is a unique piece of equipment that allows Link to withstand high temperatures in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. If you try to explore the Death Mountain Crater without this item, Link's clothes will catch fire, and he will start losing health. While entering such a dangerous place might not sound like a good idea, you can't actually avoid it, as you'll need to traverse the area to reach the Fire Temple during the story.

But don't fret. We've put this guide together to explain how to get the Goron Tunic in Zelda Ocarina of Time remake.

After you turn into adult Link, you have two options when it comes to acquiring the Goron Tunic. You can either get it for free by talking to Link (the Goron Link!) in Goron City or buy it from the Shop Owner in Goron City for 600 rupees. Even if you have enough money, I would say that paying for the tunic is not a good option.

To receive the tunic from Goron Link, you must find him in Goron City. You'll meet him as soon as you enter the city as adult Link. However, before you can talk to him, he will start rolling around the city's second layer. To stop him, you must hit them with a bomb. You can either use one of your own bombs or grab the bomb flowers that you find around the area.

Once you finally hit Goron Link, talk to him and choose "The Fire Temple?" dialogue option to hear him explain what happened to Goron City. Next, select "I'll help you!" option, and Link will give you his Goron Tunic so you can help his father and the other Gorons who were taken to the Fire Temple.

Just like the Zora Tunic, you activate the Goron Tunic's effect by equipping it in the Equipment menu. Although this tunic protects Link from the extreme temperatures inside Death Mountain Crater, it doesn't make Link immune to fire, so walking over the flames left by the volcanic rocks while wearing the Goron Tunic will still damage you.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3518. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3 Confirms A Popular Fan Theory

Meat's back on the menu, but so are spoilers for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episodes 1-4.

One of the biggest joys of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is getting to see mythical J.R.R. Tolkien characters like Gil-Galad (Benjamin Walker) and Elendil (Lloyd Owen) finally appear on screen for more than five seconds. Similarly, getting to watch the Dark Lord Sauron himself (Charlie Vickers) deceive Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) throughout Season 2 by calling himself an envoy of the Valar is hilarious (as is Sauron being haunted by Celebrimbor's ghost in the Season 3 premiere).

That said, there are plenty of engaging new additions on "The Rings of Power" as well, with Adar (Joseph Mawle and Sam Hazeldine) – the elf-turned-orc who just wants to create a safe place for his kin — being indubitably the best. Others, however, are not nearly as successful, with possibly the worst of them being Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). The character, who lived in what is now Mordor with his mother Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi) in Season 1, has the unfortunate job of serving as the annoying kid whose seemingly only purpose is to ruin everyone's fun, act racist towards elves, whine every five minutes, and make horrible decisions that end up causing a volcano eruption that engulfs the Southlands in darkness for millennia.

(Okay, that last one's not entirely on Theo, but still...)

What makes this all especially frustrating is how overtly "The Rings of Power" has foreshadowed Theo becoming someone important and evil down the line. As such, he has inspired a variety of fan theories about his true identity, like him being the King of the Dead. Now, Season 3 has confirmed that Theo is none other than one of Sauron's Ringwraiths.

In the premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3, we see Sauron recruiting allies, luring men with the promise of Rings of Power that will turn them into his Nazgnagôl (proto-Nazgûl or Ringwraiths). This includes Theo, who arrives at Mordor in order to compete for one of the rings that would give him the power to fight back against the Númenórean overlords that have been abusing the Southland refugees in Pelargir. It's clear Theo isn't really loyal to Sauron, he just wants to use him to gain power for himself.

Well, things get worse when Sauron lures Theo with talk of his ancestry, revealing that Theo comes from a long line of royalty in the Southlands and even communicating with Theo's long-dead father, Fäldred. According to the Dark Lord, Theo belongs to the "sworn stewards of Mordor", which explains why Theo was drawn to the broken sword in Season 1. Sauron then claims that Bronwyn murdered his father when she discovered the truth of his lineage, then kept it all hidden from her son.

Granted, this is Sauron, a notorious liar and expert manipulator. At the same time, it wouldn't make much sense for Sauron to casually hand Theo a ring unless there actually is something special about him. Regardless, the Dark Lord appeals to the kid's greed and ambition, saying he has it in him to be a conqueror, a sorcerer, and a king.

Unfortunately, it appears that "The Rings of Power" is setting up Theo to become the Witch-King of Angmar, as evidenced by him donning the familiar Nazgûl armor in Season 3's third episode.

While Theo's feelings about sand have yet to be revealed, we do know he's easily manipulated. Indeed, with the benefit of hindsight, we can see just how much his story has echoed Anakin Skywalker's fall to the dark side in the "Star Wars" prequel trilogy. After all, he's never known his father, used to live with his mother, and would do anything to protect those he loves, yet he has an undeniable sense of ambition and hunger for power (which Sauron recognizes, just as Darth Sidious/Palpatine did with Anakin).

Except, Theo doesn't turn to darkness while trying to save someone, so he's nowhere near as tragic as Anakin. It's his fear of being abandoned, combined with his desire for power, that make Theo an ideal candidate to become the latest victim of Sauron's lies. First, it was Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), whose thirst for vengeance made her susceptible to Sauron's trickery back when he was going by Halbrand in Season 1. Then, in Season 2, it was Celebrimbor, whose aspiration to become better and more famous allowed Sauron (passing himself off as Annatar) to gaslight him into crafting the rings of dwarves and people. Now, Theo is playing right into Sauron's hands and allowing himself to be enslaved by the Dark Lord.

It remains to be seen whether Theo is capable of coming back from this. He does seem hesitant to carry out all of Sauron's wicked biddings, yet he does it anyway. Is he beyond redemption? And most importantly, is Theo actually the Witch-King? Or will he die and get replaced by one of the Nine we know from "Lord of the Rings?" We'll see what happens as "The Rings of Power" continues.

#3517. Stacy Keach, ‘Fat City’ and ‘Mike Hammer’ Star, Dead at 85

Stacy Keach, the highly prolific screen and stage actor known to audiences for his television role as the private detective Mike Hammer and other tough guy characters, died of heart failure on Tuesday at his family residence in Magdalenka, Poland. He was 85.

Keach’s death was confirmed by his wife, Malgosia, in a statement sent by representation at Guttman Associates.

“It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach, who passed away on November 10, 2026, at our family home in Magdalenka, Poland,” reads the release. “After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength. He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life.” Related Stories How Nicholas Britell Packs Conflicting Emotions Into the ‘Jay Kelly’ Score Adam Sandler Looks Back on His Early Days in Hollywood at IndieWire Honors

She continues: “Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family. His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever.”

Keach rose to the stature of one of the preeminent classical stage actors in the United States through the ’60s and 70s, venturing into avant garde productions and playing roles like Falstaff and Hamlet in his early career. He first appeared on Broadway in 1969, playing Buffalo Bill in Arthur Kopit’s “Indians,” for which he received a Tony nomination. He was also a four-time Drama Desk award winner.

It was after establishing his onstage bona fides that Keach was tapped to play the detective Mike Hammer for CBS’ television film “Murder Me, Murder You,” adapting the character of Mickey Spillane novels that had previously been brought to the screen in noirs like “Kiss Me Deadly.” The film spawned a three-season run of “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” with nearly 50 episodes and two more TV movies featuring Keach as the tough PI. A revival, “Mike Hammer, Private Eye,” was produced in the late ’90s.

In film, Keach established his star in 1972 with early featured roles in John Huston’s classic boxing drama “Fat City” and Richard Fleischer’s intense cop thriller “The New Centurions,” along with a starring role of Doc Holliday in Frank Perry’s 1971 Western “Doc.” Though he never quite rose to marquee stardom, Keach’s character actor skills were called upon regularly by Hollywood, oftentimes playing military authorities in titles ranging from “Up in Smoke” to “Escape from L.A.” to “Truth.” In 1980, he starred in, co-wrote and executive produced the Walter Hill Western “The Long Riders,” alongside his brother James Keach.

Other notable credits for Keach include the lead of “Exorcist” creator William Peter Blatty’s horror oddity “The Ninth Configuration” (1980), the voice of the mysterious villain Phantasm in the classic superhero animated feature “Batman: Mask of the Phantasm” (1993), and the Bakersfield-loving father to George Clooney’s movie star in “Jay Kelly” (2025).

Born June 2, 1941 in Savannah, Ga., Walter Stacy Keach Jr.’s family moved to Pasadena after his drama teacher father signed a day-player contract with Universal. Keach attended University of Calfornia, Berkeley and later studied theater at Yale School of Drama and the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art.

Along with Malogisa, Keach is also survived by his their children, Karolina and Shannon; their grandchildren; their spouses; and his brother, James.

Awards Season will be here before we know it, and there are already a few projects getting early buzz. One of them is the new A24 movie Club Kid, which stars Jordan Firstman, who also wrote and directed the acclaimed dramedy. Club Kid is my favorite movie of the year, largely thanks to its heart and the authentic representation of queer nightlife. I had to ask him about bringing those sequences together, and he got honest about why the club scenes (especially in the darkroom) went so hard.

Club Kid is a new LGBTQ+ movie, and as a gay man myself I was immediately take by how real those club scenes felt. As you can see in the video above, I asked Firstman about how he brought those sequences together, especially the scene where his character Peter has sex with a woman in a club darkroom. He told me:

I got in like a fight with someone because they're like 'Darkrooms like didn't come until like 2019.' And I was like, 'They definitely came in 2016.' I like remember like at least they were popping up in New York, but I remember going to like a sex party in 2015 or 16. But I say like the Berlin-ification of New York, mama, in the movie. But I do feel like, you know, Chris Cruse started this party Spotlight in LA, which was kind of like our first like LA introduction into darkrooms. It was a cool moment for queer people because we like weren't like doing that publicly before really in my generation. So yeah, it was important for me to like show that and show what goes down at the club

For those unfamiliar, darkrooms have a long history in queer history. They're typically pitch black rooms in bars where patrons can engage in anonymous sexual activity. They were shown in the media dating back to Harvey Fierstein's Torch Song Trilogy back in 1988, and Jordan Firstman's movie brings them back to the big screen in a more modern context.

In a drug-fueled haze Peter has sex with a woman early in Club Kid in a darkroom, and that unknowingly gets her pregnant. That's how his son Arlo ends up dropped at his door over a decade later, with the party promoter suddenly forced to become a parent to a child he never knew existed.

There's been a ton of chatter lately about LGBTQ+ movies actually starring queer actors, and Jordan Firstman was able to bring a very real, niche experience to the mainstream as the director, writer, and star of Club Kid. Later in our conversation he spoke more about the way the darkroom scene was shot, telling me:

But I think also showing it in a elegant way, like I really love how that scene is shot. I think it's like very classy. And it's not, it's like, I don't know. It just it's like beautiful, but still it does, a dark room does feel that way.

He's not wrong. The darkroom scene isn't a sexually explicit scene, despite the setting. Instead it uses light in a fascinating way that's immersive, but not overly graphic. The audience sees Peter decide to have sex with a woman at the behest of a guy he's interested in, and it's that union that serves as the catalyst for the movie's primary story.

The authentic way the darkroom is shown, as well as the unique chaos of the nightlife as a whole, instantly brings Club Kid into a specific time and place. The movie shows what the club scene is like for LGBTQ+ folks, warts and all. While it's a world not all moviegoers might understand, the specificity of Firstman's work ends up making the story universal.

Club Kid is in select theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list, and will be getting more screenings as the month goes on. I laughed, I cried, and I loved how real the movie felt as a member of the queer community.

#3514. ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It

The major Hollywood studios tend to shy away from the subject of class warfare because they know they can’t pull them off with a straight face. But young people in this country are increasingly animated by radical leftist ideas like “earning a livable wage” and “being able to buy a home before they die,” and at a certain point the movies will have to meet them where they live. Perhaps that point is now. How else to explain why Jeff Bezos would fund a Robin Hood-esque heist thriller that not only encourages its target demographic to commit armed robberies, but also kinda sorta teaches them how? (No one is going to confuse a David Leitch movie for “The Anarchist Cookbook.”) At a time when internet activists like Hasan Piker have come to occupy more space in the public imagination than Marvel superheroes, selling the masses on fanciful stories about the downward redistribution of wealth might be the billionaire class’ best protection against the threat of it actually happening in real life. It’s a lot more fun than paying a proportional tax rate, at least. Related Stories Fan Edits Are Legal with Moonbeem, Distribution Network Hosts Approved Clips from Filmmakers Want a Full Scholarship to One of Our Film Festival Intensives? IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Video Contest Is Now Live

Of course, the poppy and frenetic “How to Rob a Bank” wouldn’t dare to take aim at massive corporations that widen the wealth gap by destroying small businesses, normalizing exploitative labor practices, and accelerating worldwide environmental collapse. This is very specifically a film about how banks are bad and should be fucked with, an opinion that the founder of Amazon might actually share with the average ticket-buyer.

And it’s not like the director of “Bullet Train” suddenly made a serious call to action that’s poised to inspire a wave of copycat robberies. Shot with all the propulsiveness of “Trainspotting” but almost none of its unbridled lust for life, Leitch’s YouTube-era fairy tale is no more dangerous to America’s power structures than “Verity” or “Project Hail Mary” (to name some of its studio’s other recent titles). Compared to the lawlessness of “Grand Theft Auto VI,” it might as well be the “Ocarina of Time” remake “Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.” Still, its cast is hot, its heart is in the right place, and while the Amazon Punk of it all has a tendency to make its fantasy seem more like a sale, there’s something indivisibly real and relatable to the premise of a heist movie whose characters feel like they have to steal the most basic principles of the life they were promised.

Ryan (Nicolas Hoult, channeling a very effective smidgeon of the destructive intensity that made him so terrifying in “The Order”) isn’t trying to get rich or spark a revolution, he and his accomplices just want a fair shot at the same thing that previous generations have been afforded as part of the American contract: The chance to support his family, and maybe a fair shot at revenge against the people and/or system who denied him that opportunity. In most respects, that shot has never been more unfair than it is now, but the internet — which has become the most powerful system for socioeconomic oppression this side of sharecropping — has turned attention into a currency more valuable than cash, and young people are still inventing new ways to harness those riches for themselves.

For Ryan, that process starts with stealing money the old-fashioned way, as he and his four-person crew film themselves knocking off every bank in Pittsburgh (their identities protected by giant animal masks). But the cash seems to be less important than the content that it buys them, as the gang’s real passion is reserved for the splashy, hi-octane YouTube tutorials that Hugo (an upbeat Rhenzy Feliz) cuts together and posts online after each job. “You know what’s more powerful than a gun?,” Ryan says. “An audience.” That’s us! We rule.

What the animal brigade plans to use that audience for is a mystery for most of the movie, but the big reveal is satisfying enough so long as you’re willing to accept your hard-edged socioeconomic commentary with a side of “The Thomas Crown Affair”-flavored silliness. Slapped with titles like “Lowkey Best Heist Ever,” the videos proselytize against complacency, as Ryan — still disguised as “The Wolf,” despite the fact that Hoult’s blond dye job makes his blue eyes pop like crazy — informs the masses that the odds of earning six figures in this economy are less than half the odds of pulling off an armed robbery. Sure, pulling something off isn’t the same thing as getting away with it, but who has time to quibble when they’re being fucked to death by the one percent?

And every member of Ryan’s crew has been done rather dirty. Iraq War vet Vince (an affectingly subdued Pete Davidson as the resident gun expert) has learned the hard way that “a country you fight for may not fight for you,” while Ryan shares a tragic backstory with his partner and getaway driver Emi (a wildly underused Anna Sawai) that only comes out after Mark Bianculli’s script pulls the ripcord on its propulsive first half and settles into its characters’ flimsiness during the comparatively leaden stretch that follows. We never learn anything about how the crew found each other, and unlike in the “Fast & Furious” saga, that familial energy fails to galvanize into something bigger than the sum of its parts.

Still, Hoult could get the job done by channeling even a smidgeon of the destructive intensity that he brought to “The Order,” and the religious fervor he instills in Ryan’s mission is enough to keep “How to Rob a Bank” moving forward even when the film is just spinning its wheels. Or, as the case might be, when the film pivots to a parallel track that never meaningfully overlaps with the main plot.

It’s hard to be mad at this movie for casting John C. Reilly as the Al Pacino in an eat the rich Gen-Z “Heat” (not when he gets to bark things like “Put some fucking pepper on it!” at his subordinates), or for pairing him with Zoë Kravitz as a grungy hacker who’s roped into the case in exchange for her freedom (and use of her glossed-over surveillance software), but the mild comedy of their mismatched vibe never compensates for how disconnected they both are from the main plot. Whatever inter-generational friction is gained — and then smoothed over — between them in a movie that makes bizarrely little attempt to weave them into Ryan’s tale. For all of its hashtag agitprop, “How to Rob a Bank” isn’t nearly high-minded enough to justify putting ideas before its plot, and it’s an enormous self-own that Kravitz never so much as interacts with the Hoult side of things.

Be that as it may, Leitch leans into the movie’s digital revolution as hard as circumstances allow, and what his film sometimes lacks in detail or precision it strives to compensate for with smiling verve and some bone-crunching action (there isn’t enough physical violence for this to stack up to the rest of 87North Productions’ body of work, but it’s nice that Leitch shoehorns a few solid brawls into the mix just because he can). Not since “The Perks of Being a Wallflower” has a studio movie gotten so much out of Pittsburgh, and the overbroad political messaging of “How to Rob a Bank” is sharpened by its rich sense of place, and specifically the way its locations reflect the story’s larger collision between the old world and the new.

That temporal confusion is well-served by a film that resolves as more of a fairy tale than anything else — a heist movie full of talking animals, and one that hinges on YouTube as a modern form of spellcasting. It’s all just real enough to suggest that we have the power to make it realer.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “How to Rob a Bank” in theaters on Friday, November 13.
