#3513. How To Rob A Bank Producer Explains How The Movie Reinvents The Heist Genre [Exclusive]

It's easy for novices to make the mistake that if you've seen one heist film, you've seen them all. As the genre junkies among us know, it takes a little more effort than most to make these sorts of movies stand out from the crowd. Steven Soderbergh found lightning in a bottle with his "Ocean's Eleven" remake in 2001, while Christopher Nolan added a mind-bending spin with "Inception" less than 10 years later. Classic cinema is rife with examples of how to craft memorable heist movies, from Michael Mann's "Thief" to Sidney Lumet's "Dog Day Afternoon" to Stanley Kubrick's "The Killing."

So when David Leitch came across writer Mark Bianculli's script for "How to Rob a Bank" and chose this as his next directorial effort after "The Fall Guy," it quickly became apparent how this could become a heist flick like nothing we've ever seen before. As the title implies, the unconventional heroes of this story are a group of social media influencers who've become viral sensations — not just for pulling off bank robberies like they were born to do it, but for creating a YouTube channel teaching others how to stick it to the man and perform heists of their own.

Not long ago, I had the chance to talk to the creative team of Leitch and "Violent Night" producer Kelly McCormick (who happens to be Leitch's longtime producing partner at 87North, as well as his wife) during the "How to Rob a Bank" press junket about what drew them to the script. According to McCormick:

"In this case, it's like, 'How do you turn a heist movie on its head — not your daddy's heist movie?' And it's the [idea of] thieves hiding in plain sight, as opposed to not wanting to be seen."

It's a staple of practically every heist story ever told, from "The Italian Job" to "Heat" and everything in between: In order to pull off the perfect caper, our protagonists must cover their tracks, don some clever disguises to maintain a low profile, and escape the scene of the crime without anyone being the wiser. It's definitely not advised for robbers to film themselves while on a job, edit and upload those tutorials to YouTube, and revel in the viral fame that comes with being the most well-known crew the internet has ever seen. It's all about avoiding detection — not seeking it out.

But "How to Rob a Bank" isn't exactly interested in the conventional approach. With Nicholas Hoult's Ryan as the ringleader, this motley group of Robin Hood-like revolutionaries have figured out how to successfully weaponize simmering anti-capitalist sentiments among a generation fed up with living under a broken system. They just happen to do so with a GoPro strapped to their masks and a knack for live-streaming their crimes to an eager audience. According to director David Leitch, this was the main appeal behind taking the screenplay by Mark Bianculli and bringing it to life:

"That's what we saw in it and that's why we really wanted to do this material. It had all of those elements where you could create something fun, but yet also with a bigger message. That was one of the things we haven't gotten to do: maybe have something that has a little bit more of a commentary. There's usually a moral tale [in heist movies], but this has a little bit of ... it's asking you big questions about where we are in the world right now."

Where studios like A24 and Blumhouse deserve credit for establishing themselves as high-minded horror destinations, 87North has cornered the market with the most exciting action films. Upon seeing David Leitch's name attached to any given film, audiences can safely expect more visceral set pieces, an emphasis on practical effects, and a certain, undefinable je ne sais quoi when it comes to mixing and matching genres. After "Atomic Blonde," "Deadpool 2," and "Bullet Train," "How to Rob a Bank" seamlessly fits into Leitch's ongoing interests.

Or, as Kelly McCormick aptly puts it in our conversation, "I believe one of David's pillars is that he always is doing a little bit something different with the genre every time out, and wants to and enjoys changing genres and the subgenres within action and really wanting to tell a lot of different tales." It's one thing to identify that branding, however, and another to actually put it into action. As she went on to explain:

"So then, how can you make that Leitchian? How can you make that atonal? And ['How to Rob a Bank'] had all the things, with regards to the drama versus the social media content and all those kinds of aspects. And then, I think the extra unique part is being able to have a bigger message, more front-and-center than what we do a lot of times out with our commercial propositions."

That "bigger message" may hit particularly hard at a time when working-class struggles remain at the forefront of the national conversation as the rich only get richer. "How to Rob a Bank" hits theaters on November 13, 2026.

#3512. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: up to 15 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks when I tested it. The company says some users are finding the latest software update extends battery a bit further.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

Updated 11/10/2026 to note that the Ultrahuman Ring Pro's stated battery life is up to 15 days, not 8-10 days.

#3511. Diablo Meets Hades in New Conan the Barbarian Game

Robert E. Howard's fantasy hero stars in a new 'sword & sorcery meets cosmic horror' roguelike

Conan the Barbarian has managed to remain relevant in pop culture for more than 90 years, thanks to literature, film, and video games. In 2028, Conan will return in a new adventure that combines the fantasy franchise's sword-and-sworcery themes with a dash of cosmic horror.

Developer Games Farm announced Conan: The Black Pyramid on Wednesday, revealing a reality-warping action roguelike that will see Conan aligned with other characters created by author Robert E. Howard, including pulp heroes Solomon Kane and Dark Agnes.

According to an announcement from Games Farm, Conan, Solomon Kane, Dark Agnes, and two other unannounced heroes "wake up inside the Black Pyramid, a labyrinth that ignores the rules of space and time and changes with every descent." Conan: The Black Pyramid is an action-RPG roguelike, and each run through the pyramid promises to get players closer to discovering who summoned them across time... and why.

Conan: The Black Pyramid promises a mix of melee, swordplay, magic, and gunplay. The game will feature solo and two-player cooperative play.

"We’re thrilled to bring a legendary hero like Conan back to the modern gaming world," said Peter Nagy, CEO of Games Farm, in a statement. "Robert E. Howard’s stories mean a lot to us, as they do to generations of readers, and we’re approaching them with all the care and respect they deserve. We want players to step into the world they’ve imagined while reading those stories, in all its savage and strange glory."

"Eldritch horrors, reality-warping sorcery, ancient beings from other worlds, these lesser-known aspects are some of the coolest parts of Conan, and players will finally get to experience them," added Marcos Cronander, president of Heroic Signatures, which licenses the Conan IP. "Conan and Robert E. Howard's many other mighty characters are in good hands with the Games Farm and we are excited for players to get their hands on them and see how cool they all really are."

Howard is perhaps best known for his sword and sorcery works that starred characters such as Conan, Kull, Solomon Kane, and Bran Mak Morn. But the author worked in a variety of genres, including detective stories, horror, and Westerns — as well as blends of those genres. Conan: The Black Pyramid could bring together a wild and interesting mix of Howard's heroes and weirdos in playable form for the first time.

Conan: The Black Pyramid is slated for release on Windows PC via Steam — where the game's available to wishlist — in 2027. Console versions are expected to follow the game's PC release.

Arnold Schwarzenegger announced earlier this year that he's returning to the role of Conan in King Conan, which he says will be written and directed by Christopher McQuarrie, who made the last four Mission: Impossible films. According to Schwarzenegger's comments, the project is in development at Disney's 20th Century Studios arm.

Genndy Tartakovsky has been pitching the project since 2008

#3510. How To Watch Avengers Endgame: Encore At Home

What if you could take the same movie that swept up the entire globe in hype and watch it all over again ... but, this time, with a little extra #brandsynergy? That was the (admittedly cynical) gimmick behind "Avengers Endgame: Encore," the buzzy re-release that ruled the box office again earlier this year and will no doubt do so on the streaming charts in the days and weeks ahead. The blockbuster, at one time considered the capstone to the grand Marvel Cinematic Universe experiment, now comes with a whopping four minutes of new footage meant to tie things together with the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday." That includes a noticeably altered ending and new post-credits scenes, all of which will serve as a bridge to the multiverse-focused chaos to come.

That means you can expect to get your Infinity Vision on (no, we're still not quite sure what that means) with just a snap of your fingers, now with added scenes and new color grading.

Party like it's 2019, folks, because everything old is (slightly) new again. Back then, we had no inkling of a certain novel virus making its way across the globe, we had not yet had the privilege of seeing Palpatine somehow return in "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker," and we certainly didn't think the MCU could ever top its grand finale of Earth's Mightiest Heroes assembling against the Mad Titan Thanos. Less than a decade later, Marvel Studios is hoping to keep the hype train going on the road to "Doomsday" with "Avengers Endgame: Encore."

In short, it's a good time to be a Disney fan ... and a Disney stockholder, for that matter. For those looking for an excuse to revel in some nostalgia, "Endgame: Encore" fits the bill. "Avengers: Doomsday" will finally arrive in theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3509. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3508. Fan Edits Are Legal with Moonbeem, Distribution Network Hosts Approved Clips from Filmmakers

Film lovers can make and post their fan edits legally thanks to Moonbeem, a distribution network for independent film. Fan edits are among the most-watched film content on social media, and nearly all of them are made from footage whose rights nobody cleared. But on Moonbeem, the rights holder decides which scenes to open and creators cut from those scenes. Moreover, every fan edit points viewers back to where the film can be rented, bought, or watched. Fan edits made this way have been viewed more than 190 million times across the network.

The company has unveiled its free panel for Adobe Premiere Pro, which is where the approved scenes will be available. The announcement comes during Adobe MAX, the tech company’s annual conference in Miami Beach, Florida. The company believes it’s one of the first times fans can cut real scenes from released films, with the rights holders’ permission, in the editing software they already use. Related Stories Want a Full Scholarship to One of Our Film Festival Intensives? IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Video Contest Is Now Live Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

With the panel, an editor picks a scene the filmmaker has cleared to use, pulls it onto the timeline, cuts, exports, and posts. The edit links back to the film, and approved edits can earn on funded campaigns. The panel is built on UXP and is live on Adobe Exchange.

Campaigns include “Erupcja,” released by 1-2 Special, whose fan edits have passed 4.6 million views,and “Bob Trevino Likes It,” from Roadside Attractions, at 5.6 million. Distributors on Moonbeem alsoinclude Magnolia Pictures, Oscilloscope Laboratories, and Antenna Releasing. The network isexpanding its list of partners globally.

“Every fan edit on Moonbeem exists because the film’s owner wanted it to,” said Dan Sickles, co-founder and CEO of Moonbeem and the director of the films “Dina” and “Mala Mala.” “Editors get real scenes inside the tool they already use, filmmakers get an audience sharing their stories, and we get to see what they make.”

The panel arrives as independent filmmakers look for a new home to host their work. Vimeo On Demand has been slowly phased out and will close on November 20. Moonbeem says it offers a “free migration bridge” that moves a seller’s films, prices and artwork without requiring a new upload. Past buyers will keep the films they paid for. Moonbeem said dozens of storefronts carrying over 350 films have moved so far.Moonbeem was incubated through the Sundance Institute’s Catalyst program and is based in Brooklyn.

#3507. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3506. One Of 2025's Biggest TV Shows Is Now A Box Office Success As Well

One of the biggest breakout TV shows of 2025 has now found success at the box office. The "Heated Rivalry" Season 1 finale ended last year with a barnburner and the show's popularity has only continued to grow since then. While fans eagerly await Season 2, Regal Cinemas partnered with HBO Max and Crave to bring the first season to theaters. Fans turned up to see Shane and Ilya on the silver screen.

As "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office with a $30.5 million opening, much further down on the weekend's chart, "Heated Rivalry" pulled in a respectable $1.4 million on just over 1,000 screens, making for a solid $1,409 per-screen average. That's certainly not bad for a show that anyone could stream right now from the comfort of home with the price of a subscription they likely already pay for. But this speaks to the rabid fanbase that has developed around the romantic hockey show.

"Heated Rivalry" focuses on two rival hockey stars at the top of their game who develop feelings for each other, complicating their careers and the sport's expectations. It's based on the book series by Rachel Reid. Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie lead the cast as Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, respectively.

To say that the show took off in a way that surprised people would be a bit of an understatement. It dominated HBO Max's charts and became a downright cultural sensation. So much so that a former NHL player hopes "Heated Rivalry" can change pro hockey culture. It made a real impact.

For Regal, Crave, and all involved, the millions the show makes in its theatrical release is a cherry on top of the sundae. Regal is charging $9.99 for two episode blocks of the series, which fans can watch in order if they choose to go three times to watch all six episodes.

This is just the latest example of an already successful TV show finding success on the big screen. Netflix's "Stranger Things" finale was a huge hit for theaters even if it didn't impact the box office, as those tickets were for "concessions vouchers" and not actual tickets. But lots of people still turned up nonetheless. "Doctor Who" has also had multiple theatrical events for various episodes over the years, sticking in the sci-fi realm.

More recently, an unlikely savior emerged at the box office in 2024, with two very different shows doing meaningful business. "Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba — To the Hashira Training," which is just several episodes of the TV show fashioned into a feature, helped establish anime as a true, blue way to sell a lot of tickets. At the same time, the faith-based series "The Chosen" was finding lots of success by screening episodes in theaters. All together, those episodes have grossed more than $100 million worldwide.

Not every show is a good fit for this sort of thing but the right show at the right time can certainly benefit from catering to more hardcore fans. Meanwhile, "Heated Rivalry" Season 2 is in the works, but that's just the tip of the iceberg. Deadline recently reported that Season 3 is also being filmed, along with a movie. So there's much for fans to look forward to.

#3505. Marvel Makes VisionQuest’s First Episode Free To Stream

It joins the first few episodes of WandaVision on YouTube

VisionQuest came to an end this week, putting a bow on one of Marvel's best Disney Plus shows ahead of the Marvel Cinematic Universe's next blockbuster film, December's Avengers: Doomsday. If you're curious about the show, but don't have a Disney Plus subscription (and after its recent price hikes, who can blame you), Marvel and Disney have made the first episode of VisionQuest free to watch on YouTube.

VisionQuest concludes the story of Wanda Maximoff and Vision that was first started in 2021's WandaVision, the MCU's first foray into streaming TV. (That show's first three episodes were uploaded to YouTube ahead of VisionQuest's premiere last month.) Together with Agatha All Along, the shows make an interconnected trilogy. VisionQuest builds off storylines from both shows, so you should watch them first lest VisionQuest spoil the previous series.

The resurrected Vision from WandaVision tries to sort out just who he is in VisionQuest. He'll work through that question with other AI characters at his side, like FRIDAY (Orla Brady) and Ultron (James Spader), who seemingly perished at the end of Avengers: Age of Ultron. But, these are comics characters we're talking about, and only Uncle Ben will remain dead forever. (Probably. Maybe.)

Like WandaVision and Agatha All Along before it, VisionQuest has received critical acclaim. "Thanks to some clever, non-linear storytelling, a handful of unpredictable twists, and a slew of standout performances — Paul Bettany puts on an absolute masterclass as Vision, but everyone here is pulling their weight — Marvel's streaming era gets the sendoff that it needs, and the one fans deserve," Polygon's Jake Kleinman wrote in his VisionQuest review.

All eight episodes of VisionQuest are now streaming on Disney Plus. Like so many MCU projects before it, VisionQuest ends with a major tease of what's coming up next.

#3504. Jeremy O. Harris EPs ‘American Theater,’ About a Canceled MAGA Theater Director’s Bizarre Attempted Comeback — Watch the Trailer

Can a conservative “canceled” theater director rise from the ashes of his own ruination — and in this climate? That’s one of the questions top of mind for filmmakers Nicholas Clark and Dylan Frederick, whose provocative, Christopher Guest-style nonfiction film “American Theater” (except it’s a docu-, not mockumentary) is rolling out in select theaters now. A Slamdance Grand Jury Prize winner for documentary in 2025, the film is also executive-produced by Jeremy O. Harris.

“American Theater” follows Brian Clowdus — openly gay, conservative, and formerly of the Serenbe Playhouse in Georgia, who was taken down in 2019 over allegations of racism, misconduct, unsafe working conditions, and a gamut of other accusations. Clark and Frederick follow Clowdus, now a MAGA Republican, and a troupe of other conservative actors to an abandoned cabin in middle-of-nowhere Georgia where Clowdus plots the ultimate revenge: a community musical theater retelling of, of course, the 1692 Salem witch trials, riffing on Arthur Miller’s “The Crucible” (which, published in 1953, isn’t yet in the public domain). Related Stories Fan Edits Are Legal with Moonbeem, Distribution Network Hosts Approved Clips from Filmmakers ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It

“This film was about a really fucked-up figure and a person with really fucked-up politics,” Harris told IndieWire over the phone from Copenhagen, where the Tony nominee is rehearsing a new play. “When you have unwelcoming and fucked-up politics, or a person who has unwelcoming, fucked-up politics at the center of the art you’re making, it can feel like potentially you’re endorsing their politics or celebrating them, especially because we don’t live in times that are deeply discursive or critical. At least having my name in the headline should be an invitation to certain people that maybe would’ve been like, ‘I’m not watching that,’ that maybe this is something for them.”

In taking on someone who was once a formidable presence in the Southern regional theater space, Harris said the filmmakers saw “this opportunity to embed themselves in the company for his comeback show. They realized there was a chance to look at the type of fringe character that utilized MAGA for the grifting machine that it is. MAGA is a magnet for a lot of displaced people, and theater has so many displaced people. Even thinking about the fact that one of the most famous people that stormed the Capitol was in the regional production of ‘Jesus Christ Superstar’ meant that there were ways in which the theater community wasn’t looking at some of the foxes among the lambs in our own community. This gave them the opportunity to be those foxes, or not even foxes, but to be flies on the wall of this maker who was exploiting a lot of displaced people.”

A recent Cobble Hill Cinemas screening of “American Theater” was moderated by journalist Ludwig Hurtado. Next up, the film will be available to rent on the Letterboxd Video Store, so locally driven screenings also aim to bring audiences to that platform.

“One of the things that’s very sad to me is that amongst the distributors, the ones that one would think have the most bandwidth and power to really uplift these microbudget filmmakers who are truly keeping the torch burning for that independent American brio that put American independent cinema on the map and right next to so many other stalwarts of world cinema, a lot of them are being, I think, more cautious about who they’re distributing,” Harris said. “Distribution costs are so large right now that I think that they don’t really know what to do with movies so small. And so Letterboxd has become this really great outlet because there’s such a vibrant community there who are just excited to see films and excited to learn that filmmakers who maybe are in circumstances similar to their own as movie watchers are making films.”

In a separate statement, Frederick said, “The film takes place in 2021, when Trump was facing the possibility of spending the rest of his life in prison, his political future was uncertain, and conservatives were batching DeSantis ‘24 tank tops. Democrats just had the best night of their lives in the midterms, and MAGA folks may find themselves at a low point, but it’s useful to remember that we’ve actually been here before.”

Clark added, “There was a moment when many people assumed the Trump era had come to an end. ‘American Theater’ tells a story of the Trump supporters during that time who were dedicated to figuring out what would come next. In this instance, their idea was an allegorical cancel culture musical about the Salem witch trials. It did not go anywhere near as planned, and our movie tells that story. But ultimately, everything that has happened to us as a nation ever since has only recontextualized what we saw within this brief moment in time.”

#3503. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Finally Solves A Major Lord Of The Rings Lore Mystery

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching the Season 3 premiere episodes for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

"The Rings of Power" Season 3 is here, and it finally feels like the series we were promised from the start (i.e. the one that showrunners J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay wanted to make all along). At this point, the introductions are done and the show's characters, lore, and locations have all been established. Most importantly, the very silly mysteries around the identity of certain characters all disappear in the first four episodes of Season 3. Because of this, we now know that Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) are a big part of the story, that the insufferable kid Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin) is actually a Ringwraith, and the truth about Ciarán Hinds' Dark Wizard.

As you might recall, the reveal that Weyman's "The Stranger" is actually Gandalf didn't mean all that much in Season 2, given how Gandalf-coded the character was from the get-go. By comparison, the Dark Wizard has been quite Saruman-coded from the start, be it the color of his beard or the way he calls Gandalf an old friend. Yet, the notion of him being Saruman has never made much sense, given how blatantly evil he is. After all, it's meant to be a huge shock when Saruman aligns with Sauron in "The Lord of the Rings," so the idea that he was known as the "Dark Wizard" for centuries would seem to undermine that.

Thankfully, "The Rings of Power" has now confirmed that the Dark Wizard is really Pallando the Blue Wizard, not Saruman.

While Sauron is very much the focus of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 (something that's been praised in early reactions to the show's latest batch of episodes), Pallando is an important part of the story. Except, Pallando doesn't exactly ally himself with Sauron out of greed, ambition, or evil the way that Saruman does in "The Lord of the Rings" (nor does he seem all that afraid of the Dark Lord). Instead, he's already murdered his fellow Blue Wizard and Istar companion Alatar prior to his first appearance on the series.

Pallando's betrayal, it turns out, was an act so malevolent that it turned the once-green realm of Rhûn into a desolated wasteland. The wizard isn't entirely repentant by the time "The Rings of Power" takes place, but he does acknowledge that it's his fault the region has turned to desert, and he seeks specifically to fix it. Hence, his submission to Sauron and the power of Mordor represents a desperate last attempt at correcting his greatest mistake.

All we know from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material is that the Blue Wizards failed their mission and their fates are unknown when "The Lord of the Rings" begins (although they're presumed dead). In other words, "The Rings of Power" can resolve a major "Lord of the Rings" mystery by revealing what ultimately became of Pallando in particular. This should also make Gandalf's mission in Season 3 all the more interesting, as he might yet have a chance at saving the Blue Wizard. Either way, there's much we've yet to learn about the character.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is currently streaming on Prime Video.

2027 brings the iPhone’s 20th anniversary, and all signs indicate Apple has something special planned. Similar to the debut of iPhone X for the 10th anniversary in 2017, Apple may introduce a bold new iPhone design next year.

New iPhone Pro models are rumored to get quad-curved displays that wrap around the edges for a visually bezel-free appearance. Screen size is expected to increase too.

Now today, a new post from leaker Instant Digital on Weibo says this new design will also come with a loss.

I feel like I’m the only one here, but I like the camera control button. Yes, I don’t use it for the actual camera control features, but to open up the camera quickly from any screen, and still practically use the phone one-handed to snap a picture quickly (for right handed people), is really convenient. It frees up the two app options on the lock screen and it allows the action button to be used for something else.

The leaker says the Action button’s functionality won’t be lost altogether, though. Instead, he says Camera Control will continue to launch the Camera app with a standard press, but a long-press will offer Action button-like functionality.

When iPhone Duo dropped the Action button, some users expressed disappointment that the button’s versatility was lost. Our own Chance Miller, for example, said he would gladly give up Camera Control to keep the Action button.

It sounds like Apple plans to integrate the two, a pattern that will likely apply to the next-generation iPhone Duo and other future models too.

Maybe you’re the kind of person who thinks about the first 10 minutes of “Up” from time to time, and wishes there was a film out there that would emotionally break you like that again. Maybe you long for less-processed-looking Minionesque animation and more painterly, natural worlds that find as much beauty in negative space as in color. Maybe it’s been a minute since “Flow,” and you would like a protagonist to hang out with another very good animated dog.

If your answer to any of the above is “yes,” then IndieWire has good news for you. The Annecy and Cannes Un Certain Regard Special Jury Prize-winning film “Iron Boy” is coming to U.S. theaters for a one-week awards-qualifying run in December, then launching in select cities on January 22, 2027. Writer/director Louis Clichy is a veteran of Pixar’s most undefeated run of films, including “Wall-E” and “Up,” as well as two fantastical “Asterix” adventures in France. With “Iron Boy,” he shows how big a seemingly small story can feel. Related Stories Kate Berlant and John Early to Host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards Jeremy O. Harris EPs ‘American Theater,’ About a Canceled MAGA Theater Director’s Bizarre Attempted Comeback — Watch the Trailer

Young farmboy Christophe starts tilting his head unintentionally, which eventually leads to a scoliosis diagnosis and an iron corset he has to wear everywhere. But, of course, his spine is far from the only thing out of alignment in Christophe’s life — straightening those emotions and ambitions out, discovering who he wants to be, is the real journey. But it’s one that occasionally turns its entire watercolor world sideways like the most beautiful magical realist snowglobe you’ve ever seen.

It’s one that, as Rafael Motomayor said in IndieWire’s review, “makes ‘Iron Boy’ stand out even amongst European animated films. The film employs mostly non-professional voice actors, including Clinchy’s own son (who plays Christophe), and the director would often record the lines on location, to give the performances a less constructed sound than if they were done in the clear confines of a studio. It makes the story feel quasi-documentary in its approach, an intimate and deeply personal story of a boy searching for more than what life has offered him, restrained by a physical affliction that nevertheless allows him to live an extraordinary life.”

#3498. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3's Two Big Character Deaths Explained

The land of Mordor is where the shadows lie, and this article is where major spoilers lie. Read no further if you haven't watched the Season 3 premiere episodes of "The Rings of Power."

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" has one thing in common with the TV phenomenon that was "Game of Thrones" — they're both exercises in enduring misery. After all, the show is all about watching stupid sexy Sauron (Charlie Vickers) make everyone in Middle-earth suffer season after season. And sure, the series is willing to kill beloved characters, but it really excels at killing hordes of people and turning entire kingdoms into desolated volcanic wastelands where the sun never shines.

Things are even worse at the start of Season 3, between Sauron trying to forge the One Ring, Mordor's Ringwraiths spreading across Middle-earth, and a Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) ruling Rhûn. Elsewhere, when it comes to the civil war plaguing Númenor, the realm's only hope is Eärien (Ema Horvath), who was responsible for the King's Men usurping the Númenórean throne in the first place. In fact, Eärien is an unexpected main character early in Season 3, acting as a faithful servant and the head torturer for the usurper Ar-Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) while at the same time operating as a double agent for her brother Isildur (Maxim Baldry) and father Elendil (Lloyd Owen) as they try to restore Queen Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) to power.

Unsurprisingly, things don't go well, as "The Rings of Power" Season 3 kills off two original characters made for the show in its first four episodes. First, Eärien dies in the second episode, followed by the wood elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) being tragically betrayed and murdered in Episode 4.

Let's start with Eärien. The character has always felt out of place on "The Rings of Power," with her scenes slowing down the pace and taking away from other, better storylines. Frustratingly, the show simply doesn't have time to cover all the ground it wants to, with the limited number of episodes per season forcing it to jump around too quickly. That being said, Eärien aiding the rise of the King's Men in the secluded and isolated island of Númenor due to her mistakenly believing that following Queen Míriel had gotten Isildur killed was interesting, as was her becoming a double agent once she learned the truth.

Unfortunately, Eärien's double age storyline — her best so far — doesn't last long. By Episode 2, she's already been discovered. So, rather than be subjected to torture and forced to become truly loyal to the King's Men, she dies by suicide by jumping off a balcony.

Likewise, when he was first introduced, Arondir was a great character. Sure, he didn't actually do much, with much of his screen time being dedicated to an attempt at a romance between him and the now-deceased Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi). And yet, Ismael Cruz Córdova has always played his role with great gusto, giving Arondir a strong personality that makes him feel like more than just a Legolas knock-off. But that just makes his departure all the more upsetting.

Indeed, Arondir gets little more to do in Season 3 than worry about Bronwyn's annoying son Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin). This all leads to a confrontation in Episode 4 when Sauron orders Theo — now a Ringwraith — to murder the elf. A tragic end, sure, but with little buildup.

With Arondir and Eären's deaths, "The Rings of Power" is quickly getting rid of its original characters. After all, the show had already killed off one of its best brand-new additions in Adar (Sam Hazeldine and Joseph Mawle), while the Harfoots that were so essential in Seasons 1 and 2 are nowhere to be found in Season 3 so far. Granted, Theo's still around, but he's likely to be killed soon as well (due to that whole being a Ringwraith thing). That just leaves Kemen (Leon Wadham), the tiring nepo baby at the center of the Númenor story.

Instead, it's clear "The Rings of Power" is currently more focused on bringing in previously missing characters from J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, like Isildur's brother Anárion (Andrew Richardson) and Middle-earth's own Odysseus, i.e. Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), who's married to Morfydd Clark's elfish warrior Galadriel. It makes sense for the show's writers to be doing this right now, too, as we're getting closer and closer to the end of the series' reported five-season plan. But that means "The Rings of Power" will also have less and less time to explore any of its original characters from this point on.

Another problem is the show's condensed timeline, as "The Rings of Power" is trying to tell a story that spans thousands of years in Tolkien's literature over a much, much shorter period. That means we still have a lot of major "Lord of the Rings"-related developments to get through, be it Elendil and his sons founding the kingdom of Gondor or Celeborn creating Lothlórien with Galadriel. Will all that and more to cover, there's just no more room for the likes of Arondir the wood elf.

#3496. All Bomb Bag upgrade locations in Ocarina of Time

You can upgrade your Bomb Bag in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, allowing you to carry more bombs and make more enemies explode. While not required to beat the game, if you want to be able to fling bombs freely, you should definitely upgrade your Bomb Bags and max out their capacity.

Below, we explain where to find both Bomb Bag upgrades in the Ocarina of Time remake.

After unlocking the Bomb Bag in Dodongo Cavern, you'll be able to hold 20 bombs off the bat. You can upgrade the bag twice to hold 10 extra bombs each, giving you a final total of 40 bombs.

The first Bomb Bag upgrade is in Goron City and the second is in Hyrule Castle Town in the famous Bombchu Bowling Alley. That being said, you can access both of these upgrades pretty early.

Both of these upgrades can only be obtained by young Link.

This is likely the first place you'll find a Bomb Bag upgrade.

In Goron City, there's a Goron on one of the middle floors rolling around. In the northeast area of the town, there's a sign that says, "If you can stop my wild rolling here, you might just get something great!" When you see the rolling Goron turn the corner, place a bomb down in the middle of the pathway. He'll hit it and blow up. Talk to him and he'll give you a Bomb Bag upgrade.

This is likely the second place you'll go to upgrade your bombs.

The Bombchu Bowling Alley is in Hyrule Castle Town, to the west of the fountain. It only opens for business after you clear Dodongo Cavern. It's open both during the day and nighttime.

The Bombchu Bowling Alley Attendant will offer her minigame in exchange for 10 rupees. Take her up on her deal, and then place the bombchus so that they hit the yellow target. After you beat the minigame once, you'll permanently unlock bombchus for your use. You'll need to play and beat the game a second time to get a Bomb Bag upgrade. During the second playthrough, the rules will be the same, but there'll be little wooden Cuccos running back and forth to try to block your bombs. You can also play a third time for a Piece of Heart.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, ahead of Black Friday, it’s down to $179 from $269, which price trackers show is the lowest it’s ever been.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. It’s compact enough to clip onto a backpack using its built-in nylon strap, and tough enough to handle getting knocked around, and sealed against dust and full water submersion with an IP67 rating. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. On the connectivity side, there’s Bluetooth 5.4 with AAC and AptX Adaptive support, as well as the ability to keep two devices paired for smoother switching. What you don’t get is a microphone, an aux port, or any voice assistant support, which is worth considering if you prefer wired options or use speakers for calls.

As for its sound profile, it leans into mid- and high-bass, which gives electronic and pop tracks a lively pulse, though at higher volumes, you may notice some compression (which is common in speakers this size). It also doesn’t reach into true low-bass territory, so anyone who wants thumping sub-bass may not get it here, but the punch it does deliver feels clean for its size, notes this PCMag review. And while you won't get the width and separation of a stereo mix since the SoundLink Plus plays audio in mono, its directivity is good—meaning its sound remains clear from different listening positions, so you don't have to sit directly in front of it to get a good experience.

#3493. iOS 27.2 adds three new ways to customize your iPhone

iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization.

Inside Settings ⇾ Siri there’s a new ‘Excluded Apps’ section in iOS 27.2. This makes it easier than ever to remove certain apps from being accessible to Siri, Search, and more. Apple says:

Apps added to the list below will be excluded from Siri, Search, and suggestions.

iOS 27.2 adds a new Messages feature called Suggestions that I’m a big fan of. When relevant content is detected in a conversation, you might see a Suggestion appear underneath a message. For example, if a friend asks you to do them a favor, you might see “Add to Reminders” below the message.

By default there are five supported categories of Suggestions:

You can fully customize these to your own preferences and needs. Just go to Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions to disable whichever Suggestions you don’t want to see.

Historically, Apple TV has only ever supported user profiles on tvOS. It’s an odd limitation considering every other streaming service offers profiles across platforms.

But finally with iOS 27.2, profiles are now available on iPhone too, letting you customize the content in the Apple TV app based on who’s watching.

Choosing a profile not only gives you personalized recommendations from Apple TV, it also lets you keep the ‘Continue Watching’ queue separate for each person. And if you’re setting up a profile for a child, you can set content restrictions too.

#3492. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3491. The Best Ways For Star Trek Fans To Play Magic's New Set: A Guide For Beginner Players

When I sat down at my friendly local game store to participate in a pre-release drafting event for Magic: The Gathering's new "Star Trek" set, several players saw the Enterprise tattoo on my forearm and asked me the same question. If a longtime Magic player wanted to sample "Star Trek," what was the best place for them to start?

Ironically, I was there to ask the Mirror Universe version of that same question: If a longtime "Star Trek" fan wanted to sample the new Magic set, what's the best place for them to start?

I am new to Magic, having only picked up the game a few months ago to prime myself for the new "Trek" release. And one thing Magic and "Star Trek" have in common is that they're both absolutely daunting at first blush. One is a collectible card game with over 30 years of history and dozens of ways to play. The other is a sci-fi universe with nearly 1,000 episodes of television and 13 movies, with dozens of possible entry points.

I can answer one question immediately. "Trek" newbies should start with "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," with its glossy production values and modern streaming sensibilities, before backtracking and sampling the various other shows and finding the one that connects with their tastes. (This is a sometimes controversial opinion, but I stick by it.)

But the other question involved some legwork, a lot of time spent at a gaming table, a great deal more time sorting through cards, and even a question proposed to the lead designers of the set itself. So, what is the best way for a "Star Trek" fan to sample the new Magic: The Gathering set? Here's what I learned.

One thing I will not do here is explain the rules of Magic: The Gathering, which are intuitive and easy to learn, but challenging to master. There are countless online resources to learn before you try anything I recommend below. I'm writing this piece under the assumption you intend to seek those out on your own.

The best way to truly dive in headfirst is to visit your local gaming shop and participate in a sealed or drafting event. Naturally, this is dependent on your location and whether your local gaming shop is an inviting and safe space (shout out to Mothership Games in Austin, Texas for playing host to my first sealed event). If such a place exists for you, check the calendar and see what's on offer. The good news is that the "Star Trek" set is brand new and there should be plenty of opportunities.

At events like these, players are organized into one-on-one matches and construct their decks from scratch, tearing open booster packs, examine their cards, and trying to build the most effective strategy possible around a 40-card deck. While experienced players will have an edge, they can't bring finely honed and powerful decks from home to immediately wipe the floor with you. Everyone starts at square one. And "Star Trek" fans should take very easily to this format, since the characters you'd expect to be powerful tend to have cards that are powerful. It also leads to some amusing team-ups, like how my winning deck involved an unlikely alliance between Deanna Troi and Gul Dukat.

In a friendly shop with a friendly crowd, this is Magic at its purest: a direct, competitive game where tactics at the table are as important as the strategy behind your deck construction. And the mechanics in the "Trek" set are intuitive and mesh well, meaning that creating a deck that functions as needed is fairly straightforward, and going with your gut choices (i.e., building around characters you like) often leads to strong results.

I can hear your next question: You don't have access to a local shop, or you don't feel comfortable going to one, so what's the best way to play at home? Once again, there are options.

You and a friend (or more) could always buy booster packs, tearing them open and building personal collections and constructing 60-card decks for standard play. However, I would recommend booster packs being the start of your collection, and once you have bought a few, track down single cards to complete your strategy rather than buying more and blindly hoping for strong pulls.

Another option is for you and a friend to buy a pre-release kit, as there are always plenty leftover after the initial week of special event. Use these to construct imperfect but fun starter decks to learn the game, and then grow and expand those decks as you see fit, doubling down on the characters and strategies you're enjoying.

However, the best at-home experience would be to pick up one of the set's Draft Night boxes, which are pricy but offer bang for your buck: enough cards for four friends to craft decks and go head-to-head for an evening, leaving everyone with enough cards to build upon in the future.

However, all of these options require tinkering, and suggest that you'll enjoy the process of building a deck as much as playing one. These options require additional legwork, additional financial investment, and even a bit of luck (although that can be mitigated by buying single cards from reputable online and brick-and-mortar shops). If you want to truly just dive into the game itself and skip the rest of the process, there is another way.

When I had a chance to speak to the key designers behind Magic: The Gathering's "Star Trek" set during a launch event in Los Angeles, I asked if the new set was friendly for "Star Trek" fans with no gaming experience, and if they had a recommendation on where to start.

First, they noted that the set was designed with new players in mind and puts narrative first. A card will generally behave like its counterpart in the "Star Trek" universe, so a fan knows that a Captain Kirk card will be a bit more headstrong and aggressive while Spock will allow for more wily, thoughtful strategy. This means a "Trek" fan should be able to grasp the new cards fairly quickly, using their existing knowledge as a crutch.

Second, they highlighted their recommendation for the best way to sample the game: the "Star Trek" commander decks.

Commander is the most popular format in Magic, where players utilize 100 card decks in four-player games that are slowly paced, socially driven, and generally take an entire evening to play. Think of them as more of a board game experience — or a nerd poker night — than a standard Magic set. Many Magic sets are accompanied by a few pre-constructed commander decks, which players can purchase, open, and play immediately without any prep. The "Star Trek" set has four of them: Federation Fleet, We Are the Borg, Klingon Fury, and Landing Party.

Specifically, the designers recommended the Federation Fleet commander deck as their choice for a "Star Trek" fan hoping to play the game.

Naturally, the next step was to test the designers' suggestion. I rounded up three friends and assigned them each a different Star Trek commander deck, taking Federation Fleet for myself. It's easy to see why this one was recommended: With Picard on the cover and a deck full of '90s "Trek" staples, it's the most popular era of the franchise in one 100-card deck.

Our four-player game took over three hours, and frankly, it was some of the best Magic I've ever played, with all four decks interacting in surprising and wild ways that left everyone at the table screaming and laughing. The "Trek" fans were impressed by the thematic touches, and how the mechanics relate to character personalities and motives, while the Magic players simply relished in the new design elements. I squeaked out a win, but only after the Borg player staged a comeback that essentially wiped out the table. My victory told a story in of itself: Dr. Bashir threw himself at the Borg player, perishing, but in the process, activated his ability to resurrect Ro Laren from the dead, activating her ability and ending the Borg threat once and for all.

After seeing the commander decks in action, I'm inclined to agree with the designers' recommendation. The Borg deck is scary and powerful, but makes them an immediate threat the other players will team up against to defeat. The Klingon deck is pure aggression, which may work against a new player's inherent shyness. The Landing Part deck, with its focus on Original Series characters, is fairly straightforward, but has a lot of moving pieces to consider. The mechanical simplicity of the Federation Fleet deck, and its arsenal of beloved characters, makes it easy to grasp and understand quickly.

Much like with "Star Trek" itself, there are countless ways to get into Magic: The Gathering, and no incorrect way. Ultimately, I agree with the designers: the pre-constructed commander decks, and specifically the Federation Fleet deck, are the best point of entry. Ideally, you'd buy all four and learn with friends for the best possible experience.

But like with "Star Trek" itself, you should be warned: once Magic has sucked you in, be prepared to be sucked in for the long haul.
