#3490. ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 16, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release the film in theaters Friday, November 13.]

It’s the final weekend of summer in 1986, upwardly aspirant Jewish families across Queens are still crowding around country club pools to make sure they get their annual money’s worth, and — in a little less than two months — the Mets are going to win the World Series for what might be the last time in team history. But nebbishy engineer Irwin Pearl (Miles Teller) doesn’t know that yet. He doesn’t know that this is his golden age. He doesn’t know that this is as good as it’s ever going to get.  Related Stories Kate Berlant and John Early to Host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards ‘Iron Boy’ Trailer: Beloved Animated Feature Oscar Contender Throws a Whole Watercolor World Out of Whack

What Irwin knows is that greed is good. That the income gap is widening at an unprecedented rate, that economic mobility is slowing to a crawl, and that his giant older brother Gary (Adam Driver) — a divorced ex-police officer who swans around the city like a majestic bird in a blue Mercedes — has started to make him feel even smaller than usual. What Irwin knows is that his mother-in-law wants him to move the family to Great Neck, that the older of his two bickering teenage sons wants an expensive party for his 18th birthday, and that his beautiful wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) wants fewer things to worry about. Irwin isn’t the overly ambitious sort, but a man can only live in the suburbs of Mt. Olympus for so long before it starts to feel like the gods are taunting him to claim a small piece of it for himself.

And so the stage is set for James Gray’s deft and devastating “Paper Tiger,” a Jewish-American tragedy in a teapot that — like all of the writer/director’s best films — is both sweepingly mythic and hauntingly personal all at once. That double effect, once a magic trick that Gray’s movies would manage to pull off by the time they ended, has since become the de facto starting condition of his singular auto-cinema, which continues to pick at his formative wounds by processing them through the classics.

As indebted to Aeschylus as “Ad Astra” was to Joseph Campbell, or “The Lost City of Z” was to Henri Rousseau, “Paper Tiger” begins with a telling quote from the ancient playwright’s most famous text: “Let there be wealth without tears; enough for the wise man who will ask no further.” Even more telling, however, is the opening shot that follows, which surveys the same reedy marshland — or at least one identical to it — from the end of “We Own the Night.” It’s no surprise that a project first conceived as a direct sequel to 2022’s “Armageddon Time” should point back to Gray’s previous work, but never before has it been so clear, so fast, that he’s trying to process his own, highly specific experience by assimilating it into the curriculum that first taught him how to make sense of the world. The more acutely self-referential his films get, the more broadly they speak to the soft and immortal agony that propels their characters forward.

It’s an agony that goes by many (sur)names, but is colloquially referred to as “family.” “Paper Tiger” is many things, chief among them a textbook parable about the American Dream, a breathless thriller about a working-class schmuck who gets mixed up with the Russian mafiya, and a pleasantly open question about why Miles Teller has rededicated his career to cosplaying as “Lost in America”-era Albert Brooks (to my mind, a canny, convincing way of aging up the nonconformist spunk that first defined his screen image in the days of “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now”). But, at its most nuclear level, “Paper Tiger” is — to an even more explicit degree than “Little Odessa,” “The Yards,” and any of the other James Gray movies that it hungrily mulches into something all its own — a remarkably knowing and perceptive film about how family is, and has always been, the ultimate devil’s bargain. Our greatest strength and our heaviest cross to bear. The reason our most dangerous risks can seem worth taking, and the most valuable thing we risk by taking them.

Irwin gives “Paper Tiger” its shape, but it’s how Gary navigates those dilemmas that gives the film its soul. Heartbreakingly portrayed by Adam Driver in a career-best performance that stretches across flash, menace, and pure sincerity like a foot stepping down on a bed of nails without drawing blood, Gary is a vintage ’80s showboat who only knows how to show affection by offering to share in his apparent success. He strides into Irwin and Hester’s living room — after months of radio silence — with the razzle dazzle of a local celebrity and a fully catered feast from Peter Luger’s Steak House in tow for good measure. Irwin’s sons marvel at the gun their uncle still keeps holstered around his ankle (cool!), and his wide-eyed wife looks across the kitchen table and imagines what her life might have been like had she held out for the shinier Pearl.

At least, that’s what Irwin seems to imagine that his wife is imagining, though he’d sooner let such fears fester inside of him for the rest of his natural life than to speak them aloud. For all of the character’s frustrated aspirations for a better life, Teller endows him with the wizened humility of a second-generation Jewish immigrant who knows that it would be gauche to forsake what his late father-in-law — tempting to picture as Anthony Hopkins for continuity’s sake — sacrificed to make possible for their family. Irwin might even be smart enough to recognize that his brother is an empty promise in a tailored suit, but, in a less literal expression of the double vision that will soon cause his wife to crash her car into a tree, being smart isn’t the same as seeing things clearly.

Whatever the case, Irwin is powerless to resist his brother’s sales pitch when Gary lures him into the basement to reveal the reason purpose of his visit: An ambitious new business venture is seeping its way into the Gowanus Canal, and it could use a sharp engineer to help facilitate their plans for the waterway. Still connected to the gills after getting rich in the private sector, Gary doesn’t tell his naive kid brother that said venture is the Russian mob, but the beauty of it is that he doesn’t have to. It can just be another one of the many different things that Irwin doesn’t know. He’ll go down there, sketch a few diagrams for some bald and scary men straight out of central casting, and take home a healthy paycheck to his family (“Paper Tiger” won’t score any points for bucking mafia stereotypes, as Gray plays up their ruthlessness in order to stress how far Irwin is out of his depth).

The only problem is that Irwin takes the job as seriously as he would any other, and — to his profound regret — takes his two sons to go scope out the canal one night, where they see the Russians illegally dumping their waste into the water. The Russians don’t like that. They don’t know what he’s doing there. And, in the aftermath of a stomach-churning stick-up that twisted my guts with the queasy horror of a repressed memory, Gary is given a week to make the problem go away. Spoiler alert: Appeasing the leader of an organized crime ring isn’t as simple as cutting a check, and wouldn’t be even if Gary had access to $125,000.

It doesn’t take long for things to spiral out of control from there, as Irwin and his boys soon find themselves in the crosshairs of a turf war they are comically ill-prepared to survive, while Hester — kept in the dark for her own protection — is thrust into a different crucible that she chooses to keep secret from her husband for similar reasons. (Despite being heavily affected by period drag, Johansson’s performance is too limpid to be mistaken for caricature, growing more hollowed out and heartsick with every scene until it assumes the same void-like power that Brad Pitt once found in the farthest reaches of outer space.) Plotted with a fatalistic velocity that would make Aeschylus proud, Gray’s script corkscrews towards ruin at a sickening pace, its slick road to hell paved with a well-textured mixture of imperfect intentions.

For all of the red meat that “Paper Tiger” gets to chew off the bone, this is still a small and maybe slightly underfunded movie, its outsized impact only made possible because of the micro-details that Gray traces within and between his characters. And I’m not talking about the assortment of beepers and TaB cans, or the load-bearing shots of ’80s New York, which are all Joaquín Baca-Asay’s 35mm cinematography needs to complete the illusion of time travel. While the film is buttressed by a handful of exquisite setpieces (including a nightmarish home invasion sequence that transposes the film’s title into a piece of shadowplay, and a climactic shoutout that binds it even closer to the rest of Gray’s body of work), it’s ultimately fueled by the atomic frictions inside Driver’s performance.

To that point, the real tragedy of “Paper Tiger” isn’t that messing with the mob tears these brothers apart, but rather that it brings them together. There’s not a lot of time for fun and games, but it’s never lost on Gray that this is the most time Gary and Irwin have spent with each other in years — maybe even since they were kids. “We’ve never played in the dirt,” Gary tells Irwin as he lies to his brother about how everything  about the Gowanus deal is above board. But they’re playing together now. The worse things get, the more they expose the extraordinary bond that allowed things to get so fucked up in the first place (a dynamic that becomes all the more wrenching because of how Gray transposes it onto Irwin’s sons). The worse things get, the more this movie sympathizes with Gary and Irwin for their parts in it.

It’s not that Gary is trying to do something nice for his brother, or that he’s shamelessly using Irwin to broker a lucrative deal with the Russians, but rather that everything that happens after that fateful offer stems from an inextricable braid of love and leverage. Gray is no stranger to saga about fraternal strains, but never has he so forcefully tugged at the ties that bind, or more sensitively observed how they can suffocate an entire family when a certain force pulls on them hard enough.

“Paper Tiger” is a story about a household gripped by a self-inflicted event that chokes the life out of its lungs, and precious few films have better conveyed what it feels like when the oxygen gets sucked out of a home without any hope of coming back. “We already had everything,” Irwin will eventually mutter under his breath. The deepest cut of this unshakeable tragedy is that, for the very first time, it leaves him begging for more.

“Paper Tiger” premiered in Competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. NEON will release it in theaters later this year.

#3489. HomeKit Weekly: Airversa’s Humelle is the Thread humidifier my house needs this winter

I love natural gas heat for a few reasons, but one is avoiding AUX heat from a heat pump and watching the bill rise. The downside is when the gas heat kicks on, the air in mt house is bone dry. My nose ends up being super dry for months. A humidifier like the Airversa Humelle works with Apple Home over Thread, so it can run itself based on what the air actually needs, and with the temps in my area getting into the 40s in the next week, I am glad I have one.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Airversa Humelle humidifier uses Thread, so it does join your existing Thread network via a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K and communicates with Apple Home locally. In my experience, Thread accessories always respond faster and drop connections less than Wi-Fi-only ones, and they don’t add to the pile of devices fighting for airtime on your router either. Especially since most smart home devices are 2.4 GHz only.

Once the Airversa Humelle is paired with Apple Home, it appears in the Home app as a humidifier with a built-in temperature and humidity sensor. The latter sensor is the key for automations as well. You can set a target humidity level, and in Auto Mode, it ramps the mist up or down on its own to hold that number. For most people, that’s all the automation they’ll ever need. Set it to 45%, and it’ll run forever. By including that sensor in the device, you don’t need to pair it with a separate Apple Home-compatible humidity sensor for the automations. In fact, that is probably the only automation to run with this device.

The Humelle has a 3.2L tank that Airversa rates at up to 60 hours of runtime, and the mist reaches about 40 inches high, so it covers a bedroom or an average-sized living room pretty easily. It’s a top-fill design, which honestly is the only way these should be made at this point. Flipping them over always ends with some water on the floor.

Sleep Mode runs at 28dB, which is good for a baby’s room, etc. There’s a multicolor LED on the base that you can set to whatever color you want from the Home app or the Sleekpoint app, or turn off completely. There’s also a tray for essential oils if you want it to double as a diffuser to improve a room’s smell.

One thing to know about the Airversa Humelle going in: you’ll still want the Sleekpoint app for a few things, like setting a cleaning reminder that pings you when it’s time to rinse the tank. Day-to-day control lives in Apple Home, but the setup and maintenance features live in the manufacturer’s app. That’s just where Matter is as a protocol right now.

Natural gas heat dries out your inside air, and the Airversa Humelle fixes it. It allows me to avoid regretting my heating choice when I built my house. A humidifier that knows when the air is dry and turns on is the secret sauce. The Humelle does that in Apple Home with Thread, giving you a humidity sensor you can build the rest of your winter automations around. If you need a Thread Border Router, one of the new HomePod mini 2 units is the best to get started.

The Airversa Humelle is available on Amazon and directly from Airversa.

Grand Theft Auto fans are so shook they're question if Rockstar’s new footage is AI-generated

With only a week left before the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, there's little in Rockstar Games' marketing that players haven't seen before. That familiarity is true of new GTA 6 features, at least. In terms of visuals, the game developer just proved it still has plenty of Leonida to show off.

The new clip that has fans talking was shared via Rockstar's Instagram stories on Wednesday, and it's based on a video originally uploaded on the OnlyInDade account. The regional social media account chronicles some of the wackier things that happen in the Florida county. A quick swipe through many of OnlyInDade's posts will explain exactly why Rockstar made the gator state the setting of its new open-world game. Some Miami-Dade incidents sound like a parody of a Florida Man headline.

The video is only 15 seconds long, but it has repeatedly left viewers with their mouths agape. Many watched it initially and fully believed they were looking at real-world footage. They weren't.

If it seems convincing, it's because the GTA 6 clip is a near replica of a video that originally captured a scene in Dade. When you compare the two, GTA 6's simulacrum becomes more obvious. The "real" video has way more humans walking about, and the colors aren't saturated to make a screenshot pop. The video game clip also features some shaky cam, which creates the illusion there's an actual person holding the phone. Mind you, based on the NPC density of areas like the beach, GTA 6 seems capable of rendering the number of people present in the original footage. Paradoxically, the sidewalk's sparseness in the video game makes it look more convincing.

"this ain’t no gameplay footage this is in real life," one viewer wrote on X.

On Reddit, the top replies are dozens of people arguing over whether the clip was made by AI. While Rockstar has not outright said the clip is real, it seems unlikely that the developer would share fake footage that could confuse fans. The OnlyInDade account also claims the clip is 100% gameplay. Many are theorizing this is what GTA 6 might look like when the player records the world with their in-game phone.

Previously, GTA 6 fans couldn't believe how realistic the digital mud looked — and had plenty to say about the game's trailers. Rockstar has also made it sound like the game will be full of unexpected graphical flourishes, like Red Dead Redemption 2's infamous horse balls. Perhaps the 30 frames-per-second limitation that keeps making people melt down online won't be that big of a deal after all.

#3486. Henry Cavill Comments On Superman Return After James Gunn's DC Studios Exit

Henry Cavill was a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie, and that should have been the end of it. But it's now 2026, and we're still talking about whether Cavill will return as the Man of Steel. With James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future is very much up in the air, and now Cavill is saying he'd always be open to returning as Supes.

During an Inverse interview, the actor was asked if he'd ever play the DC hero again and seemed open to the idea. "Look, there's lots of fantastic storylines," he replied. "There's always a lot of opportunity. As the pigeon sang to Fievel in 'An American Tail,' "never say never." And I buy into that." It's hardly surprising, given that Cavill and his former DC Extended Universe colleague Dwayne Johnson once launched a pretty bizarre attempt to remain in the cinematic universe, most pointedly with 2022's immediately forgettable "Black Adam." At the time, Cavill proudly announced his return as Superman in a social media post following the film's release, but it never actually amounted to anything more than that and left Gunn deeply (and understandably) confused about what was even happening.

Since then, Gunn has introduced us to an all-new Man of Steel in David Corenswet, who made his debut in the charming crowd pleaser that was 2025's "Superman" and is set to return in the 2027 follow-up "Man of Steel." But with Gunn out at DC Studios it remains to be seen where the Corenswet version of the character and his story will go from there. Meanwhile, we've got Cavill telling Inverse he "had such a wonderful time playing Superman in the past" and "would never say never now." It's a bit tiresome, no?

Directly after the extremely perplexing return of Henry Cavill's Superman in "Black Adam," the DCEU collapsed with back to back flops in 2023. Meanwhile, James Gunn was gearing up to launch his DC Universe, which is why the whole situation left him baffled – especially since he was already actively preparing his DC reboot at the time. He wasn't the only one, either. Audiences thought they'd seen the last of the so-called Snyderverse after 2023, but Gunn chose to soft reboot DC with a new cinematic universe that retained elements of the old one. What's more, calls to reinstate the DCEU persist even today.

Now that Gunn and Peter Safran have been removed (er, "stepped down") from DC Studios, it looks as though Skydance CEO David Ellison — who's running the newly-merged Warner Bros. and Paramount — is planning to pretty much dismantle everything Gunn built at DC to prepare for yet another reboot.

Whatever Ellison and his new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios, Jeremy Latcham, have planned for the brand, I think it's safe to say we really don't need more talk of Cavill suiting back up. Had the actor left this character alone following 2017's "Justice League," it might have been a thrill to hear of his possible return a decade later. As it stands, like calls to restore the Snyderverse, this seems to be the discussion that never dies. Perhaps it's that lingering feeling that Cavill never got the movie he deserved, or the fact that Superman remains his best-known character. But for now it would be nice to go a few years without hearing about anything from the Snyderverse era coming back.

#3485. Apple’s DOJ antitrust battle sparks disputes with Epic, Samsung, Oura, Roblox, more

Several tech companies are pushing back against subpoenas issued by Apple and the DOJ in their ongoing antitrust battle. Here are the details.

In March 2024, the Department of Justice and 15 states, plus the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, despite recent reports of settlement talks happening behind the scenes, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, which is the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case.

As part of its effort to refute the DOJ’s arguments, Apple has subpoenaed several third-party companies and organizations, seeking documents and information relevant to its defense. That includes Epic Games, Samsung Electronics America, Meta, Oura, Garmin, Playco, Ultrahuman, PayPal, Match Group, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, among others.

The DOJ and plaintiff states, in turn, have issued their own subpoenas, including to Roblox, Epic Games, Snap, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, seeking evidence to support their allegations against Apple.

Google, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Capital One are also named in legal documents.

In essence, both sides are trying to use data from Apple’s competitors and companies with which it has commercial relationships to establish how its policies affect competition, and whether those policies are justified or constitute anticompetitive behavior.

Over the past couple of days, multiple letters submitted to the court reveal disagreements over the scope of the subpoenas, the information being requested, and whether the companies should be required to produce certain documents.

Epic Games, for instance, argues that Apple’s requests for documents from three previous lawsuits (Epic v. Apple in the US, Epic v. Apple in Australia, and Epic v. Google in the US), along with extensive searches of internal files belonging to three senior executives, including its CEO, would be disproportionately burdensome.

Still, the company has offered to produce several categories of information, including Fortnite user and revenue data, contracts with Google and Samsung, and records relating to Apple’s Core Technology Fee.

Samsung, in turn, has agreed to search documents belonging to two executives, which the company says have yielded nearly 900,000 documents matching the agreed-upon search terms.

However, Apple wants to expand the searches to six additional executives, including Samsung Electronics America’s current and former CEOs, and obtain deposition transcripts from Samsung executives who testified in the DOJ’s antitrust lawsuit against Google.

The companies also disagree over whether Samsung Electronics America should be required to produce documents held by its South Korean parent company, which is a dispute we covered here before.

As for Oura, the company is pushing back on several fronts, including whether Apple should reimburse it for reviewing more than 32,000 additional documents, and whether it may withhold or redact certain information it considers trade secrets.

Garmin has raised similar objections to Apple’s requests for confidential financial and strategic information.

Roblox, which is the only company among these recent filings subpoenaed by the DOJ and plaintiff states rather than Apple or other plaintiffs, is disputing requests for information about its relationship with Apple and how Apple’s App Store policies are applied. The government, meanwhile, argues that the documents could help establish whether Apple consistently applies its App Store Guidelines to developers.

Another interesting dispute involves Japan-based instant gaming company Playco, which is resisting Apple’s requests for documents concerning its efforts to influence App Store policies, including lobbying activities.

Playco argues that producing these materials would violate its First Amendment rights, citing a 2021 court decision involving similar requests Apple made to Match Group.

Several of the companies have also requested until November 11 to continue negotiations before their disputes are formally declared at an impasse, potentially avoiding further court intervention.

All of this is happening against the backdrop of another dispute between Apple and the DOJ involving the company’s efforts to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies.

Although a special master has twice sided with Apple, the order remains on hold while the court considers the government’s appeal.

#3484. DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues

When they were hired to run DC Studios, James Gunn and Peter Safran were tasked with turning the struggling comic book company into a true rival to Marvel. Four years later, the two have been handed their walking papers before they were able to accomplish their task.

Skydance, which recently bought Warner Bros. Discovery and with it the rights to heroes like Superman, Batman, and the other DC staples that Gunn and Safran were trying to reinvigorate, opted to go in another, cheaper direction. They brought in Jeremy Latcham, a low-profile executive who, like Gunn, had spent years working for Marvel, to oversee DC’s latest reboot. Related Stories ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy ‘Iron Boy’ Trailer: Beloved Animated Feature Oscar Contender Throws a Whole Watercolor World Out of Whack

There have been mutterings that the change was because of the commercial performance of DC’s films, and the track record has been a mixed bag. “Superman” did what it needed to do, earning $618.7 million worldwide on a $225 million budget, but it wasn’t a blockbuster on the level of Christopher Nolan’s “Dark Knight” films or “Aquaman.”

But “Supergirl” was an unmitigated disaster, earning $126.5 million against a $170 million budget, resulting in losses of roughly $100 million. And “Clayface,” a body horror film produced for $44 million, has been a modest success, earning approximately $110 million. So no, Gunn and Safran had yet to produce a “Guardians of the Galaxy”-style smash that taps the zeitgeist. Though, to be fair, Marvel hasn’t made as many of those lately either. Tastes have changed, and comic book movies, at least ones not starring Spider-Man, aren’t as popular as they once were.

But look closer, and Gunn and Safran’s ouster is about something more than their films’ commercial performances. It’s about cost-cutting too, something that Skydance, with its $80 billion in net debt, needs to start chipping away at if it’s going to realize the $6 billion in savings it’s promised to find.

The duo’s deal, which was set to expire in 2027, was unusually generous. Safran not only got paid to run the comic book label, he was also allowed to run The Safran Company, the wildly successful production company behind “The Conjuring” franchise (former Netflix film chief Dan Lin, in contrast, divested from his company Rideback when he went over to the streamer). Then there was Gunn, who commanded fees for producing films like “Supergirl” and “Clayface,” as well as fees for those DC films that he wrote and directed, such as “Superman” and “Man of Tomorrow.” Gunn’s total haul for a DC film could be as high as $10 million for all his various duties, according to insiders.

When Warner Bros. Discovery chief David Zaslav offered the pair such a sweet deal, comic book movies looked more durable and he needed to make a splash after DC produced flops like “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom” and “The Flash.” To sweeten the offer, Zaslav also allowed Gunn and Safran to be relatively autonomous, reporting directly to him, whereas Skydance wanted the DC leadership to be under Skydance Motion Picture Group chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein.

Skydance has also been stunned by the financial picture of Warner Bros.’ film unit since taking over. The studio has suffered a devastating wave of flops this year, losing hundreds of millions on a slate that included bombs such as “Digger,” “The Bride!,” and last weekend’s “The Cat in the Hat.” One insider put the estimated losses at nearing $1 billion. Of course, most of those films were greenlit under Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy, who were let go as soon as David Ellison got the keys to the Warner lot, and have nothing to do with Gunn or Safran. But it does put pressure on Skydance to turn things around and improve the film division’s margins, fast. On an earnings call this week, Ellison acknowledged the film division faces “headwinds” and “has underperformed this year.” He went on to pledge to “apply the same playbook we did at Paramount: greenlighting more selectively.”

Safran remains widely respected on the lot for his stewardship of DC, and is praised for trying to keep budgets in line and for cleaning up the company’s byzantine production practices so that its films, shows, and comic books had a unifying creative voice. Gunn, though a gifted filmmaker, had a harder time adjusting to life in the c-suite, something he admitted to this week in a lengthy post on X. “What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least,” Gunn wrote. “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.” He closed by saying that he was excited to return to working purely as a creator.

Gunn’s habit of engaging with fans directly on social media raised eyebrows at Warner Bros. and, later, at Skydance. But it cut both ways, with Gunn often using his vast following to promote upcoming projects and to engage more directly with fans in a way that inspired loyalty. Insiders also credit Safran and Gunn with not only reinvigorating Superman on screen, but also backing critically acclaimed shows such as “Lanterns” and “Peacemaker.” And the pair handled a delicate situation with the production of “The Batman: Part II,” which was delayed because of personal issues involving its writer and director Matt Reeves, a situation that ultimately required Steven Soderbergh to step in to finish the sequel under Reeves’ guidance. It is expected to wrap production in the next few weeks.

Insiders also note that Gunn and Safran didn’t have a chance to fully realize their vision of making superhero films featuring a wider variety of characters across a greater diversity of genres made for a broader range of budgets. Gunn was already plotting his next move even as he edited “Man of Tomorrow,” which features a team-up of Lex Luthor and Superman. He had outlined a third “Superman” film and was working on a “Justice League” and a “Batman” film, either one of which was expected to be his next project.

In Hollywood, however, timing is everything. And Gunn and Safran had the misfortune of trying to build their own MCU just as comic book movies were declining in popularity. Will Latcham have more success? He’s widely liked and boasts ties to the Christian community that could broaden DC’s core audience. But he also doesn’t come with the kind of pedigree and profile that Gunn did.

As for DC’s fans, they are bracing for yet another reboot having seen the comic book brand they love go through three different regimes over the last decade. Will Latcham provide the kind of consistency the company so desperately needs, or will he be just the latest in a long line of executives asked to pull off a miracle without being granted much of a runway?

#3483. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

But now that we know Vision is in the movie, let's guess at his role in the narrative. If you haven't finished "VisionQuest," you should duck out now because I'm going to spoil the final episode's post-credits scene.

At the end of "VisionQuest," we're treated to a replay of the "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness" finale, where Elizabeth Olsen's Wanda Maximoff/Scarlet Witch sacrifices herself to rid the multiverse of the Darkhold. She is crushed by Mount Wundagore, which seemed at the time like a pretty definitive death, but, come on, this the MCU. No one is dead forever.

"VisionQuest" continues this scene with Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) arriving and lifting the pile of earth off of Wanda. "Scarlet Witch, awaken," says Doom. "Your power will be mine." So, shock of shocks, Wanda is back in circulation.

We know from "Avengers Endgame: Encore" that Doctor Doom has also kidnapped the Hulk, so he's amassing some serious power to wreak a heapin' helpin' of havoc. If Wanda is deep in the thrall of Doom, the only hope the Avengers have of turning her back to their side is her beloved Vision. So that "VisionQuest" reveal should've had every Marvel fan figuring that Vision would play a pivotal part in "Avengers: Doomsday." In a little over a month, we'll know how this all shakes out.

#3480. Netflix's Hit Spy Thriller Returns and Takes Over Streaming Charts

The British spy series has returned with new episodes

Keira Knightley has a knack for playing smart, determined women who refuse to back down when things get dangerous. Whether she's exposing government secrets in Official Secrets, investigating a serial killer in Boston Strangler, or navigating a deadly mystery aboard a luxury yacht in Netflix's The Woman in Cabin 10, Knightley has become a natural fit for tense thrillers.

Now, she's back in the spy business with a returning Netflix series that's attracting plenty of streaming attention.

The second season of Black Doves arrived on Nov. 5, and the spy thriller wasted little time climbing Netflix's charts. The series reached No. 2 on the global Netflix TV chart, according FlixPatrol. Netflix's own weekly figures also show that season 2 of Black Doves attracted 3.8 million views between Nov. 2 and Nov. 8, making it the fourth most-watched English-language series of the week.

Black Doves follows Helen Webb (Knightley), a seemingly ordinary politician's wife and mother who is secretly working as a spy for a clandestine organization called the Black Doves. For a decade, she has been passing along her husband's political secrets to the organization while maintaining her carefully constructed family life.

However, Helen's double life becomes considerably more dangerous when her secret lover, Jason (Andrew Koji), is murdered. Her employer calls in her longtime friend Sam Young (Ben Whishaw), an assassin with a complicated past, to protect her while she investigates the killing. Their search soon uncovers a much larger conspiracy involving London's criminal underworld and international politics.

The first season premiered on Netflix on Dec. 5, 2024, with six episodes. Its follow-up brings Knightley and Whishaw back for another six-episode adventure, continuing the story of their unlikely partnership.

Black Doves has also received a strong reception from critics. Season 1 currently holds a 92% critics' score and 64% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Season 2 has performed even better with critics, earning a 96% score, alongside a 66% audience rating.

#3479. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

#3478. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3477. Lauren Graham's 2026 Colleen Hoover Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

Is there anyone more representative of the recent romance novel adaptation trend than Colleen Hoover? Hollywood loves a BookTok phenomenon, and Hoover's novels seem designed in a lab to appeal to the "crying, screaming, throwing up" crowds on social media, who simply cannot resist what The Guardian called Hoover's "normcore thrillers."

But the film also has some other things working in its favor. For one it stars the talented Maika Monroe, and it also features Lauren Graham, who's best known for playing Lorelai Gilmore on "Gilmore Girls." Graham does a decent job with the material in "Reminders of Him," and regardless of how you feel about the film as a whole, it's nice to see her in a modern-day melodrama.

"Reminders of Him" is directed by British director Vanessa Caswill, who oversaw Netflix's 2023 romantic comedy "Love at First Sight," after honing her chops on BBC series such as "Little Women," "Gold Digger," and "Thirteen." This was another romance movie based on a popular book, and wouldn't you know, the movie went straight to the top of the Netflix charts upon its release. Now, Caswill has done it again with "Reminders of Him," though this one had a successful box office run under its belt before taking over Netflix.

The film stars Maika Monroe as Kenna Rowan, who made a tragic mistake years earlier that landed her in prison. After serving her sentence, Kenna returns to her Wyoming hometown, where she hopes to finally meet her young daughter, Diem Landry (Zoe Kosovic). Sadly, Diem's grandparents Grace and Patrick Landry (Lauren Graham and Bradley Whitford) are completely opposed to the idea. But there's also a strapping young bar owner standing between her and her daughter in the form of Ledger Ward (Tyriq Withers). Turns out Ledger has been helping take care of Diem, and he's similarly concerned about Kenna's return. But as the two get to know each other, romance blossoms, and Kenna finally gets a chance at redemption.

"Reminders of Him" hit Netflix U.S. on November 10, 2026, and according to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, became an instant hit. The film shot to number one on November 11, 2026, proving these Colleen Hoover adaptations remain perennially popular. No doubt we'll see plenty more Hoover books being adapted in the near future.

There are plenty of movies to avoid on Netflix, and "Reminders of Him" is right on the borderline. The film managed a 56% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is higher than any other Colleen Hoover adaptation. But it also has an 87% audience score, which ties it with "It Ends With Us" for most popular among viewers on the site. Now it has managed to earn the endorsement of Netflixers, does this mean you should watch it?

Well, the movie has a few plus points. For one, it stars the Maika Monroe, who's able to shift from scream queen to swoon queen with ease. Meanwhile, Lauren Graham is given some of the more emotional scenes and does a solid job of bringing them to life. Otherwise, it's sort of okay for the first half? Monroe and her co-star, Tyriq Withers, manage to wring some believable emotion out of the script. Once they throw caution to the wind and just go for it, despite their previous reluctance to besmirch Monroe's deceased husband, everything starts to get a little ridiculous.

Joey Shapiro summed things up quite aptly in his review for the Chicago Reader, when he called "Reminders of Him" a "corny TV movie" that's "made with so much sincerity and conviction by all involved that it becomes watchable, if rarely 'good' by any stretch." If that appeals, or if you simply can't get enough of these romance movies that verge on providing some sort of interesting insight into human emotion only to fall short, then why not give this lesser-known Hoover adaptation a go.

#3476. Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today

Way back in October 2024, The Fithian Group, led by former NATO chief John Fithian and founding partner Patrick Corcoran, announced plans for an ambitious new marketplace, one that would help connect filmmakers and their projects directly to theater owners looking to book their movies and effectively cut out the distribution middleman. Today, that vision is now a reality.

The Fithian Group on Wednesday at the American Film Market announced the formal launch of Attend Theatrical Marketplace, the group’s online platform and marketplace for filmmakers and exhibitors that is now live and ready for business.

Attend launches with today just a curated selection of four films, all of whose filmmakers will now be doing the legwork to connect with theaters and find venues at which to exhibit their work. But the platform is already loaded with exhibition partners who will be able to browse available films, with more to be added soon, and Attend will eventually be a fully open platform to any filmmaker who wishes to do outreach directly to theater owners. Related Stories DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy

IndieWire got an early demo of Attend and how it aims to simplify the work that distributors do every day in putting movies into theaters, as well as the work exhibitors have to do in booking movies, paying invoices, and more. And IndieWire will on Wednesday lead a panel discussion at AFM with Corcoran, Charles Beale of the site’s designer Titlepool, and filmmaker Lilian T. Mehrel, whose Tribeca award-winning film “Honeyjoon” will be one of the four inaugural films shopping for theaters.

Beyond “Honeyjoon,” the other three films available on Attend at launch are Kenny Riches’ crime drama “Mouse”; “Spoke,” which is a documentary about firefighters and the trauma they deal with after the fires; and “Censurada,” an LGBTQ+ drama from Marco Garza about forbidden love in 1969 Spain.

The vision of Attend was outlined to IndieWire over a year ago with an indie rom-com called “You, Me, and Her” serving as an early guinea pig for the idea. The thinking was, if you had a film that could demonstrate it already had an audience and you had a clear sense of where your audience was and how to target them, all you needed were the screens to showcase your movie and the means to get your movie into the hands of those theaters.

That was and remains the tricky part. Few people have the connections with theater owners to be able to reach them and get a film out in any meaningful capacity. This year has produced a number of examples in which enterprising filmmakers have done without distributors and found the audience they already knew was there to release their movies. YouTuber Markiplier went directly to theaters and made $50 million with his horror movie “Iron Lung.” The documentary “NAZA” skipped a distributor in order to get its story about the IDF out with urgency. Even an AI movie called “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is next month releasing without the aid of a distributor.

Attend seeks to use technology to simplify that process, to get your film out to an even wider audience and a more targeted one. For filmmakers, the platform is designed to eliminate the guesswork of who you need to talk to, how you reach them, and what attributes a given exhibitor is looking for in a film. For exhibitors, it filters all your titles and screens into one place, and it makes the receiving of deliverables or the payment of invoices more automated than the often tedious work it is for most exhibitors today. It’s exciting to see the whole vision come into fruition.

On the filmmaker end, the way Attend works is you as an individual can upload details and assets about your film, from simple details like its runtime, logline, and genre, to much more granular details about the aspect ratio, the available formats, the awards it has won and festivals it has played, the social networking reach of talent, and many more data points. There may be assets you don’t realize will be significant to a given exhibitor but will jump out as they browse your profile. You can then identify themes that speak to the film’s target audience and narrow the demographics for which your film is intended.

From there, you can filter and browse theaters to identify which theaters would be the best fit for your movie. For instance, Attend has data that can show a theater is within walking distance of a firehouse or that the theater has ties to a local advocacy group that aligns with the themes of the film’s story, and Attend’s predictive AI engine can recommend those theaters that would be available and the best fit for your film. Then, instead of reaching out to each of those theaters individually, filmmakers can easily select all the relevant theaters they want to message and have the option to manually add or subtract more beyond the recommended targets. You can even modify proposed theatrical terms for individual theaters or personalize messages, and as theaters come in, Attend can dynamically estimate P&A spend for those locations.

When theater owners are contacted, they’ll receive push notifications about films that are available for them to review, and they can further browse any available films in the marketplace and do their own outreach. Exhibitors can create tabs and info on any number of their circuit’s screens or locations and can upload in spreadsheets specs like screen size, audio, and seat count that filmmakers can view themselves to better get a sense of which theaters are the best fit. Exhibitors can specify rental prices for individual screens, you can mark your theater as being willing to offer simple four-walling options or that it’s capable of hosting big premieres, whether you want to offer “split screens” or “clean screens,” or you can set terms for how long you’re able to hold a movie. And not only does it also itemize marketing costs, Attend clearly indicates what the share of a film’s box office would be if they were to accept it and program it.

This helps theater owners in a number of ways. It takes the busy work out of things like paying numerous individual vendors or distribution partners, and it lets you download and easily generate a W9 form based on that film’s booking, being able to do so across multiple locations. But for theater owners that generally don’t know what they’re playing until the Monday before, this gives theaters far more advanced leeway and awareness to then be able to do the necessary marketing, put tickets on sale, and actually get butts in seats. All that is especially important for the smaller indies that need that word of mouth.

For now, theaters haven’t linked their loyalty data or other point of sales or scheduling tools to Attend, but that could come with time, and as people actually begin to use the platform, the predictive functionality will improve in the long run.

Corcoran and Fithian see Attend being useful for smaller distributors themselves in the long run, not just individual filmmakers who want to cut out the middleman. Distributors can use it to plan the campaigns of multiple titles and use its automation features to save time and costs. And while today Attend just supports new releases, there’s no reason why older library titles couldn’t be marketed here to exhibitors as well.

Time will tell if filmmakers find Attend an effective form of reaching theaters or if exhibitors adopt the platform widely to make it a useful tool for all parties. But it’s an ambitious vision that if implemented properly could have enormous impacts for the independent film world. And after two years of effort and hype, that day could finally be here.

#3475. Report: Apple faces congressional scrutiny over ICE tracking apps and Trump donations

Reuters and The Washington Post report that Apple is among the tech giants potentially facing congressional investigations as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers in January. Here are the details.

Earlier today, The Washington Post reported that “Democrats are laying the groundwork to investigate some of the country’s largest companies, setting off a scramble among executives who courted the president.”

The report notes that Washington law firms are advising companies and executives on how to prepare for potential congressional investigations, with some also pitching their services to Elon Musk:

Multiple firms have crafted pitches for why they should serve as Musk’s personal counsel, aware that the world’s richest man is likely to receive a barrage of subpoenas and that any casework stemming from those investigations will be both lucrative and the highest-profile investigative work available in the coming year, according to two of the people.

When it comes to Apple, the report noted that lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the company “over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

While the report refers to Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by ICE, the company has previously faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over its decision to remove apps used to track ICE agents from the App Store.

Last year, Apple removed ICEBlock and several similar apps from the App Store following pressure from the DOJ, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents.

The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

Since then, Apple has faced questions from Democratic lawmakers over the extent of the Trump administration’s involvement in the decision and whether the removals infringed on constitutionally protected speech.

 or no , oversight needs to happen. If  did bad, let it come out; if not, let that come out as well. There should be no sacred cows here, oversight and accountability need to be our national, collective goal. Anyone who says otherwise is trying to sell you something.

Reuters, meanwhile, reported that Senator Richard Blumenthal, “who is set to take over as chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations,” called on Apple “and others who donated to [President Trump’s new White House] ballroom project to turn over records” or “face possible subpoenas in January.”

As The Washington Post reported last month, Apple and Nvidia each pledged $25 million toward the ballroom, making them two of the project’s largest donors.

Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters or The Washington Post.

#3474. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

It’s been a long time for Tears of the Kingdom fans

All eyes are on The Legend of Zelda right now — and for good reason. The franchise is currently in the midst of celebrating its 40th anniversary and the long-awaited remake of Ocarina of Time was released on Nov. 5, 2026, becoming the second best-selling game on the Nintendo Switch 2 less than a week after its release. But, even amid all the Ocarina excitement, it's hard to forget just how memorable earlier Switch-era Zelda titles were — particularly Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

Breath of the Wild came out on the Nintendo Switch in 2017, and Tears of the Kingdom followed in 2023. Both games are considered part of the franchise's Wilds era, marked by open-world exploration and non-linear gameplay. The titles are loved by critics and fans alike, with each holding a Metacritic score higher than 95. While there's been no official word yet on when Zelda fans might see a new Wilds era title built for the Nintendo Switch 2, there is a project in the works that will be sure to appeal to any Tears of the Kingdom fan.

A new statue of Link designed by FIGURIZMa is being released in December 2026. The statue, replicating Link's look and pose from official Tears of the Kingdom artwork, features Link kneeling on a floating island with the Master Sword strapped to his back. It is listed on the Sega Plaza website as being approximately 10 cm x 23 cm (roughly 4 in x 9 in), and a description of the product reads: "Pay attention to the meticulously crafted costumes and the sculpting of the master sword. We paid special attention to the texture of the pants. The rock pedestal reminiscent of the original Great Sky Island was crafted with special attention to recreating unique patterns."

The statue is a re-release of a 2024 FIGURIZMa figurine that could only be won in Sega Plaza crane games in Japan. It never quite made its way to the United States, and the statue currently sells for between $40 and $60 on resale markets. No price for the 2026 version has been confirmed on the Sega Plaza website, but the release date is listed as Dec. 25, 2026. The re-release is looking likely to be a Japanese exclusive once again, but there's good news for Zelda fans worldwide — the re-release should drive down resale prices, so more people can get their hands on this Tears of the Kingdom collectible.

The statue is the latest in a line of releases coinciding with The Legend of Zelda's 40th anniversary. Other items that have been released this year include a lineup of Hasbro action figures and a limited-edition Nintendo Switch 2 console.
