Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.  He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms.  His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director.  In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

Thanksgiving week is stacked with a football slate, as it seemingly has always been. The NFL has scheduled five games in three days for the first time ever. The eventful holiday weekend begins with the Packers at Rams on Netflix on Wednesday the 25th, and ends with the Broncos at Steelers on Black Friday. The Thursday triple-header brings the Bears at Lions, Eagles at Cowboys and Chiefs at Bills. It's a lot of downtime with family, and a lot of time for football and movies. So I decided to combine the two.

The ten movies below cover pretty much every flavor of football, from prison yard scrappy comedy to a Superbowl terror plot. They span 1971 to 2014, and include true stories, a literary thriller adaptation and a TV movie that made an entire sports generation cry. I ranked them by how well they hold up on a rewatch, which rewards the stronger character work over box office value and the flashier trophy-like blockbusters of the football film.

A few notes on the edges. Jerry Maguire spends most of its time with an agent, but football runs through every scene. Several connect to this week's games, from the Bears in Brian's Song to the Cowboys and Steelers in Black Sunday. The Longest Yard is the 1974 original with Burt Reynolds, while the Sandler 2005 remake takes a seat on the bench. So, in between kickoffs, here are some iconic football flicks to put on while the turkey rests and the stuffing settles.

Picture a prison yard in the sun, a warden with a plan, and a disgraced quarterback who knows he is being used. Robert Aldrich directed The Longest Yard, and Burt Reynolds built a movie star persona on Paul Crewe, a former pro quarterback with a sneer and a bruised ego. He was thrown out for shaving points, and the warden wants him to now put together an inmate team for a game against the guards. He pressures Crewe into organizing it, and he ends up getting the strongest and angriest convicts he can find.

The inmates call themselves the Mean Machine, and they relish every chance they get to hit a guard. The training sequences give the movie a fun and rowdy charm. Ed Lauter plays the head guard, Captain Knauer, with a snarl and menacing grin. Aldrich keeps the camera very close to the action, so the audience feels up tight with the game's most violent hits. The warden expects his guards to win and Crewe's early willingness to go along puts him at odds with his own teammates. Michael Conrad, an old football coach in the yard, gives the team a crusty voice of experience. Ray Nitschke, the Green Bay Packers linebacker, appears as an inmate for those Packer fans gearing up for Wednesday night.

Rudy Ruettiger grows up in a big family in a steel town, where the normal trajectory is to work at the local mill and keep your head down. His father and brothers do so, but Rudy's less inclined. He fully wakes up when a close friend's death at work makes him bolt for South Bend on a bus with little more than a dream. Sean Astin plays him with a squint of determination, a kid who stands about five foot six and keeps a Notre Dame pennant on his wall. He naturally cannot get in right away, so he enrolls at nearby Holy Cross Junior College, where a priest helps him with his grades. David Anspaugh directs from Angelo Pizzo's script, and the two had already made Hoosiers together, which should tell you everything about their creative tone of voice.

Charles S. Dutton is warm and gruff as the Notre Dame groundskeeper who gives Rudy a job. He gives him some of the best advice in the movie amidst the scout team practices, where Rudy keeps getting knocked around daily. Vince Vaughn, in an early role, appears as one of the Notre Dame players. Late in the story, the players lay their jerseys on the coach's desk, so Rudy can dress for the final game, and the chants begin from there. Rudy finally dresses for the last game, gets in for a few plays, and sacks the quarterback to end it, just as the real Ruettiger did. The crowd chants his name some more as his teammates carry him off, and Jerry Goldsmith's music swells to match every emotional beat.

Bobby Boucher has the world's strangest job. He hauls water for a college football program, and Adam Sandler plays him with a squeaky voice and a heart full of passion. Bobby lives in the Louisiana bayou with his Mama, played by Kathy Bates, who is convinced that football is a sin and girls are traps. He promptly loses his job and lands at South Central Louisiana State University, where Henry Winkler's Coach Klein is in desperate need of a spark. A locker room tease turns Bobby into a human wrecking ball, and the Mud Dogs have finally gotten their defense back. Frank Coraci directs and lets the jokes run wild, from the over-the-top swamp accents to the oddly specific rules Mama sets down.

Fairuza Balk plays Vicki, a childhood friend with a bad reputation but whose loyalty to Bobby never wavers. The movie grossed more than $160 million domestically on a fairly modest budget. Its quotes spread through schoolyards and dorm rooms for years after its release. The Mud Dogs' games get bigger and louder as the season goes on, and Bobby's anger becomes the biggest laugh. The movie pokes fun at college football's culture of worshiping its stars, and it shows little mercy in doing so.

Reacher just pulled 66 million viewers, and Fallout is back in 2027.

Black Sunday starts with a raid in Beirut, then moves to the Superbowl. John Frankenheimer (The Manchurian Candidate) adapted the novel for the screen, and Robert Shaw, fresh off of Jaws, plays Mossad agent David Kabakov. Kabrakov is opposite Bruce Dern's Michael Lander, a Goodyear blimp pilot and Vietnam veteran who has lost faith in everything. Dern plays Lander as a bitter man who has been passed over and ignored. Marthe Keller is chilling as a Black September operative who recruits Lander for the mission and convinces him of its justification.

Their target is Super Bowl X in Miami, and the weapon is the blimp itself. Frankenheimer directs it like a procedural, with stakeouts, tips and a countdown. He shot the climax inside the Orange Bowl during the real Super Bowl X between the Steelers and Cowboys. The crowd of over 80,000 is one of the more elaborate stunts of that era and gives the finale a scale most thrillers cannot come close to. The legendary John Williams wrote the score, and its brass swells over the blimp's final approach. Black Sunday asks its audience to imagine the worst day in sports, and it takes the question with a deep seriousness.

Ivan Reitman, best known for Ghostbusters, directed Draft Day, and Kevin Costner plays Sonny Weaver Jr., the Cleveland Browns general manager. The movie takes course over one day, as Weaver hopes to make the biggest trade of his career. Sonny's father, the former Browns coach, has just passed, and the weight of that loss colors every decision. Costner has a long sports resume, with Bull Durham, Field of Dreams and Tin Cup, and he is comfortable living in the psyche of these kinds of men. Frank Langella plays the owner who pushes for a flashy move, and Denis Leary plays Coach Penn, who wants Sonny to stay out of his way.

Reitman uses split screens and a ticking clock to foster the tension in the room. Jennifer Garner plays Ali, whose news about their personal life complicates a stressful day. Sonny trades the Browns' future picks to move up to the top of the draft. He then quickly second guesses himself when he takes a closer look at the quarterback everyone loves. He is drawn to linebacker Vontae Mack (Chadwick Boseman), whose character impresses Weaver more than the scouting report. Terry Crews plays running back Earl Penn, and Tom Welling is the incumbent quarterback, Brian Drew. Real NFL figures, including Commissioner Roger Goodell, appear as well, and the draft's logos are everywhere.

John Lee Hancock adapted Michael Lewis's book, with Quinton Aaron starring as Michael Oher, a gentle giant who has spent his life moving from home to home. The Blind Side uses the famous Lawrence Taylor hit on Joe Theismann to explain why the left tackle is such a crucial position to a football team's success. Sandra Bullock is Leigh Anne Tuohy, a Memphis interior designer with a Southern drawl and a steel spine. She spots Michael walking in the cold on Thanksgiving night and brings him home.

Tim Mcgraw plays her husband, a fast food franchise owner with a soft spot for Ole Miss football, and Kathy Bates is his school tutor. Bullock netted an Oscar for Best Actress and the movie got a nomination for Best Picture. It ended up grossing more than $300 million, making it one of the biggest sports movies ever. Michael Oher became a first round pick of the Baltimore Ravens in 2009. Real college coaches such as Nick Saban appear while they recruit Michael. The real Michael filed a court petition in 2023 claiming he was never formally adopted by the Tuohys, while the family fully disputes the account.

Cameron Crowe's script starts with a sports agent typing a mission statement in the middle of the night about caring for clients. He's fired the next day and nearly everyone abandons him. Tom Cruise plays Jerry as a charming man whose honesty ends up costing him his lifestyle. Cuba Gooding Jr. plays Rod Tidwell, the Arizona Cardinals receiver who becomes Jerry's last client and demands to be shown the money. Jonathan Lipnicki's Ray famously tells Jerry that the human head weighs eight pounds. Kelly Preston plays Jerry's fiancée and Jay Mohr plays the rival agent who smiles while he steals away his clients.

Football appears around the edges, with Rod's Cardinals playing on Monday night and a college quarterback prospect named Frank Cushman anchoring the early scenes. The movie runs on lines people still quote, including "You had me at hello," and Rod's celebration after a big touchdown catch gets a huge laugh. Gooding won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor, Cruise earned a Best Actor nomination and the movie itself got a nomination for Best Picture. Jerry Maguire grossed more than $270 million, and is engrained in pop culture for all of its quotable moments.

In 1971, Alexandria, Virginia, integrated its high schools, and the T.C. Williams football team became front page news. Denzel Washington is new head coach Herman Boone, a stern black man hired over the beloved white coach Bill Yoast (Will Patton). Yoast agrees to stay on as an assistant, and the two fight before they learn to respect each other. Wood Harris is defensive end Julius Campbell, and Ryan Hurst stars as All-American Gerry Bertier, two teammates who start out at odds and end up as brothers. Ethan Suplee, Donald Faison, Kip Pardue, and Ryan Gosling round out the young but remarkably talented cast.

The training camp at Gettysburg College in Remember the Titans is a focal point. Coach Boone puts the players through rigorous drills till the early hours of the morning and gives a memorable speech about the historical battlefield beneath them and the men involved who sacrificed their lives. The team's chants, including the famous call of "left side, strong side," give it an emotional depth and tonal richness. The soundtrack mixes 1970s hits with a stirring score by Trevor Rabin that keeps the energy high. Real events were reshaped for the screen, but the 1971 team did go undefeated and win the state championship. The movie ended up grossing more than $136 million and stands the test of time as a classroom and football season favorite.

Brian's Song aired on ABC on November 30th 1971, marking this year as its 55th anniversary right after Thanksgiving. It is a TV movie that people still talk about like a theatrical classic. James Caan plays Brian Piccolo, a bold, slightly resentful undrafted free agent out of Wake Forest who plays his way onto the Chicago Bears. Billy Dee Williams is Gale Sayers, a quiet yet gifted star. The two begin as fierce rivals playing the same position and grow into good friends after Sayers tears up his knee.

Piccolo helps him rehab, and their unlikely friendship becomes the story's center. When Piccolo is diagnosed with cancer, the movie follows his decline with a restraint that surprised audiences at the time. Sayer's speech for the George Halas Award is dedicated to Piccolo, and it's a moment that audiences remember decades later. Brian's Song won multiple Emmys and a Peabody Award. The Bears of the movie travel to Detroit on Thanksgiving Day, which gives the classic a timely connection. A 2001 remake starred Sean Maher and Mekhi Phifer, but most fans still talk about the original.

Friday Night Lights starts in Odessa, Texas, where the high school football team is the town's biggest event. Billy Bob Thornton is coach Gary Gaines, a man who gets called out at the grocery store when the team loses. Derek Luke plays running back Boobie Miles, a talented kid whose knee injury changes the course of the season. Lucas Black is the quarterback and Garrett Hundland is a kid whose father (Tim McGraw) pushes him a little too hard and wears his old championship glory like a warrior's armor. Peter Berg directs with handheld cameras that put you on the sideline.

The score by Explosions in the Sky and David Torn gives the movie a dreamy, restless sound. H.G. Bissinger's book about the 1988 Permian Panthers supplies the story, and Berg keeps the film close to its real people. Connie Britton stars as Sharon Gaines, the coach's wife, and she would later become famous as Tami Taylor on the TV series. The season ends at Texas Stadium, and Gaines's pregame speech about being perfect is regarded as the movie's most recognized sequence. The TV series premiered on NBC in 2006, and a Peacock reboot is currently on pause.

#3435. This Low-Profile Roborock Vacuum and Mop Is $500 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, but prices aren’t always what they seem. Use a price tracker to make sure you’re getting the best deal, or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3434. Chromagraph Camera is exactly the camera app I’ve been looking for on iPhone

Last week, movie director Rian Johnson announced a surprise new camera app for iPhone that reimagines what a smartphone photo should look like. Many people would agree that Apple’s iPhone photos are a tad bit overprocessed.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo introduced a new film texture option, but in my view, it’s a bit too exaggerated. Chromagraph Camera, on the other hand, feels pretty perfect.

Attempts have been made to improve iPhone photos for years, but they all feel a little bit too heavy, in my view. Most camera apps for iPhone require you to dial settings in. While that can be appropriate for certain settings, I ultimately want my iPhone to just be a point and shoot experience. If I wanted the perfect photo, I’d be using my camera.

That said, iPhone photos just don’t look super excellent out of the box. It’s not a limitation of hardware. If you take a RAW iPhone photo and edit it yourself, you can actually get surprisingly good results. Apple’s camera app just has poor defaults.

When Apple introduced the film grain feature on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, I was actually quite interested in it. It was certainly my favorite camera feature of the phone when I briefly tried out the iPhone 18 Pro. For some reason though, the film look just feels a bit exaggerated on iPhone Duo.

Apps like Adobe’s Project Indigo have gotten really close in terms of look, but the fact that there’s so much time spent post-processing means it’s often inconvenient. I’ve also had a few instances of losing photos because the app closed in the background while it was still processing the photo.

User reviews tell a different story. No trial option is a non- starter for me.

When Chromagraph Camera was announced, I was quite interested. I paid the $12.99, and I’ve been happy with the results. I tweeted some of my sample photos when I just got the app, and it’s been well worth it.

$12.99 may be a higher starting price, but if you really want an iPhone camera app that just takes good looking photos without a lot of hassle, it works really well.

#3432. Apple aiming to make Siri ‘more like an agent’ as soon as next year: report

Apple finally shipped its long awaited personalized Siri with iOS 27. The company lived up to its promises, and delivered on its hefty goals that it set out back in 2024.

That said, Siri still lacks in terms of proactively taking actions for you, a feature that many AI companies are actively working towards. Apple might come around on that next year, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The company is also experimenting with a new engineering pipeline that might make faster development possible.

In recent months, companies like Meta and SpaceXSI have gone all-in on new agentic AI interfaces that can carry out tasks for you. Muse and Grok Bot are agents that have their own virtual machines and can proactively handle tasks in the background for you, then deliver results.

Apple has a lot of potential to deliver in this space, especially given all of the frameworks they’ve built up over the years, like App Intents. With Apple, you hypothetically wouldn’t need to depend on as much computer-use ability, making certain tasks a lot less expensive.

According to Mark Gurman in his Power On newsletter, Apple could debut its own proactive version of Siri as soon as next year:

Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

It remains to be seen what Apple will ultimately ship here, but with the right execution, Apple certainly has high potential to compete in this space.

A major part of better execution is having a better process. According to Gurman, Apple is also giving engineers more time to code and explore, rather than spend as much time integrating features within the operating system.

Typically, each of these stages is four weeks. With the first cycle of iOS 28 development, Apple is allotting 6 weeks to coding and 2 weeks to integration. This change was likely driven by the massive advances in agentic coding tools in the past couple years:

For this cycle, though, Apple has done things differently for the M1 milestone. Instead of the normal split between two four-week efforts, Apple engineers were tasked with six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development, and then only two weeks of convergence. Employees say they like the change, indicating that it creates more time for coming up with ideas and exploring them before needing to lock things in.

#3431. 10/10 Fallout Replacement Officially Added As PlayStation Plus Free Game

There simply aren't enough games like Fallout. With Bethesda's lackadaisical approach to the series resulting in just two entries over the past 11 years, fans have been left with few ways to engage with the franchise beyond the abundance of available mods. However, even they prove to be insufficient at retaining one's interest, especially when the foundations are so old, unstable, and ill-equipped to serve a contemporary audience looking to get even more out of their gaming experiences.

Fortunately, while there are few Fallout games and fewer pretenders, there is one title that promises to be a suitable replacement for those whose apocalyptic appetites had yet to be satiated. This title, which proved to be a sleeper hit back in 2025, has finally been added to PlayStation Plus as a free title, making it so that those who've never heard of it and those who had but didn't want to buy it at full price finally have the next best Fallout replacement they've been searching for accessible at the press of a button.

Atomfall was released back in March 2025 and offered an experience that was as close to Fallout as one could have hoped for. Developed by Rebellion, the same folks behind the Sniper Elite series, Atomfall marked a rather significant departure from the studio's usual style of game. It featured a vast open world filled with towns and cultist settlements that had to be discovered rather than pinpointed on your map with markers, a mysterious narrative packed full of meaningful choices, factions, survival mechanics, and a retrofuturistic aesthetic, all of which would feel right at home under the Fallout moniker.

Atomfall proved to be a huge success for Rebellion, garnering more than enough sales to warrant the production of DLC, which expanded the game's narrative and world significantly. Now, it joins numerous other games coming to PlayStation Plus on November 17. This is the first time Atomfall has been on the platform, with it previously finding success on Xbox Game Pass when it initially launched. It has been available on PlayStation since launch, but only as a full-price title, with the occasional sale bringing down its price a tad.

Atomfall will join the pantheon of amazing games on PS Plus, of which Fallout 4 is also proudly included. It isn't clear how long Atomfall will remain on the platform, especially as PlayStation Plus titles seem to come and go at the drop of a hat, but one can reasonably expect it to be around for at least a few months. To be clear, Atomfall's two DLCs, Wicked Isle and The Red Strain, aren't included in its PlayStation Plus release, and will still need to be bought separately.

If you've been looking for a first-person, narrative-focused, survival-based shooter like Fallout, then Atomfall is absolutely the game for you. While it isn't perfect (Atomfall's initial reviews were favorable, if a little mixed), there is a lot to love about it, especially if you're already a huge fan of Fallout. Rebellion may not have referred to Atomfall as the Fallout killer at launch, but it very much feels like one, especially considering that Bethesda has yet to release a new mainline entry.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

#3429. Report: John Ternus pushing Craig Federighi to speed up Apple software engineering

In the past few years, a major Apple story (especially in the age of AI) has been that the company isn’t moving fast enough in the space to keep up with competitors. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, new Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly pushing on software chief Craig Federighi to ‘accelerate’ Apple’s roadmap for software.

At the moment, there’s no indication that Apple’s well known software SVP Craig Federighi will be leaving the company. In fact, Craig has made it a very low priority of his to develop a succession plan in any sense, per Mark Gurman. That said, Ternus still wants to see change in how Craig Federighi thinks about Apple’s software strategy:

In recent weeks, Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Craig Federighi, who became Apple’s AI czar following last year’s dismissal of its former AI leader. Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri.

A large part of Federighi’s approach has been how hands-on he is, resulting in his viewpoint shaping how Apple’s software development goes to a large extent. That’s left team members feeling that they have ‘limited influence’ over what happens:

Federighi is known for taking an especially hands-on role in meetings and major decisions, with some employees describing a management style that can leave little room for competing ideas to gain traction. He is also known for vigorously debating opposing viewpoints, using his command of technical details and ability to argue his position to push back against proposals he disagrees with. That approach has at times frustrated members of the software engineering and design teams, some of whom believe they have limited influence over the direction of products.

Another part is that Federighi reportedly only plans for a 12-18 month timeframe, versus the years-long roadmaps used in hardware engineering. These are some of the gaps that Apple may want to bridge in the coming years.

Separately, Vision Pro and Siri AI leader Mike Rockwell is still seriously considering stepping down. He’s currently vice president of Siri engineering:

The management concerns go beyond Federighi. Mike Rockwell, who created the Vision Pro headset in addition to leading the development of Siri AI, continues to seriously consider stepping down. That could mean leaving his role as vice president of Siri engineering — or Apple altogether — next year. Such a move would be a major blow, given his role in bringing the new Siri to market after an embarrassing two-year delay.

Interesting timing on this article. I’m sitting here with two laptops: one running Tahoe and the other one running Golden Gate, both of them full of bugs and issues that should’ve never been released outside of Apple, and thinking how great Apple’s hardware is, but how terrible their software has become. I don’t know the inner workings of Apple, so I’ve never wanted to outright blame Federighi, but given that he’s at the top of the software ladder, I can only think that he’s most likely the problem. For all I know he could be holding it altogether, but then I read something like this and makes me think that it might be time for him to go.

I don’t know about accelerating their software, I feel like their software has felt rushed and unfinished for the last 10 years or so, and increasingly so each year, but I think what the article really means is speed up the advancement in the AI aspect of Apple’s software, not actually rushing out their software in general.

In the same report, Gurman also reported that Apple is experimenting with a new development pipeline, giving engineers 50% more time to code and explore more, and spend less time on integration, as coding agents have improved.

It remains to be seen what else might change at Apple to enable faster development timelines, though it seems likely that Craig Federighi may have to release his ‘firm grip’ on the software engineering org, and instead allow some other leaders to blossom and act on their own accord.

#3428. 15 Movies To Watch if You Love 'MobLand'

Guy Ritchie has long been the go-to Guy when it comes to British crime movies. Ever since his 1998 feature-length debut, Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, it has been clear that this British director has a keen eye for the wickedly violent and the devilishly funny. With the premiere of the second season of The Gentlemen and Prime Video's Young Sherlock, there's no better time to be a Ritchie fan.

This is especially true when considering the unquestionable success of his latest foray into the world of crime, MobLand (the series was created by Ronan Bennett, with Ritchie attached as a director). With the stars aligning to take on Ritchie's big-budget caper, including Tom Hardy, Pierce Brosnan, Helen Mirren, and Paddy Considine, this modern-day series has received plenty of high praise thus far, including a strong 83% approval rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes. For fans craving more movies like MobLand, several films deliver the same beats. With all that in mind, here's a look at the best movies to watch if you love MobLand.

There's no better place to start when recommending a movie following MobLand than 2019's The Gentlemen, not to be confused with Ritchie's series of the same name. Directed by Ritchie, the film follows Matthew McConaughey's American expat who, while trying to find the highest bidder for his marijuana empire, ends up sparking all-out criminal chaos.

Featuring a star-studded ensemble worthy of rivaling MobLand's — including the aforementioned McConaughey, Charlie Hunnam, Jeremy Strong, Hugh Grant, and more — The Gentlemen is a fast-paced, stylish run through the best of Ritchie. Effortlessly funny and often brutal, this is a winding crime web spun to perfection.

Mobland's brilliance lies in its distinct mix of witty charm and hard-hitting crime action, making the overall experience an absolute blast to watch, a strength shared by the underrated 2000s crime comedy Smokin' Aces. The film follows a magician turned mafia informant on the run after the mob gets word of his betrayal, placing a $1 million bounty on him as well as looking to take him for their own personal reasons.

The initial setup is about as classic as crime comedies get, seeing various personalities with ties to the mob converging and facing off in an attempt to make it on a high bounty. However, as the intricacies of these crimes and an array of shocking twists come to light, it becomes largely apparent that the film is hiding a much larger web of lies, deception, and madness between intersecting parties. Similar to Mobland, the film has an absolute slam-dunk cast to help elevate its story, featuring the likes of Ben Affleck, Ray Liotta, Jeremy Piven, Ryan Reynolds, Alicia Keys, and Jason Bateman. —Robert Lee

For those who like Hardy in MobLand, Legend is the next port of call. The man behind fixer Harry Da Souza takes on not one but two of the most infamous criminals in British history, portraying both of the Kray twins in this journey through their lavish, tragic lives in 1960s London.

Perhaps Hardy's best performance to date, his ability to switch between both twins, offering evolving and nuanced perspectives on both their lives, is nothing short of remarkable. Add to that a stellar supporting cast, a neat script, and several action scenes that live long in the memory, and a recipe for British crime movie success is born.

Mobland doesn't simply follow a singular mob family, but instead the infighting and squabbles that come up as a result of conflicting mob families, a facet that has consistently found strength within crime storytelling. Lucky Number Slevin takes this classic archetype and provides the engaging dark comedy of taking a completely unrelated third party, throwing him in the middle of this conflict, but having completely mistaken him for a friend who is in deep with the mob.

It covers a similarly dark comedy tone that Mobland expertly utilizes, with Lucky Number Slevin getting a lot of comedic mileage out of not just the inherent miscommunication of its concept, but all of the different moving pieces and wild characters that end up intertwined in this dilemma. The film also features a standout cast, including Josh Hartnett, Morgan Freeman, Bruce Willis, Lucy Liu, Ben Kingsley, and Stanley Tucci. —Robert Lee

Brosnan's patriarch, Conrad Harrigan, is one of the standout characters in MobLand, with Die Another Day the best next stop for the actor at his suave and stylish best. The movie follows Brosnan as the iconic James Bond as he attempts to bring down an international criminal enterprise that plans to build a world-threatening space weapon.

Brosnan is still as effortlessly cool as ever in MobLand, but rewind 23 years to 2002, and his portrayal of 007 marks the actor's peak. An action-packed Bond entry that also marked the end of an era for the series, Die Another Day might usher in an even greater period for the franchise, but let that take nothing away from just how impressive it is on its own.

While Mobland was undeniably the standout gangster story worth watching in 2025, one other gangster film from the year that parallels its strengths in distinct ways is Caught Stealing, the most recent film from Darren Aronofsky. Similar to Lucky Number Slevin, the film follows an unaffiliated third party who finds himself at the center of an ongoing feud between a bunch of different criminal groups. From Russian mobsters to Hasidic brothers to corrupt police, all of the different moving pieces prove to make the film that much more of a striking watch.

Leading star Austin Butler is one of the key selling points of the film; he exceptionally navigates the chaos and death that constantly follow him both as a result of these criminals and the guilt of his past haunting him. The aesthetic of '90s New York also does wonders for the feel and look of the film, harkening back to iconic New York crime movies of the '90s like A Bronx Tale and Carlito's Way. —Robert Lee

For many, Snatch is Ritchie's magnum opus. Featuring a cast that includes a young Stephen Graham and Brad Pitt at the peak of his powers, Snatch follows the theft of a priceless diamond and the many invested criminal minds attempting to beat the competition and track it down.

Snatch feels like Ritchie let loose. Packed from start to finish with iconic one-liners, unapologetically violent action, and even a terrifying Irish action from Pitt for good measure, Snatch is an enigmatic, bloody imprint on Ritchie's wonderful legacy. MobLand might show Ritchie at his most mature, but Snatch will showcase him at his best.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

While this crime comedy certainly leans more toward comedy than crime in its tone, the overwhelming amount of violence and dark humor present in Seven Psychopaths helps the film never stray away from its roots as an unrestrained story of crime. The setup is about as goofy as a crime story gets, with a screenwriter getting into hot water with the Los Angeles criminal underworld after his friends kidnap a gangster's beloved Shih Tzu. However, the pain and carnage that this kidnapping sets in motion is very real, emphasized by the immaculate directing of Martin McDonagh.

This strange blend of killers, blackmail, and extravagant personalities at times feels like a distillation of classic gangster films down into an absurdist satire on crime culture, Hollywood, and everything in between. The film was largely celebrated when it first released, but has largely been lost in the shadows due to McDonagh's career being elevated to Academy prestige in his subsequent films. Still, there is a charm and brilliance within Seven Psychopaths that makes it still worth watching almost 15 years later. —Robert Lee

MobLand boasts an extremely talented cast, with one of the more underrated performances in the series coming from Considine. Back in 2004, Considine once again put in a highly underrated supporting turn as Phil in Paweł Pawlikowski's My Summer of Love. Two young women from either end of the class spectrum end up entwined in a burning romance across a hot British summer, only for the reality of their situation to rear its ugly head.

Considine's performance as the reformed criminal Phil in My Summer of Love underpins almost every emotional beat in the story. Perhaps underrated due to this movie marking the breakout of one Emily Blunt, experiencing Considine's skin-crawling turn with knowledge of his impeccable career that followed certainly makes this a worthy follow-up to MobLand.

MobLand is seen as this glorious collaboration between English filmmaking talent, most notably with director Guy Ritchie and A-list leading star Tom Hardy. However, this actually isn't the first time that these two have collaborated on a creative work, as Hardy appears as one of many icons of English cinema in RocknRolla, one of Ritchie's most often forgotten crime comedy films. The film sees various members of London's criminal underworld pursuing their share of a lucrative fortune brought about by a Russian mobster's real estate scam.

Hardy's role in the film isn't front and center, as it is largely balanced with its prominent cast of other English talent, including Gerard Butler, Mark Strong, Idris Elba, and Thandiwe Newton. Still, even in this side role, released 17 years before they would collaborate again in MobLand, Hardy fits into Ritchie's signature style of directing perfectly. It certainly also helps that MobLand and RocknRolla are both crime stories that act as a workaround for exceptional English ensembles. —Robert Lee

#3427. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3426. macOS 27.3 could change how you grant AI agents Full Disk Access, here’s how

In its blog post, Apple announced that apps will require “very explicit user action” to have Full Disk Access on your Mac. At the time of the announcement, Apple didn’t make it super clear what that would actually mean. Now, we have an idea of what’s to come.

Code sifter pdfu posted on X that Apple will be getting rid of a clever loophole that developers could use to make it easier for users to enable Full Disk Access. In current versions of macOS, if an app requests a file that would require Full Disk Access, the system denies the request and logs the app as an option in the Settings app for enabling Full Disk Access.

At that point, developers often prompt users to open that section of the Settings app and flip the toggle.

Starting as soon as macOS 27.3, apps that request files outside of the permission scope will no longer get logged, and as a result, won’t show up as an option for quickly toggling Full Disk Access, per leaker pdfu.

macOS 27.3 starts implementing changes to Full Disk Access (FDA). Here’s what ‘very explicit user action’ may mean.When an app tries to read a protected file without FDA, macOS doesn’t prompt the user to grant permission. Instead, it automatically denies access and records that… https://t.co/zjUuEh7EIb

At the moment, developers can still request users to drag an app icon to the Settings panel to enable Full Disk Access, even once the feature flag for the aforementioned change is enabled. To me, it still doesn’t quite feel like you’ll need “very explicit user action” to enable Full Disk Access, but it’s possible this will change in the future. This is all still in development.

All in all, I’m not fully convinced that this solves the core problem. Developers are requesting Full Disk Access because they’d like to tap into things like iMessage, and there hasn’t been a better way of doing so. As long as that demand is there, users will likely still have to enable Full Disk Access and risk all sorts of other data, just so they can share their texts with an agent.

Granted, pdfu also mentions the idea of Private Folders, which could potentially allow users to grant scoped access to just the iMessage database folder. It’s unclear if that’ll be possible since there’s little detail on how Private Folders will work. If that’s the case, then hopefully Full Disk Access can stop being the default permission you have to provide for any personal data.

Tubi is less well known than some other streaming services, but it does have a solid selection that is frequently refreshed. The platform also boasts some exclusives under its Tubi Originals label, such as Lowlifes in 2024.

Hercules offers a fun spin on the Greek legend. Most notably, Hercules is a mercenary in the 2014 movie, and we're not even sure if he's truly a demigod. Ergenia (Rebecca Ferguson) approaches Hercules with a proposal. She wants him to help her father, Lord Cotys (John Hurt), fend off Rhesus (Tobias Santelmann), a brutal warlord. He agrees to help when he learns that Rhesus has burned down villages, even though it's an uphill struggle.

Lord Cotys' soldiers lack training. Hercules and his crew attempt to make them battle-ready, but will he succeed before Rhesus's forces close in?

2014's Hercules rarely comes up in conversation today, which is surprising, considering its performance at the box office. The movie reportedly made $243.3 million worldwide, not including physical sales. Financials vary by project, but movies typically need to make 2.5x their production budget to be considered a success. Hercules was very close to that target, with an estimated production cost of $100 million.

The movie itself tells an entertaining dark fantasy adventure story. Hercules is famous across Ancient Greece, and his legendary 12 labors are known across the land. Interestingly, during his first fight, we notice that his teammates contribute far more than the stories may suggest. Hercules is supported by several fighters, including Atalanta (Ingrid Bolsø Berdal), a skilled archer, and Amphiaraus (Ian McShane), a seer.

Iolaus (Reece Ritchie) is a unique member of the team, as he's Hercules' nephew. He's not a fabled warrior like his uncle, but he is a storyteller who can inspire others, even if he embellishes the truth. Hercules' group is just as important as the legendary warrior himself, and the movie offers a multilayered take on the character. He's charismatic and strong, not unlike the Scorpion King in many ways. Hercules also has a troubled past, thoroughly explored as he tries to prepare Lord Cotys' army for battle.

#3423. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3421. This New Sci-Fi Novel From a Pulitzer Prize Winner Could Be the Next Hunger Games

For only having three books under his belt, author Hernan Diaz has added an impressive number of literary prizes to his trophy case. The Argentine and American writer won the New American Voices Award for his 2017 debut novel In the Distance, and was also a finalist for both the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction for the same book. Later, his follow-up novel, Trust, won both the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the Kirkus Prize. This year, Diaz has made a triumphant return to the page – except this time, he’s playing in the science fiction sandbox.

Diaz's newest novel, Ply, came out in September 2026. This refreshing book takes a sharp detour from the author's usual route. Usually, Diaz writes historical fiction novels. Ply tackles Diaz's usual themes – power, wealth, American mythology, loneliness – except, this time, in a futuristic, hardscrabble world. The novel takes place centuries from now in a ruined American city, where citizens have to struggle for even the most basic necessities, including food, shelter, and, most importantly, electricity. Overall, Ply is a dark dystopian take on America’s future, featuring a savant female protagonist whose great intellect and razor-sharp edge might just pull her out of obscurity. Sound familiar? This surprising sci-fi take from an award-winning literary novelist will remind readers of The Hunger Games series by Suzanne Collins and Station Eleven by Emily St. John Mandel – and it just might be the next big thing in dystopian fiction.

Like many dystopian epics, Ply begins with a girl. The book’s unnamed protagonist is introduced to readers simply as “the Pincher.” She is an orphan, hustling her way through life in a derelict cityscape. Set centuries from now, the Pincher’s world is one of decay, pollution, and rugged individualism. Citizens of this crumbling America are left to fend for themselves; they scavenge for food and trade wares with their neighbors, all the while living in fear of the powerful corporations that control society’s water and electricity output – simply called Flow and Tensor.

There’s also the terrorizing group known as CTS, a blurry security conglomerate that polices the city’s streets with hawk-like eyes. This is the context in which readers are introduced to the Pincher. As the book unfolds, readers soon learn more about her world. She lives in a deteriorating building on the wrong side of the city’s heavily polluted river, and makes her living by stealing electricity from the grid and selling it secretly on the black market – this is where her title of “Pincher” comes from.

While the Pincher has many clients, one of her passions is fueling the city’s underground music concerts. Over the years, she has earned a reputation for being exceptionally good at her job; she is both swift and undetectable. However, while surreptitiously delivering a brick of power to a concert one night, the Pincher gets the eerie feeling that she is being followed. But who is following her, and what do they want? It’s not long before the Pincher finds herself pulled into a complicated web of tinkerers, power players, and black market dealers – all of whom are scrambling to get their hands on a groundbreaking experiment. If the Pincher is able to provide the electricity to power this new machine, she could revolutionize the world as she knows it.

Like The Hunger Games and the Divergent series before it, Ply is the story of a spiky female lead who is forging not only a new path for herself but is also breaking new ground for society as a whole. While Katniss Everdeen changes the world through her physical prowess in the arena and her political cunning, and Tris challenges the status quo with her very brain functions (by being naturally immune to mind-control serum, of course), the Pincher in Ply stands out from the rest thanks to her technological genius. Diaz’s novel may be a portrait of a dystopian America, but the star of the show is, undeniably, this electrician whiz; readers will care about her character's evolution first and foremost.

Looking at these books, sci-fi is in great hands.

Hernan Diaz is anything but a newcomer to the literary scene. When his debut novel, In the Distance, was released in 2017, it quickly became the talk of the proverbial town. The prestigious publication, The Paris Review, listed it as one of the top books of the year, while Literary Hub listed it as one of “The 20 Best Novels of the Decade.” He followed up his success with Trust – Diaz’s second book published in 2022. This sophomore release upped the ante, earning the Argentine-American writer a spot on the longlist for the 2022 Booker Prize and taking home the 2023 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. It, too, found its way on many “best of” lists – including the New York Times’s “10 Best Books of 2022” list.

With such a sterling reputation, fans of Diaz may have been expecting more of the same with his third release. After all, why depart from a winning model? However, Ply marks new territory for Diaz and sees him dipping his toes into the sci-fi genre, which comes with its own unique conventions and history. Did Diaz stick the landing? Both In the Distance and Trust are historical fiction novels that look to the past to help make sense of the present.

Set in the 1800s, In the Distance tells the story of a Swedish emigrant named Håkan who is searching for his brother across the American West. Along the way, he faces poverty, hardship, and discrimination. Likewise, Trust is a puzzle-like novel that takes place in the early 1900s, examining the world of extreme wealth in New York City before and after the cataclysmic event that was the Great Depression. By setting his third novel in the future, in an unspecified year, Diaz expands his toolkit, bringing in techno-thriller elements to craft a dystopian setting.

While Daniel Kraus took home the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction with his World War I novel Angel Down, Diaz and his team could potentially be eyeing up next year's competition. According to the Pulitzer committee, any book published in the 2026 calendar year is eligible to be considered for the 2027 award. Having hit US shelves on September 29 of this year, Diaz’s name is sure to be thrown into the ring for his experimental third novel.

If Diaz were to take home the 2027 Pulitzer Prize, he would join an elite club of writers who have two Pulitzer Prizes under their belt, including Booth Tarkington, William Faulkner, John Updike, and, most recently, Colson Whitehead, who won for The Underground Railroad in 2017 and The Nickel Boys in 2020.

Fans of Ply will have to bide their time, though, as the 2027 Pulitzer Prize winners won’t be announced until May of next year. If Ply does take home any big literary awards in the coming season, it may herald a new exciting era for sci-fi novels. Announced on November 9, 2026, the 2026 Booker Prize winner, The End of Everything by M. John Harrison, has been celebrated as the first winner in Booker history to come from the science fiction world. Could Ply be the next big sci-fi literary champion? Only time will tell.

#3420. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3419. Prime Video's #1 Global Hit Series Takes Advantage Of Massive Streaming Trend

Although every streaming service and cable network has cashed in on one popular trend recently, Prime Video’s worldwide number one hit proves that the streaming service is at the vanguard of this particular cycle. Despite TV’s infamous reputation for chasing trends, the entertainment industry can sometimes move surprisingly slowly when it comes to riffing on popular titles thanks to the slow speed of television production.

While HBO’s Game of Thrones became a huge hit when the show debuted in 2011 and was a massive worldwide success by 2013, Netflix’s The Witcher didn’t reach screens until the HBO show’s series finale aired in 2019. Prime Video’s ambitious Lord of the Rings prequel The Rings of Power took even longer, with the fantasy adaptation only arriving in 2022 even though the series was clearly intended to act a Game of Thrones replacement or substitute.

Similarly, even though Grey’s Anatomy creator Shonda Rhimes had a massive global hit in 2020 with the alternate history romance novel adaption Bridgerton, it took almost half a decade before the rest of the industry caught onto this trend. In 2025, Heated Rivalry became a colossal success, and this hit was followed by a flurry of romance novel adaptations including Prime Video’s Off Campus, Every Year After, and, most recently, Campus Drivers.

Based on the bestselling book series by author CS Quill, Campus Drivers is a six-episode romance novel adaptation that aims to recapture the success of Prime Video’s earlier 2026 hit Off Campus. The story of the series follows Carmen Kassovitz’s Lois as she arrives at Belrose University with her love interest, Max, only to end up living with Baptiste Madeline’s Lane. Lane is famous on campus for inventing the titular ride-share app, and what starts out as awkward cohabitation soon blossoms into something else entirely.

Campus Drivers immediately proved a massive breakout hit when the series arrived on the streaming service, rocketing to number one worldwide despite stiff competition from high-profile shows like The Terminal List. This might seem surprising, but the consistent success of Bridgerton and its spinoff, Heated Rivalry, and Off Campus, as well as original romance shows not based on novels, such as Prime Video’s small-town story Sterling Point, make the development less shocking.

Much like Shonda Rhimes’s underrated political thriller Scandal was part of a massive genre resurgence that also included Designated Survivor, Madam Secretary, Veep, House of Cards, and even The Newsroom, her Bridgerton success was just the tip of the iceberg when it came to successful streaming adaptations of romance novels. Like Bridgerton, Heated Rivalry, and Off Campus, Campus Drivers is also a multi-book series, meaning there are two more seasons of material ready to go if the show is renewed.

This in-built longevity is particularly useful at a time when even the biggest streaming projects are struggling to maintain their fan bases. Wednesday season 2 saw a major drop-off in viewers when the Addams Family spinoff released its second volume in 2025, but romance novel adaptations are a safer bet for streaming services since they tend to be less expensive than flagship fantasy or sci-fi shows.

Meanwhile, the arrival of Prime Video’s upcoming romance thriller Perfect Liars proves that the genre has a winning flexibility that allows these shows to incorporate elements from other genres seamlessly. Anyone who was around for the Twilight saga’s Team Edward and Team Jacob fan wars knows that fantasy romance is big business, but the success of Campus Drivers proves that contemporary romance, romantic comedies, romantic thrillers, and historical romances clearly also have the viewing public’s heart in 2026.
